Noach נֹחַ

BereshitNoachLekh Lekha

Genesis 6:9–11:32. Select a Hebrew word for its morphology, lemma, root, senses and the comments anchored to it. A dotted underline marks a word a commentator quotes.

6:9

These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generations; Noah walked with God.

these generations-of Noah Noah man righteous blameless was in-generations-his with-the-God walked-habitually Noah

Grammar
  • תּוֹלְדֹת is in the construct state, bound to נֹחַ; the account that follows begins not with Noah's sons but with his praise (so Rashi: הוֹאִיל וְהִזְכִּירוֹ סִפֵּר בְּשִׁבְחוֹ).
  • The zaqef qaton on the first נֹחַ closes the heading אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ; the repeated נֹחַ, which carries the revia, begins a new clause as its subject: 'Noah was a righteous man'.
  • אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים: the two adjectives stand side by side, each describing 'man'; this predicate is placed before the verb הָיָה.
  • הִתְהַלֶּךְ is a hitpael perfect with no vav; Rashi notes that in this stem the same form serves for the future (imperative) and the past, here the past.
  • The etnaḥta on בְּדֹרֹתָיו divides the verse: the first half describes Noah, the second his relation to God.

'Generations' for תּוֹלְדֹת keeps the word's range (descendants, history, account); Ibn Ezra reads it as 'events', Ramban as the plain sense 'descendants'. The phrase בְּדֹרֹתָיו is left as 'in his generations', which keeps both readings (in his own age, and in the ages after the flood) and the disputed praise/blame reading of Rashi's rabbis. 'With God' for אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים follows the preposition אֵת; the old 'walked before' of Abraham is a different construction.

Commentary (24)
Rashinormativefollows אֵ֚לֶּה תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת נֹ֔חַ נֹ֗חַ אִ֥ישׁ צַדִּ֛יק
Rashi: since the text mentions Noah, it goes on to praise him, as 'the memory of the righteous is for a blessing'; or it teaches that the true generations (offspring) of the righteous are their good deeds. The English keeps 'generations', which allows this.
Hebrew
הוֹאִיל וְהִזְכִּירוֹ סִפֵּר בְּשִׁבְחוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה (משלי י'). דָּבָר אַחֵר לִמֶּדְךָ שֶׁעִקַּר תּוֹלְדוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים מַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים:
Rashinormativerecords בְּדֹֽרֹתָ֑יו
Rashi: some of our rabbis read בְּדֹרֹתָיו as praise (he would have been more righteous in a righteous generation) and some as disparagement (righteous only relative to his generation; beside Abraham he would count for nothing). The English leaves the phrase as 'in his generations' and does not decide between them.
Hebrew
יֵשׁ מֵרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דּוֹרְשִׁים אוֹתוֹ לְשֶׁבַח, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן אִלּוּ הָיָה בְדוֹר צַדִּיקִים הָיָה צַדִּיק יוֹתֵר; וְיֵשׁ שֶׁדּוֹרְשִׁים אוֹתוֹ לִגְנַאי, לְפִי דוֹרוֹ הָיָה צַדִּיק וְאִלּוּ הָיָה בְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם לֹא הָיָה נֶחְשָׁב לִכְלוּם (סנה' ק"ח):
Rashinormativefollows אֶת הָֽאֱלֹהִ֖ים הִֽתְהַלֶּךְ נֹֽחַ׃
Rashi: of Abraham it says 'before whom I walked', but Noah needed support to hold him up, while Abraham strengthened himself and walked in his righteousness on his own. The English 'walked with God' keeps the preposition אֵת; the contrast with Abraham is in the commentary.
Hebrew
וּבְאַבְרָהָם הוּא אוֹמֵר אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלַּכְתִּי לְפָנָיו? (ברא' כ"ד), נֹחַ הָיָה צָרִיךְ סַעַד לְתָמְכוֹ, אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם הָיָה מִתְחַזֵּק וּמְהַלֵּךְ בְצִדְקוֹ מֵאֵלָיו:
Rashinormativefollows הִֽתְהַלֶּךְ
Rashi: הִתְהַלֵּךְ is past in meaning; in the pattern of this stem the same form serves for the future and the past, as with קוּם הִתְהַלֵּךְ (future) against הִתְהַלֶּךְ נֹחַ (past). The English uses the past tense.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן עָבָר, וְזֶהוּ שִׁמּוּשׁוֹ שֶׁל לָשׁוֹן, בְּלָשׁוֹן כָּבֵד מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת לְהַבָּא וּלְשֶׁעָבַר בְּלָשׁוֹן א', קוּם הִתְהַלֵּךְ (שם י"ג) לְהַבָּא, הִתְהַלֶּךְ נֹחַ לְשֶׁעָבַר; הִתְפַּלֵּל בְּעַד עֲבָדֶיךָ (שמואל א' י"ב) לְהַבָּא, וּבָא וְהִתְפַּלֵּל אֶל הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה (מ"א ח') לְשׁוֹן עָבָר, אֶלָּא שֶׁהַוָּי"ו שֶׁבְּרֹאשׁוֹ הֲפָכוֹ לְהַבָּא:
Ibn Ezranormativerecords אֵ֚לֶּה תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת
Ibn Ezra: תּוֹלְדֹת means 'events', as in מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם and אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת יַעֲקֹב. The English 'generations' does not exclude it, and the note records it. Ramban rejects this and keeps 'descendants'.
Hebrew
כמו הקורות כטעם מה ילד יום (משלי כז א) וכמוהו אלה תולדות יעקב (בראשית לז ב):
Ibn Ezranormativefollows אִ֥ישׁ צַדִּ֛יק
Ibn Ezra on אִישׁ צַדִּיק: 'in his deeds'. Righteous is read as righteous in conduct, which is the plain English.
Hebrew
במעשיו
Ibn Ezranormativefollows תָּמִ֥ים
Ibn Ezra: תָּמִים is 'in his heart', as צַדִּיק is 'in his deeds' (6:9:2). Grammatically תָּמִים is an adjective (תֹּאַר הַשֵּׁם) from the geminate verbs (פַּעֲלֵי הַכֶּפֶל), root תמם. The English 'blameless' is read as sound and whole, so the pair means righteous in act, whole in heart.
Hebrew
תמים. בלבו ותמים תאר השם מפעלי הכפל והוא תמים,
Ibn Ezranormativefollows בְּדֹֽרֹתָ֑יו
Ibn Ezra: בְּדֹרֹתָיו means in his generation at the time of the flood and in the generations after, for Noah lived until Abraham was fifty-eight. The plural 'in his generations' in the English admits this reading.

וטעם בדורותיו בדורו בעת המבול, ובדורות שהיו אחריו כי הוא חיה עד שהיה אברהם בן נ"ח שנה והסימן הוא ואברהם אבינו בן נ"ח כאשר מת נח:

Hebrew
טַעְמוֹ פֵּרְשׁוּ בּוֹ (הראב"ע והרד"ק) קוֹרוֹתָיו, כְּטַעַם "מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם" (משלי כז א), וְיִרְמֹז אֶל כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה. וְאֵינוֹ נָכוֹן בְּעֵינַי, כִּי אֵין קוֹרוֹת הָאָדָם תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו. וְהַנָּכוֹן שֶׁהוּא כְּמַשְׁמָעוֹ, כְּמוֹ "אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ" (בראשית י':א'), "וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת יִשְׁמָעֵאל" (בראשית כ"ה:י"ב), יֹאמַר אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת נֹחַ שֵׁם חָם וָיָפֶת, אֲבָל הֶחְזִיר "וַיּוֹלֶד נֹחַ" בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁהִפְסִיק וְאָמַר "נֹחַ אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים הָיָה", לְהוֹדִיעַ לָמָּה צִוָּהוּ בַּתֵּבָה. וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר אָמַר לְמַעְלָה (ה לב) "וַיְהִי נֹחַ בֶּן חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַיּוֹלֶד נֹחַ אֶת שֵׁם אֶת חָם וְאֶת יָפֶת", חָזַר לְהַזְכִּירָם פַּעַם אַחֶרֶת, לְהַגִּיד כִּי לֹא הָיָה כְּכָל אֲבוֹתָיו שֶׁיּוֹלִידוּ בָּנוֹת וּבָנִים. וְזֶה טַעַם "שְׁלֹשָׁה בָּנִים", כִּי יַזְכִּיר מִסְפָּרָם לֵאמֹר כִּי אֵלֶּה שְׁלֹשָׁה לְבַדָּם הָיוּ תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו וְנִצְּלוּ בִּזְכוּתוֹ, וּמֵאֵלֶּה נָפְצָה כָל הָאָרֶץ:
Ramban אִ֥ישׁ צַדִּ֛יק תָּמִ֥ים הָיָ֖ה
Hebrew
יַזְכִּיר הַכָּתוּב שֶׁהָיָה זַכַּאי וְשָׁלֵם בְּצִדְקוֹ, לְהוֹדִיעַ שֶׁרָאוּי לְהִנָּצֵל מִן הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ עֹנֶשׁ כְּלָל כִּי הוּא תָּמִים בְּצֶדֶק, כִּי הַצַּדִּיק הוּא הַזַּכַּאי בַּדִּין, הֶפֶךְ הָרָשָׁע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר "וְהִצְדִּיקוּ אֶת הַצַּדִּיק וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ אֶת הָרָשָׁע" (דברים כה א), וְכֵן "וְאַתָּה צַדִּיק עַל כָּל הַבָּא עָלֵינוּ כִּי אֱמֶת עָשִׂיתָ" (נחמיה ט לג), וְכֵן "בְּצֶדֶק תִּשְׁפֹּט עֲמִיתֶךָ" (ויקרא יט טו). אֲבָל בְּאַבְרָהָם שֶׁאָמַר (בראשית י"ח:י"ט) "לַעֲשׂוֹת צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט", שִׁבַּח אוֹתוֹ בְּצֶדֶק שֶׁהוּא הַמִּשְׁפָּט וּבְרַחֲמִים שֶׁהִיא הַצְּדָקָה. וְרַבִּי אַבְרָהָם אָמַר (אבן עזרא על בראשית ו':ט') צַדִּיק בְּמַעֲשָׂיו תָּמִים בְּלִבּוֹ, וּכְתִיב (יחזקאל כח טו) "תָּמִים אַתָּה בִּדְרָכֶיךָ", וְאַחַר שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁהוּא אִישׁ צַדִּיק, כִּי אֵינֶנּוּ אִישׁ חָמָס וּמַשְׁחִית דַּרְכּוֹ כִּבְנֵי דּוֹרוֹ הַחַיָּבִים, אָמַר שֶׁהָיָה מִתְהַלֵּךְ אֶת הַשֵּׁם הַנִּכְבָּד לְיִרְאָה אוֹתוֹ לְבַדּוֹ, אֵינֶנּוּ נִפְתֶּה אַחֲרֵי הוֹבְרֵי שָׁמַיִם וּמְנַחֵשׁ וְעוֹנֵן, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אַחֲרֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְאֵינֶנּוּ שׁוֹמֵעַ לָהֶם כְּלָל, רַק בַּשֵּׁם לְבַדּוֹ הוּא דָּבֵק תָּמִיד וְהוֹלֵךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר בָּחַר הַשֵּׁם אוֹ אֲשֶׁר יוֹרֶה אוֹתוֹ, כִּי נָבִיא הָיָה, וְזֶה כְּטַעַם "אַחֲרֵי ה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם תֵּלֵכוּ וְאֹתוֹ תִירָאוּ" (דברים יג ה) הַנֶּאֱמָר בְּהַרְחָקַת הַמִּתְנַבֵּא לַעֲבֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְנוֹתֵן אוֹת וּמוֹפֵת, כַּאֲשֶׁר אֲפָרֵשׁ, וְעוֹד אַזְכִּיר זֶה בְּפָסוּק "הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי וֶהְיֵה תָמִים" (בראשית י"ז:א') אִם יִהְיֶה תְּמִים דֵּעוֹת עִמִּי. וְהִנֵּה אַחַר שֶׁהָיָה נֹחַ צַדִּיק וְאֵינֶנּוּ רָאוּי לֵעָנֵשׁ, גַּם בָּנָיו וּבֵיתוֹ רְאוּיִים לְהִנָּצֵל בִּזְכוּתוֹ, כִּי הָיָה עֹנֶשׁ עָלָיו אִם יִכָּרֵת זַרְעוֹ. אוֹ יֹאמַר כִּי הוּא צַדִּיק שָׁלֵם וְגַם בָּנָיו וּבֵיתוֹ צַדִּיקִים כִּי הוּא לִמְּדָם, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁכָּתוּב (בראשית י"ח:י"ט) "כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו וְאֶת בֵּיתוֹ":

6:10

Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

and-fathered Noah three sons ACC-Shem ACC-Ham and-ACC-Japheth

Grammar
  • וַיּוֹלֶד is hifil wayyiqtol of יָלַד; the hifil is the usual form for a father's begetting.
  • שְׁלֹשָׁה has the ending ־ָה yet goes with the masculine בָּנִים: from three to ten, the cardinal takes in form the opposite gender to its noun.
  • The three names are each marked with אֶת, in apposition to שְׁלֹשָׁה בָנִים.
  • The etnaḥta on בָנִים separates the number from the list of names.

The verse repeats what 5:32 already said; the commentators (Radak, Ramban, Sforno) explain why, but the English simply states it. In this unit the lexicon gives the lemma of שֵׁם as 'Sem'; the English form is Shem, following the decisions.

Commentary (4)
Rambannot-applicable אֶת שֵׁ֖ם אֶת חָ֥ם וְאֶת יָֽפֶת׃
Ramban: Japheth is the eldest (10:21 אֲחִי יֶפֶת הַגָּדוֹל; his sons are listed first in chapter 10) and Ham the youngest (9:24 בְּנוֹ הַקָּטָן). Shem is put first for his eminence, Ham follows him in birth order, and so Japheth comes last; the verse does not say 'Shem, Japheth and Ham', which would set all three out of birth order. The English keeps the Hebrew order, so the comment does not change it.

Radak: the sons were already named above (5:32); they are named again here, right after 'Noah walked with God', to teach that as he devoted himself to serving God, so he taught and trained his sons to turn from the ways of the wicked and to serve the LORD. 6:11

The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.

and-was-corrupted the-earth before the-God and-was-filled the-earth violence

Grammar
  • The two verbs are nifal wayyiqtol, both 3rd feminine singular, to agree with הָאָרֶץ.
  • וַתִּשָּׁחֵת and וַתִּמָּלֵא are parallel: the first says the earth was corrupted, the second what filled it.
  • חָמָס follows וַתִּמָּלֵא directly, with no preposition: a verb of filling keeps the thing that fills as an accusative even in the nifal, and English supplies 'with'.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאֱלֹהִים divides the verse into two parallel halves, each with the earth as subject.
  • שָׁחַת and its related forms recur in the next verse (נִשְׁחָתָה, הִשְׁחִית) and make a play on the one root.

'Earth' is kept for הָאָרֶץ; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the people of the earth (BDB 1.c, 'earth = inhabitants of earth'), and the English leaves the metonymy for the reader. 'Was corrupt' gives the nifal of שָׁחַת, 'be spoiled, ruined'; Rashi specifies the corruption as sexual immorality and idolatry, which 'corrupt' allows. 'Violence' for חָמָס covers Rashi's robbery and Ibn Ezra's robbery, oppression and seizing women by force.

וְאִתְחַבָּלַת אַרְעָא קֳדָם יְיָ וְאִתְמְלִיאַת אַרְעָא חֲטוֹפִין:
Apparatus
  • לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים: 'before God' as 'in God's sight' or 'in God's presence'; Ibn Ezra's note at 6:11:2 (given under 6:12) discusses the two readings.
6:12 · ס

God saw the earth, and indeed it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.

and-saw God ACC-the-earth and-behold was-corrupted for corrupted all flesh ACC way-its upon the-earth

Grammar
  • וְהִנֵּה marks what God sees, from the point of view of the one who sees: 'and there, it was corrupt'.
  • נִשְׁחָתָה (nifal, 'was corrupted') and הִשְׁחִית (hifil, 'corrupted') are the same root in two stems: the earth is ruined because all flesh ruined its way.
  • כׇּל־בָּשָׂר, 'all flesh', can mean every living creature or all humankind; here Rashi and Ibn Ezra include the animals, while Ramban and Radak take it by the plain sense as humankind.
  • The suffix in דַּרְכּוֹ is singular, referring back to 'flesh' taken as a whole.
  • The etnaḥta on נִשְׁחָתָה divides the seeing from the reason.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that 'all flesh' here includes the animals (beasts and birds mating with kinds not their own), and that 'its way' is the natural way of begetting: Ibn Ezra endorses the ancients' כָּל חַי לֹא שָׁמַר דֶּרֶךְ תּוֹלַדְתּוֹ. The English 'all flesh had corrupted its way' carries this reading without narrowing it. Ramban, by the plain sense, and Radak take 'all flesh' as humankind, and Onkelos adds אֱנַשׁ. The hifil הִשְׁחִית is taken as a pluperfect ('had corrupted') because it gives the cause of the state just described (נִשְׁחָתָה).

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows כִּֽי הִשְׁחִ֧ית כׇּל בָּשָׂ֛ר
Rashi on כִּי הִשְׁחִית כׇּל בָּשָׂר: even beasts, wild animals and birds joined with kinds not their own. The English 'all flesh' does not exclude animals, so this is kept open.
Hebrew
אֲפִלּוּ בְהֵמָה חַיָּה וָעוֹף נִזְקָקִין לְשֶׁאֵינָן מִינָן:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows כִּֽי
Ibn Ezra on לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (6:11): some say it means 'openly'; others say they corrupted themselves in secret, in hidden matters known only to God. The nearest reading in his view is that the Torah speaks in human language so that the hearers understand: like a servant who commits a transgression in front of his master and does not fear him. Those who say that אֱלֹהִים here is not holy (that is, means judges or rulers) have said nothing. The English 'before God' fits his reading.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: what our ancients said, that הִשְׁחִית כָּל בָּשָׂר אֶת דַּרְכּוֹ means every living creature failed to keep the way of its generation and twisted the known, planted path, is correct (נָכוֹן הוּא); he also praises the homily that they corrupted themselves with 'water' and God judged them with water, from above and below. With Rashi, he takes 'all flesh' to include the animals and 'its way' as the natural way of begetting; the English 'all flesh had corrupted its way' carries that reading.

Ramban: if 'all flesh' is taken literally, with Rashi (beasts, animals and birds mating with other kinds), then 'filled with violence because of them' (6:13) means because of some of them, and only man's punishment is told; or the animals too broke their nature, every beast preying and every bird tearing, so that they also did violence. But by the plain sense כָּל בָּשָׂר here is all humankind, as in Isa 66:23, while below (6:19, 7:15) it means every living body. The English keeps the wider 'all flesh'.

Apparatus
  • Subject of 6:12.1: אֱלֹהִים without the article, 'God'; Onkelos renders it יְיָ, 'the LORD'.
  • 'All flesh' including the animals (Rashi; Ibn Ezra, endorsing the ancients) or all humankind (Ramban by the plain sense, Radak, Onkelos with אֱנַשׁ): the English keeps the wider phrase.
6:13

God said to Noah, "The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is full of violence because of them; now I am about to destroy them with the earth."

and-said God to-Noah end-of all-of flesh has-come to-before-me for has-been-full the-earth violence from-before-them and-behold-I destroying-them [with/from] the-earth

Grammar
  • קֵץ כׇּל־בָּשָׂר is a construct chain: 'the end of all flesh'; the pashta on בָּשָׂר closes the subject.
  • The perfect בָּא ('has come') and מָלְאָה ('is full') state the present result of what has happened.
  • וְהִנְנִי with the participle מַשְׁחִיתָם is the idiom of imminent action: 'and behold I am about to destroy'.
  • אֶת־הָאָרֶץ: אֶת is the usual object marker, but the commentators read it as 'from' or 'with' because the object of מַשְׁחִית is already -ם.
  • The etnaḥta on מִפְּנֵיהֶם divides the verse: reason for the decree, then the decree itself.

אֶת־הָאָרֶץ: Rashi first reads אֶת as 'from the earth' (like כְּצֵאתִי אֶת הָעִיר), and then, as a second explanation, as 'with the earth', so that the earth too is ruined. Ibn Ezra lists 'from' and 'with' but prefers that מַשְׁחִיתָם does double duty: 'I am destroying them and destroying the earth'. The English takes 'with', the reading the two share; the other readings are recorded. The pack's parse gives אֶת as a preposition, which agrees. חָמָס is the word on which Rashi (Sanhedrin 108) says the decree was sealed.

Apparatus
  • Ibn Ezra's preferred reading: 'I am about to destroy them and to destroy the earth' (מַשְׁחִית has a second, implied object).

  • The Targum Onkelos renders 'with the earth' (עִם אַרְעָא), agreeing with 'with'.
6:14

Make yourself an ark of gopher wood; make the ark with compartments, and cover it with pitch inside and out.

make for-you ark-of wood-of gopher nests you-shall-make [obj]-the-ark and-you-shall-cover it from-inside and-from-outside with-the-pitch

Grammar
  • The two verbs עֲשֵׂה (imperative) and תַּעֲשֶׂה (imperfect) repeat 'make', the second adding what the ark is to have.
  • קִנִּים is placed first for emphasis; it is the object of the idea 'make the ark with nests'.
  • וְכָפַרְתָּ is a denominative verb built on כֹּפֶר 'pitch', with the cognate noun after it (figura etymologica): 'pitch it with pitch'.
  • מִבַּיִת וּמִחוּץ: 'from the inside and from the outside', an idiom for 'inside and out'.
  • The etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה separates the building from the sealing.

גֹּפֶר is a hapax and the species is not known; the English keeps the Hebrew word. Rashi connects it with גָּפְרִית 'brimstone'; Ibn Ezra says only that it is a light wood that floats. קִנִּים is 'nests' and so 'compartments' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak). כֹּפֶר is 'pitch' (Rashi: Aramaic זפת; BDB agrees).

בַּזְּמַן הַקָּצוּב לָהֶם לְמַעַן יִרְאוּ וְיָשׁוּבוּ:
Apparatus
  • Rashi: כֹּפֶר is pitch (זֶפֶת) in Aramaic, the Talmud's כּוּפְרָא. Moses' basket (Exodus 2:3) sat in calm water, so clay inside and pitch outside was enough, and the righteous child was spared the smell of pitch. Here, because of the force of the water, the ark was pitched inside and out.
  • Onkelos: 'of kedrom wood' (קַדְרוֹם), a cedar kind, per Radak.
  • Radak: the outer coat may fail under the force of the water, while the inner holds.
6:15

This is how you shall make it: the ark's length shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.

and-this which you-shall-make it three hundreds cubit length-of the-ark fifty cubit its-width and-thirty cubit its-height

Grammar
  • וְזֶה is a masculine demonstrative: 'this (measure) which you shall make it'.
  • The numbers precede אַמָּה in the singular, as is usual after a number; the nouns אֹרֶךְ, רֹחַב and קוֹמָה follow.
  • The three dimensions are set out in a rhythm: the zaqef gadol on וְזֶה, the etnaḥta on אֹתָהּ and the revia on אַמָּה.
  • The verse is a list of measures: 300 x 50 x 30 cubits, a ratio of 30 : 5 : 3.

The cubit is the unit of the Torah; the commentators give no other reading of the numbers.

Commentary (3)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְזֶ֕ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֖ה
Ibn Ezra: the sense is 'this is the measure that you shall make'; its height is a tenth of its length, so that it floats on the water and the wind does not overturn it. The English 'this is how you shall make it'.

Grammar
  • צֹהַר תַּעֲשֶׂה לַתֵּבָה puts the object first: 'a skylight you shall make for the ark'; the ׀ (paseq) after צֹהַר marks a pause.
  • וְאֶל־אַמָּה תְּכַלֶּנָּה מִלְמַעְלָה: 'and to a cubit you shall finish it from above'; the sense is that the roof ends in a single cubit.
  • The adjectives תַּחְתִּיִּם שְׁנִיִּם וּשְׁלִשִׁים are used as nouns for the three storeys: 'lower, second, third'.
  • The tevir on תַּחְתִּיִּם and the tipḥa on וּשְׁלִשִׁים divide the three storeys from the verb.
  • The final verb תַּעֲשֶׂהָ has a feminine object suffix: 'you shall make it (the ark)'.

צֹהַר: the pack gives BDB 'roof'; Rashi says a window or a precious stone that shone for them (Bereshit Rabbah); Ibn Ezra: a place by which light enters, derived from צָהֳרַיִם, made at the top. The English 'skylight' keeps the two commentators' 'light opening at the top' and does not decide between window and gem; the roof sense is recorded. וְאֶל־אַמָּה תְּכַלֶּנָּה מִלְמַעְלָה is hard: Rashi takes the roof as sloping up until it is only a cubit wide at the top, so that water runs off; Ibn Ezra takes the top as a cubit long and a sixth of a cubit wide. The English keeps the sense 'finish off the top to a cubit'. The pack notes that the WLC reads תְּכַלֶנָּה, without the dagesh.

Apparatus
  • צֹהַר: roof (BDB), window (Rashi, Radak), a gem (Rashi, Radak), an opening for light (Ibn Ezra).
  • Rashi: וְאֶל־אַמָּה is the roof narrowing to a cubit. Ibn Ezra: the ark is a triangle in section, with its top a cubit long.
  • Radak on תַּחְתִּיִּים: the yod is the yod of relation, and the yod of the plural has been dropped, like עֲבָדִים נָכְרִים.
  • Sforno: תַּחְתִּיִּם שְׁנִיִּם וּשְׁלִשִׁים means those that are used to ships (הַמּוּרְגָּלִים בָּאֳנִיּוֹת), that is, ships' decks.
  • תְּכַלֶּ֣נָּה — WLC reads תְּכַלֶ֣נָּה (vowels)
6:17

As for me, I am about to bring the flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life from under the heavens; everything that is on the earth shall perish.

and-I behold-I bringing [obj]-the-flood waters upon the-earth to-destroy all-of flesh which in-it breath-of life from-under the-heavens all which in-the-earth shall-expire

Grammar
  • וַאֲנִי הִנְנִי: the pronoun וַאֲנִי is emphatic, with הִנְנִי and a participle for what is about to happen.
  • הַמַּבּוּל מַיִם: the second word explains the first; Ibn Ezra reads 'the flood, (a flood of) waters'.
  • The infinitive לְשַׁחֵת (piel) gives the purpose of the flood.
  • The relative clause אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים describes the creatures meant by 'all flesh'.
  • כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע: the verse closes on the single verb 'shall expire'.

וַאֲנִי: Rashi hears God agreeing with those who urged him (Psalm 8:5); Ramban reads 'I also', as in וְיִסַּרְתִּי אֶתְכֶם אַף אָנִי. The English keeps the emphasis ('As for me') without choosing. מַבּוּל is the word for the flood; Rashi and Ibn Ezra give derivations (from בלל, בלה, נבל) but the sense is 'flood'. Radak (6:17:4) says כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ means on dry land, not fish.

Apparatus
  • Ramban on וַאֲנִי: 'I too', as in וְיִסַּרְתִּי אֶתְכֶם אַף אָנִי; the flood is God's own act against those who ruined the earth.
  • Radak on הַמַּבּוּל מַיִם: the construct is understood (מַבּוּל מַיִם), and מַבּוּל is a descriptive name for whatever falls from heaven.
  • Radak on כֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ: on dry land; fish are not included (the creatures of the sea did not share the wicked way, on the view of the Sages).
6:18

I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall enter the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives with you.

and-I-will-establish [obj] my-covenant with-you and-you-shall-enter into the-ark you and-your-sons and-your-wife and-wives-of your-sons with-you

Grammar
  • וַהֲקִמֹתִי is a weqatal verb continuing the speech; the vav is not 'and' in the English, and the verb is future.
  • The suffix of אִתָּךְ is written with a final ךְ and a qamets: this is the pausal form of 'with you' (masculine) before the etnaḥta and silluq.
  • הֲקִמֹתִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי: the hifil of קוּם takes בְּרִית with the sense of 'confirm, carry out' a covenant.
  • The list אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ וְאִשְׁתְּךָ וּנְשֵׁי־בָנֶיךָ names the eight persons: men before women, as the commentators note.
  • The zaqef gadol on אַתָּה begins the list of those who enter.

הֲקִמֹתִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי: the first mention of בְּרִית in the Torah. Ibn Ezra first explains it as God's oath that Noah and his sons would not die in the flood, then says the view nearest his own is that the covenant alludes to the rainbow. Ramban takes the plain sense as a covenant of survival (the commitment to bring them safely through). The English keeps 'covenant' without deciding. Rashi, citing Bereshit Rabbah, takes it as a pledge that the food would not spoil and that the wicked would not harm Noah.

Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): a covenant was needed so that the food would not rot or spoil and that the wicked of the generation would not kill him. A reading of what the covenant covers; the English leaves the content open and records this.

Ibn Ezranormativerecords וַהֲקִמֹתִ֥י אֶת בְּרִיתִ֖י
Ibn Ezra: a sign that God had sworn to Noah that he and his sons would not die in the flood, though this was not stated before (compare Deuteronomy 1:22). וַהֲקִמֹתִי means 'I will fulfil my oath'. The view closest to his own is that this covenant alludes to the rainbow. בְּרִית is an agreement chosen by two parties, from בְּרוּ לָכֶם אִישׁ; others take it as a boundary cut.

Apparatus
  • Ramban: the plain sense is a covenant of survival: that Noah and his household and two of every kind would live and come out alive.
  • Sforno: the covenant is made after the flood (אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל).
  • Radak: the covenant that I make with you, that you and all who are with you will be saved from the waters, I will confirm for you.
6:19

And of every living thing, of all flesh, you shall bring two of each into the ark to keep them alive with you; they shall be male and female.

and-from-all the-living from-all flesh two from-all you-shall-bring into the-ark to-keep-alive with-you male and-female they-shall-be

Grammar
  • The verse begins with two phrases in a row, וּמִכׇּל־הָחַי מִכׇּל־בָּשָׂר: the general term, and its explanation.
  • שְׁנַיִם מִכֹּל 'two from each' is the distributive: two of every kind.
  • The verb תָּבִיא is a hifil imperfect: Noah must bring them in; the infinitive לְהַחֲיֹת gives the purpose.
  • זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה יִהְיוּ: a plural verb for a pair; the subject is the 'two'.
  • The telisha gedola on הָחַי and the gershayim on בָּשָׂר divide the opening phrase.

The verb in יִהְיוּ is plural, agreeing with שְׁנַיִם. לְהַחֲיֹת אִתָּךְ: the object is implied: the animals are kept alive with Noah, and the English supplies 'them'.

Commentary (11)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וּמִכׇּל הָ֠חַ֠י
Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah): 'even demons'. A homily on the scope of 'every living thing'.
Hebrew
אֲפִלּוּ שֵׁדִים (ב"ר):
Rashinormativefollows שְׁנַ֧יִם מִכֹּ֛ל
Rashi: from the smallest of them, not fewer than two, one male and one female. The English 'two of each'.
Hebrew
מִן הַפָּחוּת שֶׁבָּהֶם לֹא פָּחוֹת מִשְּׁנַיִם, אֶחָד זָכָר וְאֶחָד נְקֵבָה:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: after saying 'two', the text explains that they are male and female. After the general 'of all the living, of all flesh', it lists the particular kinds: birds, cattle, and creeping things of the ground, the last covering the wild animals, small and great, born of male and female. Excluded are all creatures born without the mating of two, and so are the water creatures. The fish too is called 'flesh' (Numbers 11:21–22), so 'all flesh' alone could have included them.

Apparatus
  • Ramban: it is a miracle that the ark held them; it was made large so that people would see it and repent.
  • Radak on תָּבִיא: once they come of themselves in front of the ark, Noah brings them in; on לְהַחֲיֹת: Noah provides their food day by day.

6:20

Of the birds according to their kind, and of the animals according to their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground according to its kind, two of each will come to you to be kept alive.

from-the-bird to-its-kind and-from-the-animal to-its-kind from-all creeping-thing-of the-ground to-its-kind two from-all they-shall-come to-you to-keep-alive

Grammar
  • The three classes are introduced with מִן: birds, animals, creeping things; each takes לְמִינוֹ.
  • עוֹף, בְּהֵמָה and רֶמֶשׂ are collectives in the singular; the suffixes of לְמִינֵהוּ and לְמִינָהּ agree with them.
  • שְׁנַיִם מִכֹּל יָבֹאוּ אֵלֶיךָ: the verb is now 'come' (qal) where verse 19 had 'bring' (hifil): they come to him.
  • The infinitive לְהַחֲיוֹת is hifil: 'to keep alive'.
  • The verse picks up the list that verse 19 summarised with the 'all flesh' phrase.

The English reads לְהַחֲיוֹת as 'to be kept alive' (the animals are the ones who survive). The hifil is active, 'to preserve life', and the agent could be Noah (as in verse 19, 'with you'); the Hebrew is not explicit. The English gives the plural 'their kind' for the first two phrases and 'its kind' for the third; the Hebrew has the singular suffix each time.

מֵעוֹפָא לִזְנוֹהִי וּמִן בְּעִירָא לִזְנַהּ וּמִכֹּל רִחֲשָׁא דְאַרְעָא לִזְנוֹהִי תְּרֵין מִכֹּלָּא יַעֲלוּן לְוָתָךְ לְקַיָּמָא:
Apparatus
  • Ramban: the animals come of themselves two by two, but those taken for sacrifice (seven of each clean kind) Noah took himself.
  • Radak: הַבְּהֵמָה includes the wild animals, since the two classes overlap.

6:21

As for you, take for yourself some of every kind of food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself, so that it will be food for you and for them.

and-you take-(imperative) to-you from-all-of food that is-eaten and-you-shall-gather to-you and-it-shall-be to-you and-to-them for-food

Grammar
  • וְאַתָּה begins with an independent pronoun, which contrasts Noah with everyone else.
  • קַח is an imperative; וְאָסַפְתָּ is a weqatal continuing the command.
  • The etnaḥta on אֵלֶיךָ divides the verse: the gathering, then the purpose.
  • לְאָכְלָה is a feminine noun 'food' with prefixed ל, giving 'as food'.

The 'them' of the last clause are the animals of 6:19-20. Radak says even the predators ate the same plant foods and no meat, as at the beginning of creation.

Commentary (3)
Radakfollows וְאַתָּ֣ה קַח לְךָ֗
Radak: since the animals come to Noah to be kept alive, he must prepare food for himself and for them; the food is fruits, seeds and plants, and even predators eat them.

6:22 · ס

Noah did according to all that God had commanded him; so he did.

and-did Noah like-all that commanded him God so he-did

Grammar
  • The wayyiqtol וַיַּעַשׂ narrates; the closing כֵּן עָשָׂה is a qatal that sums up.
  • The etnaḥta on נֹחַ divides the report 'Noah did' from its measure, 'according to all that God commanded him'.
  • The telisha gedola on כְּכֹל is a disjunctive accent of low rank. It is prepositive, written on the first letter of the word, and is written again on the stressed syllable.
  • אֹתוֹ is the object marker with a 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'him'.
  • Obedience is stated twice, in וַיַּעַשׂ נֹחַ and in כֵּן עָשָׂה, around the clause כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים.

The English keeps the Hebrew order, with 'so he did' at the end. Ramban: the double statement, 'Noah did' and 'so he did', shows that he left out nothing of all he was commanded. Rashi takes the doing as the building of the ark; Ramban and Radak include the gathering of the food.

  • Onkelos has יְיָ ('the LORD') for אֱלֹהִים; this is Targum Onkelos's rendering, not a variant of the Hebrew.
7:1

Then the LORD said to Noah: Come, you and all your household, into the ark, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation.

and-said the-LORD to-Noah come-(imperative) you and-all-of house-your to the-ark for you-(object) I-saw righteous before-me in-the-generation the-this

Grammar
  • אֹתְךָ is the object marker with a suffix, fronted before the verb; it stresses 'you, and no one else'.
  • בֹּא־אַתָּה uses an independent pronoun after the imperative for emphasis.
  • The etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה separates the command from its reason.
  • צַדִּיק is the predicate of the object: 'I saw you (as) righteous'.

Rashi stresses that the text says only 'righteous', not 'righteous and blameless' as in 6:9: a person is praised in part to his face, in full behind his back. Ramban and Sforno hold the emphatic 'you' implies that the household is saved for his sake only. The English keeps 'you' plain; the emphasis goes in the notes.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows רָאִ֛יתִי צַדִּ֥יק
Rashi: the verse does not say 'righteous and blameless'; one says part of a man's praise in his presence and all of it in his absence (Genesis Rabbah). The English says only 'righteous'.

Hebrew
, כִּי בִּשְׁבִילְךָ בִּלְבַד אֲמַלְּטֵם:
7:2

Of every clean animal take for yourself seven each, a male and his mate; and of the animals that are not clean, two, a male and his mate.

from-all-of the-animal the-clean you-shall-take to-you seven seven man and-his-wife and-from the-animal that not clean it two man and-his-wife

Grammar
  • תִּקַּח is an imperfect used as a command; the accent on לְךָ is tevir.
  • שִׁבְעָה שִׁבְעָה is distributive repetition. It can mean seven individuals of each kind or seven pairs; the text itself says 'a male and his mate' after it.
  • אִישׁ וְאִשְׁתּוֹ are the words for a human husband and wife, here applied to animals (Radak: a figurative use).
  • לֹא טְהֹרָה הִוא ('that is not clean') stands for 'unclean'. Radak: Scripture often puts a quality in the negative, as in כִּי לֹא טָהוֹר הוּא (1 Sam 20:26), and the sense is the same; the rabbis learned from this verse that one should not utter an unseemly word.

The English leaves the ambiguity in 'seven each' (seven individuals or seven pairs). Radak reads seven pairs; Rashi says only that the extras are for a sacrifice at exit. 'Clean' is not defined in the text; Rashi reads it as 'destined to be clean for Israel', Sforno as 'fit for sacrifice', and Radak that God told Noah the signs of cleanness or that he recognized them by their coming in sevens.

7:3

Also of the birds of the sky, seven each, male and female, to keep seed alive across the face of all the earth.

also from-bird-of the-heavens seven seven male and-female to-keep-alive seed upon face-of all-of the-earth

Grammar
  • עוֹף is a collective singular, so the English plural 'birds'.
  • שִׁבְעָה שִׁבְעָה is again distributive; here זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה explains it.
  • לְחַיּוֹת is a Piel infinitive construct and gives the purpose.
  • The etnaḥta on וּנְקֵבָה divides the verse: the birds to be taken, then the purpose. The tevir on הַשָּׁמַיִם and the tipḥa on the second שִׁבְעָה are lesser pauses within the first half.

גַּם ('also') joins the birds to the animals of 7:2. Rashi reads the verse as speaking of clean birds only, learning the unstated from the stated. Radak, at 7:2, weighs two readings: that all birds, clean and unclean, came in sevens, or that, as with the animals, only the clean birds did, the 'also' joining them to the clean animals. The English, like the Hebrew, does not say 'clean'.

7:4

For in seven more days I will make it rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from the face of the ground.

for to-days still seven I causing-rain upon the-earth forty day and-forty night and-I-will-wipe-out (object) all-of the-existing-thing that I-made from-upon face-of the-ground

Grammar
  • The participle מַמְטִיר expresses what is about to happen; the weqatal וּמָחִיתִי continues it.
  • יָמִים ... עוֹד שִׁבְעָה: 'still seven days'; the preposition ל marks the span after which the event occurs.
  • הַיְקוּם is rare: here, 7:23 and Deut 11:6. Ibn Ezra says it occurs only in this section; he and Radak take it as a general word for every living being.
  • The verse uses אֲדָמָה (ground), not אֶרֶץ, for what is wiped out.

The BDB entry gives `substance, existence` for הַיְקוּם; the English 'living thing' follows Ibn Ezra, 'a general term for every living being on the earth' and Radak ('all that is on the face of the ground among living beings'). Radak adds that it does not include fish or those in the ark. Rashi reads the seven days as the mourning for Methuselah and the 'still' as additional to the 120 years; neither changes the plain translation.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos renders הַיְקוּם by its cognate יְקוּמָא and אֲדָמָה by אַרְעָא, his usual equivalent; neither is a variant of the Hebrew.
7:5

Noah did according to all that the LORD had commanded him.

and-did Noah like-all that commanded-him the-LORD

Grammar
  • The narrative wayyiqtol וַיַּעַשׂ begins the report of obedience.
  • צִוָּהוּ is a Piel perfect with a pronominal suffix.
  • The divine name here is יְהוָה, where 6:22 had אֱלֹהִים.
  • The etnaḥta on נֹחַ divides subject from the measure of obedience.

The Hebrew repeats the report of 6:22, with the divine name changed. Rashi reads 'Noah did' as his entering the ark; Ibn Ezra as his coming with his household near the ark; Radak as his entering with his household and bringing in the animals. The English line gives the plain wording.

Now Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came, water upon the earth.

Grammar
  • בֶּן־שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה is the idiom for age: 'son of six hundred years'.
  • The ו of וְהַמַּבּוּל is circumstantial: 'when' (Radak).
  • מַיִם is a plural noun 'water'.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁנָה divides Noah's age from the flood.

Radak glosses וְהַמַּבּוּל הָיָה as 'a flood of water': the one word מַבּוּל serves twice, 'the flood came' and '(a flood of) water upon the earth'. The English line reads 'the flood came, water upon the earth'.

7:7

Noah went into the ark, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him, because of the waters of the flood.

and-came Noah and-sons-his and-wife-his and-wives-of sons-his with-him to the-ark from-before waters-of the-flood

Grammar
  • The verb וַיָּבֹא is singular and agrees with the first subject, Noah; the rest of the party follows in a list.
  • The telisha gedola on בָנָיו and the darga/tevir pair keep the men (sons) apart from the women (wife, sons' wives), in the order of the list.
  • מִפְּנֵי is literally 'from before' and means 'on account of'; the etnaḥta after הַתֵּבָה divides the verse before this clause.

Rashi reads the separate listing of men and women as a sign of marital abstinence; that bears on the order of the list, not on the English words. 'Because of' follows both Rashi (waters pressed him) and Ibn Ezra (fear of the flood) in taking the clause as the reason for entering.

Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וְעָאל נֹחַ וּבְנוֹהִי וְאִתְּתֵיהּ וּנְשֵׁי בְנוֹהִי עִמֵּיהּ לְתֵבוֹתָא מִן קֳדָם מֵי טוֹפָנָא:
7:8

Of the clean animals, and of the animals that are not clean, and of the birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground,

from-the-animal the-clean and-from-the-animal which not-it clean and-from-the-bird and-all which creeping on the-ground

Grammar
  • The verse continues the list begun in 7:7 and has no verb of its own; the main verb is בָּאוּ in 7:9.
  • Each of the three מִן phrases is partitive: representatives 'of' each class entered. The fourth item, וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר רֹמֵשׂ, has no מִן; the English carries the 'of' over from the series.
  • אֵינֶנָּה is the negative particle אַיִן with a feminine singular suffix, agreeing with בְּהֵמָה.
  • The etnaḥta on טְהֹרָה divides the beasts, clean and unclean, from the birds and the creeping things. Zaqef qaton on הַטְּהוֹרָה, הַבְּהֵמָה and הָעוֹף marks the lesser breaks, and the second and third וּמִן carry a conjunctive qadma.

The verse is a fragment of one sentence with 7:9, so the English ends with a comma. The clean/unclean distinction is already known in the narrative at 7:2.

7:9

two by two they came to Noah into the ark, male and female, as God had commanded Noah.

two two came to Noah to the-ark male and-female as commanded God ACC Noah

Grammar
  • Doubling a word (שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם) expresses distribution: 'two by two'.
  • The verb בָּאוּ is a qatal; it brings the list of 7:8 to its main verb.
  • זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה stand in apposition, 'male and female', explaining the pair.
  • צִוָּה is Piel; the qatal after כַּאֲשֶׁר is rendered as a pluperfect.

The verse completes the sentence begun in 7:8, whose list names those who came, so the English runs on from 7:8; 'came to Noah' is literal; Rashi and Radak both say the animals came of their own accord.

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי with a time phrase introduces a new moment in the narrative: 'and it came to be at ...'.
  • לְשִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים is literally 'at the seven of the days', the seven days announced in 7:4.
  • The subject מֵי הַמַּבּוּל is grammatically plural and takes a plural verb הָיוּ.

Radak takes ל as 'at the end of' the seven days of grace given in 7:4; the English follows that.

Grammar
  • The date is a series of ב phrases: year, month, day of the month, with the time clause leading to the main verbs נִבְקְעוּ and נִפְתָּחוּ.
  • Both verbs are Niphal qatal, plural, passive: 'were split', 'were opened'.
  • מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם רַבָּה: the springs of the great deep; תְּהוֹם is also found with the feminine adjective here, and Ibn Ezra notes it is both masculine and feminine.
  • The symmetry of the verse sets the springs of the earth below against the windows of the sky above.

'The great deep' keeps תְּהוֹם רַבָּה; Rashi's note sees measure for measure in רַבָּה. Of the two second-month readings in Rashi, the English says only 'second month'; the commentators' disagreement over which month that is does not affect the English words.

Ibn Ezra: תהום is both masculine and feminine, as in 'the deep raised it up' (תהום רוממתהו, Ezek 31:4). The text does not mention rivers, since they come from the springs. When the springs split the waters rose; the windows of the storehouses in heaven opened and the waters came down, and the earth was thrown into confusion, with no telling day from night, as 'day and night shall not cease' (8:22) shows. When the rain stopped Noah knew that forty days and forty nights had passed, because God revealed it to him.

Some take the aleph as a root letter, like כבודות; others as added, like the aleph of אגורת (1 Sam 2:36), from a doubled root. On the seventeenth, when the flood began, Noah and his household entered the ark and brought in the animals and birds; צפור is a general term for whatever has a wing, and the wonder is that all came of themselves, two by two.

Grammar
  • הַגֶּשֶׁם is ordinary rain, not מַבּוּל; the narrative changes terms at 7:17.
  • The number precedes the noun and the noun is singular: אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם, 'forty days'.
  • The zaqef qaton after יוֹם divides the two measures of time.

Rashi: the text says גֶּשֶׁם here and מַבּוּל afterwards because the rain began as a rain of mercy; the English keeps the distinction in 'rain'. Rashi's count of the forty days (the first day, not counted) bears on the date and not on the words.

Grammar
  • בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, literally 'in the bone of this day', means 'on this very day'.
  • בָּא is a qatal singular with the first subject, Noah; the other subjects follow after it, as in 7:7.
  • שְׁלֹשֶׁת is the construct of the number: 'three of'.
  • The disjunctive accents divide the verse into the day, Noah, his sons, and the women.

The English keeps the Hebrew order (the verb after Noah, the verb's other subjects after it) so each phrase lines up with the Hebrew words.

Grammar
  • הֵמָּה resumes the subjects of 7:13 and is followed by the list of the animals, with לְמִינָהּ/לְמִינֵהוּ repeated for each class.
  • הָרֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ is a noun with its cognate participle: 'the creeping thing that creeps'.
  • The suffix on לְמִינָהּ agrees with the feminine noun (חַיָּה, בְּהֵמָה), the suffix on לְמִינֵהוּ with the masculine (רֶמֶשׂ, עוֹף).
  • The last clause, כֹּל צִפּוֹר כָּל כָּנָף, is a construct chain: 'every bird of every wing'.

Rashi reads צִפּוֹר כָּל כָּנָף as one construct chain (דבוק): 'a bird of every kind of wing', so that winged creatures such as locusts are included. The English follows him; 'kind of' gives the sense of כָּל before a singular noun. Radak allows כָּל כָּנָף to mean 'every winged creature', in apposition.

Grammar
  • וַיָּבֹאוּ is a wayyiqtol, plural: its subject is the animals listed in 7:14, and it continues the account of the entry 'on that very day' (7:13).
  • שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם: repeating a number makes it distributive.
  • The etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה divides the verse after the entry into the ark.
  • רוּחַ חַיִּים is a construct chain: 'breath of life'.

Ramban (not normative): the verse tells that the animals were not gathered to Noah beforehand but came only on that very day, gathered by God's spirit in a moment. Radak (not normative): they came in pairs in this second entry as in the first, none missing and none added.

7:16

Those that came in, male and female from all flesh, came in as God had commanded him, and the LORD shut him in.

and-the-ones-coming male and-female from-all flesh came as commanded him God and-shut the-LORD behind-him

Grammar
  • וְהַבָּאִים is a participle with the article, 'the ones coming', the subject of בָּאוּ.
  • The sentence has a long subject separated from its verb by 'male and female from all flesh'.
  • כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים recalls the command of 6:19-20 and 7:2-3.
  • בַּעֲדוֹ: בְּעַד means 'about, behind'; Rashi reads it as כְּנֶגֶד, 'facing, against': the LORD shut the ark about him, against the water. This is the only place in the unit where the name יְהוָה appears.

Rashi gives two readings of בעדו: the homiletic one (bears and lions ringed the ark) and the plain sense (he shut it against the water). The English follows the plain sense. The name is God (אֱלֹהִים) in the command and the LORD in the shutting.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּסְגֹּ֥ר יְהֹוָ֖ה בַּֽעֲדֽוֹ׃
Rashi: by the midrash, He protected him so that people would not break the ark, ringing it with bears and lions that killed them; the plain sense is that He shut [the ark] כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, 'facing him', against the water. Every בְּעַד in Scripture means כְּנֶגֶד, as in 'pray בְּעַד your servants' (1 Sam 12:19), 'facing your servants'.

7:17

When the flood had lasted forty days on the earth, the waters increased and lifted the ark, and it rose above the earth.

and-was the-flood forty day on the-earth and-increased the-waters and-lifted DOM the-ark and-rose from-on the-earth

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי הַמַּבּוּל אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם עַל־הָאָרֶץ is a full clause, 'the flood was forty days on the earth', closed by the etnaḥta. Ibn Ezra reads it as the time of what follows: 'when the flood had been forty days, the waters increased'.
  • The wayyiqtols וַיִּרְבּוּ וַיִּשְׂאוּ וַתָּרׇם follow one another as a chain of consequences.
  • וַתָּרׇם is a short form of the Qal of רום with feminine subject (the ark).
  • מֵעַל הָאָרֶץ: 'from upon the earth', 'above the ground'.

Ibn Ezra reads 'the flood was forty days' as 'when the flood had been forty days (the rain), the waters increased and lifted the ark'; the English follows him. Rashi (11 cubits) is recorded in the commentary entry.

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativefollows וַתָּ֖רׇם מֵעַ֥ל הָאָֽרֶץ׃
Rashi: the ark sank eleven cubits in the water, like a loaded ship that is partly submerged; the verses that follow (15 cubits) prove it. The English 'rose above the earth' is compatible with this.

7:18

The waters grew strong and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark moved on the surface of the waters.

and-grew-strong the-waters and-increased very on the-earth and-went the-ark on faces-of the-waters

Grammar
  • Three wayyiqtols in a row describe the rising of the water and the movement of the ark.
  • פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם is a construct chain: 'the face of the waters'.
  • גבר and רבה are close in sense: 'be strong' and 'be many'. 7:17 used רבה; this verse has both; 7:19-20 use גבר alone.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ divides the verse: the waters rise, then the ark moves.

Rashi says the waters grew strong 'by themselves', that is, apart from the rain; Sforno says the ark moved by the force of the waters from below. The English keeps 'grew strong', which fits both.

בִּדְחִיַּת הַתִּגְבּוֹרֶת הַבָּאָה מִלְמַטָּה.
7:19

The waters prevailed very, very greatly on the earth, and all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered.

and-the-waters prevailed very very on the-earth and-were-covered all-of the-mountains the-high which under all-of the-heavens

Grammar
  • The subject comes before the verb in וְהַמַּיִם גָּבְרוּ, which marks a new stage of the story.
  • מְאֹד מְאֹד is a doubled adverb, an intensifier.
  • וַיְכֻסּוּ is a pual: the mountains 'were covered'.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ divides the verse: the strength of the waters, then the covering of the mountains. The revia on וְהַמַּיִם sets off the fronted subject.

Ibn Ezra: מְאֹד מְאֹד is as high as one can say; he takes 'all the high mountains' as every high mountain, covered by fifteen cubits, and tells us to trust the Torah against the claims of men about mountains in Greek lands.

Commentary (7)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows מְאֹ֥ד מְאֹ֖ד
Ibn Ezra: מאד מאד, said twice, is a degree beyond which there is none. Since 'all the high mountains were covered' has been said, why repeat 'and the mountains were covered' (7:20)? It means that every high mountain was covered by the water, and the fifteen cubits covered those same mountains. We believe the words of our God and leave aside the vain talk of men about a high mountain in the kingdom of Greece.

Grammar
  • The measure comes first for emphasis: חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה.
  • מִלְמַעְלָה: 'from above', 'upward'; the sense is 'higher'.
  • The etnaḥta on הַמָּיִם divides the verse; the silluq falls on הֶהָרִים, the last word.
  • The order is measure, verb, subject: the perfect גָּבְרוּ follows the fronted measure and comes before its subject הַמָּיִם.

Rashi: the fifteen cubits are above the height of all the mountains, after the waters had been made level with the tops. The English leaves the starting point open ('upward'), as the Hebrew does.

Grammar
  • וַיִּגְוַע is singular before the collective subject כׇּל־בָּשָׂר.
  • The prefix בְּ before the list of animals means 'among, including'; the list specifies the 'flesh'.
  • הַשֶּׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ is a figura etymologica: 'the swarmer that swarms'.
  • The gershayim after וַיִּגְוַע and the revia on הָאָרֶץ mark the first division; the humans come last, after the etnaḥta.

Ibn Ezra takes רֶמֶשׂ as including birds, livestock, wild animals, swarming things and humans: 'all flesh that creeps' is the whole of life, and the list that follows specifies it. He reads וַיִּגְוַע as pluperfect-like ('had died').

  • The verb מֵתוּ comes last, after a long subject, 'everything that ...'.

Rashi reads 'the breath of the spirit of life' as 'the breath that belongs to the spirit of life', and takes 'on dry land' to exclude fish. Radak agrees about fish, since they are bred in water and do not live with humans.

Hebrew
כֹּל דִּי נִשְׁמְתָא רוּחָא דְּחַיִּין בְּאַנְפוֹהִי מִכֹּל דִּי בְּיַבֶּשְׁתָּא מִיתוּ:
7:23

He wiped out every living thing that was on the surface of the ground, from humans to animals, to crawling things, and to the birds of the sky; they were wiped out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark.

and-wiped-out [object-marker] all-of the-living-thing which on face-of the-ground from-human to animal to crawler and-to bird-of the-sky and-were-wiped-out from-the-earth and-was-left only Noah and-which with-him in-the-ark

Grammar
  • וַיִּמַח (Qal) and וַיִּמָּחוּ (Niphal) are the same root: the act and its result stand side by side.
  • The list runs מִן ... עַד ... עַד ... וְעַד: 'from ... to ... to ... and to'. The preposition עַד is written three times, and the last takes ו.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ closes the first half. In the second half the tevir on נֹחַ, a disjunctive accent, makes a small pause after 'only Noah' before 'and those with him in the ark'.
  • אַךְ limits the survivors to Noah and those with him; the verb וַיִּשָּׁאֶר is singular.

The English keeps the double verb (wiped out ... were wiped out) as the Hebrew has it. The parse in the pack gives Qal for the first verb, in agreement with Rashi.

Commentary (15)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּ֜מַח
Rashi: וַיִּמַח is an active (Qal) form, not Niphal, like וַיִּפֶן and וַיִּבֶן from roots ending in he, pointed with ḥireq under the yod. The English has an active verb with God understood.

Rambanrecords וַיִּמָּח֖וּ מִן הָאָ֑רֶץ
Ramban: the doubling may be for the birds and some creeping things, to say that no eggs of theirs were left in any tree or under the ground; or the verse may be read 'all, from human to bird, were wiped out from the earth; only Noah was left'. The rabbis read 'he wiped out' of this world and 'they were wiped out from the earth' of the world to come.

Apparatus
  • 7:23.20 vowels: WLC reads וַיִשָּׁאֶר without the dagesh in yod; the base text וַיִּשָּׁאֶר is followed.

7:24

The waters prevailed over the earth for a hundred and fifty days.

and-prevailed the-waters upon the-earth fifty and-hundred-of day

Grammar
  • The merkha on וַיִּגְבְּרוּ and the tipḥa on הַמַּיִם lead to the etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ; the duration is a separate clause-end.
  • The number is written smaller number first: חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם, with the noun in the singular.
  • גָּבַר 'be strong' is used of waters 'gaining the upper hand'.

'Prevailed' keeps the sense of strength, not only rising. Ibn Ezra's point is about how the water gained: the springs broke open, and the rain fell intermittently.

Commentary (5)
Ibn Ezranormativenot-applicable וַיִּגְבְּר֥וּ הַמַּ֖יִם חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים וּמְאַ֖ת יֽוֹם׃
Ibn Ezra: the waters prevailed a hundred and fifty days because the springs had burst open, and rain also went on falling, one day yes and one day no; the 'I will rain' of 7:4 means forty days of rain without a break, and the later וַיִּכָּלֵא הַגֶּשֶׁם (8:2) is the proof that rain still fell after them. This concerns the course of the flood, not the wording of the verse.

8:1

God remembered Noah and every living creature and all the domestic animals that were with him in the ark, and God made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters subsided.

and-remembered God [object-marker] Noah and-[object-marker] all-of the-living-thing and-[object-marker] all-of the-beast which with-him in-the-ark and-made-pass God wind upon the-earth and-subsided the-waters

Grammar
  • וַיִּזְכֹּר is not a lapse corrected: Radak says memory and forgetting do not apply to God; the Torah speaks in human terms, and the word means he acted for them.
  • The Hiphil וַיַּעֲבֵר makes God the cause: he made a wind pass. The qadma on וַיַּעֲבֵר and the merkha on אֱלֹהִים are conjunctive accents; the clause runs on to the zaqef qaton on הָאָרֶץ.
  • Pashta is written on the last letter of its word. On רוּחַ it is written a second time, on רוּ, because the stress falls on the first syllable: the pataḥ under ח is a furtive pataḥ.
  • וַיָּשֹׁכּוּ is the Qal wayyiqtol of the doubled root שׁכך, the verb of Esther 7:10 (וַחֲמַת הַמֶּלֶךְ שָׁכָכָה); the dagesh in the כ makes up for the root's missing second letter (Ibn Ezra). The sense is 'settle, abate'.

The English keeps 'God' for אֱלֹהִים by decision, even though Rashi reads it as the attribute of justice turned to mercy. 'Noah' stands for Noah with his sons and wives, as Ibn Ezra says. 'Wind' (not 'spirit') because the verb is Hiphil of 'pass over' and the object is something that blows over the earth, as Ibn Ezra ('he made it pass continually') and Radak take it; Rashi's reading, a spirit of comfort passing before God concerning the affairs of the earth, is recorded.

Commentary (14)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וַיִּזְכֹּ֤ר אֱלֹהִים֙
Rashi: this name, אֱלֹהִים, is the attribute of justice, turned to mercy by the prayer of the righteous; the wickedness of the wicked turns mercy to justice. A homily on the divine name.
Hebrew
זֶה הַשֵּׁם מִדַּת הַדִּין הוּא, וְנֶהֶפְכָה לְמִדַּת רַחֲמִים עַל יְדֵי תְפִלַּת הַצַּדִּיקִים; וְרִשְׁעָתָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים הוֹפֶכֶת מִדַּת רַחֲמִים לְמִדַּת הַדִּין, שֶׁנֶאֱמַר וַיַּרְא ה' כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם, וַיֹּאמֶר ה' אֶמְחֶה, (ברא' ו') וְהוּא שֵׁם מִדַּת רַחֲמִים:

Hebrew

and-were-shut springs-of deep and-sluices-of the-sky and-was-held-back the-rain from-the-sky

Grammar
  • Both subjects of וַיִּסָּכְרוּ are in the construct (מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם, אֲרֻבֹּת הַשָּׁמַיִם); the verb is plural and agrees with the nearer.
  • Two Niphal wayyiqtols (וַיִּסָּכְרוּ, וַיִּכָּלֵא) describe the end of the flood as passives: no agent is named.
  • The Hebrew has no 'all' here, unlike 7:11 (כָּל מַעְיְנֹת): Rashi draws the lesson from this.
  • סכר and סגר are two forms of one meaning (Ibn Ezra, Radak).

'Floodgates' renders אֲרֻבֹּת, the word of 7:11. 'Shut' is chosen for סכר to match 'closed' of Ibn Ezra; 'stopped up' is the alternative.

8:3

The waters withdrew from the earth steadily, and the waters decreased at the end of a hundred and fifty days.

and-returned the-waters from-upon the-earth going and-returning and-decreased the-waters from-end-of fifty and-hundred-of day

Grammar
  • הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב: two infinitive absolutes after a finite verb express continuing action (compare 8:5, הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר).
  • The tevir on הַמַּיִם and the etnaḥta on וָשׁוֹב divide the verse after the first clause; the zaqef gadol on מִקְצֵה sets the number apart.
  • וַיַּחְסְרוּ is a stative Qal wayyiqtol of a verb with a stative vowel (חָסֵר).
  • The word order of the second clause puts the verb before its subject: וַיַּחְסְרוּ הַמַּיִם.

'Steadily' translates the idiom; the words 'going and returning' are in the literal line. The English follows the timing of Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak: the waters began to decrease at the end of the hundred and fifty days. Ramban joins מִקְצֵה with the following 'the ark came to rest'.

Commentary (5)

למטה מהארץ כמשפטם בסוף חמשים ומאת יום, גם זה החשבון, בדרך נבואה ידעו והאומרים כי הנה מצאנו מאה וחמשים יום, חמשה חדשים וזה לנו לאות שהם חדשי חמה, והנה לא דברו נכונה על דבריהם כי שנים ימים יחסרו גם האומר כי בחשבון העבור היה עושה וישים בחדש השני מרחשון ותהיה השנה שלימה, ולמה כל זה, ואפילו היה כתוב כי נח היה חשבונו על החמה או תחלת השנה מתשרי לא נתנו המועדים ע"י נח גם יתכן על מנוח התיבה לדבר דברים ארוכים לכן לא יועלו ולא יצילו כי תהו המה:

יֹאמַר שֶׁהָיוּ חֲסֵרִים מְעַט מְעַט עַד שֶׁחָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה, וַיַּחְסְרוּ הַמַּיִם מִקְצֵה חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם דָּבֵק עִם "וַתָּנַח הַתֵּבָה", לוֹמַר שֶׁחָסְרוּ בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא חֶסְרוֹן גָּדוֹל שֶׁנָּחָה בּוֹ הַתֵּבָה, כַּאֲשֶׁר פֵּרַשְׁתִּי:

Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וְתָבוּ מַיָּא מֵעַל אַרְעָא אָזְלִין וְתָיְבִין וַחֲסָרוּ מַיָּא מִסּוֹף מְאָה וְחַמְשִׁין יוֹמִין:
8:4

The ark came to rest in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on the mountains of Ararat.

and-rested the-ark in-the-month the-seventh in-seven-ten day of-the-month upon mountains-of Ararat

Grammar
  • וַתָּנַח: the verb is feminine, as תֵּבָה is feminine; a play on נֹחַ, whose name comes from נוח.
  • The date has three parts: the month by ordinal (הַשְּׁבִיעִי), the day by cardinal (שִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם), and then 'of the month'.
  • The zaqef qaton on הַשְּׁבִיעִי and the etnaḥta on לַחֹדֶשׁ separate the date from the place.

The English does not say which reckoning gives 'the seventh month'. Rashi and Radak count from the stopping of the rain (Sivan); Ramban attributes another reckoning to Ibn Ezra and others. Rashi's inference that the ark sank eleven cubits is a calculation from the days and cubits.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativerecords בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י
Rashi: the seventh month is Sivan, the seventh from the stopping of the rains in Kislev. The English leaves the starting point of the count open.
Hebrew
סִיוָן, וְהוּא שְׁבִיעִי לְכִסְלֵו שֶׁבּוֹ פָּסְקוּ הַגְּשָׁמִים:
Rashinormativenot-applicable בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂ֥ר י֖וֹם
Rashi: from here you learn that the ark was sunk eleven cubits in the water, by a calculation from the exposure of the mountain tops at a rate of one cubit in four days. A computation that does not bear on the words.
Hebrew
מִכָּאן אַתָּה לָמֵד שֶׁהָיְתָה הַתֵּבָה מְשֻׁקַּעַת בַּמַּיִם י"א אַמָּה, שֶׁהֲרֵי כְתִיב בָּעֲשִׂירִי בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ נִרְאוּ רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים, זֶה אָב, שֶׁהִיא עֲשִׂירִי לְמַרְחֶשְׁוָן לִירִידַת גְּשָׁמִים, וְהֵם הָיוּ גְבוֹהִים עַל הֶהָרִים חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה, וְחָסְרוּ מִיּוֹם אֶחָד בְּסִיוָן עַד אֶחָד בְּאָב חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה לְשִּׁשִּׁים יוֹם, הֲרֵי אַמָּה לְד' יָמִים, נִמְצָא, שֶׁבְּי"ו בְּסִיוָן לֹא חָסְרוּ אֶלָּא ד' אַמּוֹת וְנָחָה הַתֵּבָה לְיוֹם הַמָּחֳרָת; לָמַדְתָּ, שֶׁהָיְתָה מְשֻׁקַּעַת י"א אַמָּה בַמַּיִם שֶׁעַל רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים:
Rambanrecords וַתָּ֤נַח הַתֵּבָה֙ בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י בְּשִׁבְעָה עָשָׂ֥ר י֖וֹם לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ

8:5

The waters continued to diminish steadily until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains became visible.

and-the-waters were going and-diminishing until the-month the-tenth in-the-tenth on-one to-the-month were-seen heads-of the-mountains

Grammar
  • הָיוּ הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר: the finite verb 'be' with two infinitive absolutes gives the sense 'kept on diminishing'.
  • The tenth month is named twice: in full after עַד (עַד הַחֹדֶשׁ הָעֲשִׂירִי), then by the ordinal alone after בְּ (בָּעֲשִׂירִי), with חֹדֶשׁ understood.
  • The date uses בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ for 'on the first of the month', with ל for 'of'.
  • נִרְאוּ is the Niphal 'appeared, was seen'; the subject רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים is plural.

'Became visible' for Niphal of ראה. Radak: they did not all go down until the land was seen; the mountain tops were first seen in the tenth month and the decrease continued after.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativerecords בָּֽעֲשִׂירִי֙ נִרְא֖וּ רָאשֵׁ֥י הֶֽהָרִֽים׃
Rashi: the tenth is Av, the tenth from Marheshvan, when the rain began; the seventh month he counts from the stopping, but the tenth cannot be counted from the stopping. The English leaves the count open.
Hebrew
זֶה אָב, שֶׁהוּא עֲשִׂירִי לְמַרְחֶשְׁוָן שֶׁהִתְחִיל הַגֶּשֶׁם. וְאִם תֹּאמַר הוּא אֱלוּל, וַעֲשִׂירִי לְכִסְלֵו שֶׁפָּסַק הַגֶּשֶׁם, כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאַתָּה אוֹמֵר בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי סִיוָן, וְהוּא שְׁבִיעִי לַהַפְסָקָה – אִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר כֵּן, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שְׁבִיעִי אִי אַתָּה מוֹנֶה אֶלָּא לַהַפְסָקָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי לֹא כָלוּ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם שֶׁל יְרִידַת גְּשָׁמִים, וּמֵאָה וַחֲמִשִּׁים שֶׁל תִּגְבֹּרֶת הַמַּיִם עַד אֶחָד בְּסִיוָן; וְאִם אַתָּה אוֹמֵר שְׁבִיעִי לַיְרִידָה, אֵין זֶה סִיוָן, וְהָעֲשִׂירִי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִמְנוֹת אֶלָּא לַיְרִידָה, שֶׁאִם אַתָּה אוֹמֵר לַהַפְסָקָה וְהוּא אֱלוּל, אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא בָּרִאשׁוֹן בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ חָרְבוּ הַמַּיִם מֵעַל הָאָרֶץ; שֶׁהֲרֵי מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם מִשֶׁנִּרְאוּ רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים שִׁלַּח אֶת הָעוֹרֵב וְכ"א יוֹם הוֹחִיל בִּשְׁלִיחוּת הַיּוֹנָה, הֲרֵי שִׁשִּׁים יוֹם מִשֶּׁנִּרְאוּ רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים עַד שֶׁחָרְבוּ פְנֵי הָאֲדָמָה. וְאִם תֹּאמַר בֶּאֱלוּל נִרְאוּ, נִמְצָא שֶׁחָרְבוּ בְּמַרְחֶשְׁוָן וְהוּא קוֹרֵא אוֹתוֹ רִאשׁוֹן, וְאֵין זֶה אֶלָּא תִּשְׁרֵי, שֶׁהוּא רִאשׁוֹן לִבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם, וְלְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הוּא נִיסָן:
Ibn Ezranormativerecords בָּֽעֲשִׂירִי֙ בְּאֶחָ֣ד לַחֹ֔דֶשׁ נִרְא֖וּ רָאשֵׁ֥י הֶֽהָרִֽים׃
Ibn Ezra: Noah fixed the first of the month without seeing the moon, since the window was not yet open; the tenth month is counted from the day of the flood, and he sent the raven on the tenth of Shevat. The English leaves the reckoning open.

Rambanrecords וְהַמַּ֗יִם הָיוּ֙ הָל֣וֹךְ וְחָס֔וֹר עַ֖ד הַחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָֽעֲשִׂירִ֑י
Ramban: the order is inverted: the waters kept diminishing until the mountain tops were seen in the tenth month, which is Tammuz.
Hebrew
טַעְמוֹ מְסֹרָס, שֶׁהָיוּ הָלוֹךְ וְחָסוֹר עַד שֶׁנִּרְאוּ רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָעֲשִׂירִי הוּא חֹדֶשׁ תַּמּוּז, וְהוֹדִיעָנוּ הַכָּתוּב שֶׁחָסְרוּ בְּע"ג יוֹם חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה אַמָּה, אֲבָל הַחֶסְרוֹן אֲשֶׁר מִתְּחִלָּה לִמְנוֹחַ הַתֵּבָה לֹא יָדַעְנוּ כַּמָּה הָיָה, כִּי לֹא הֻצְרַךְ הַכָּתוּב לְהוֹדִיעַ הַשִּׁקּוּעַ וְלֹא הַחֶסְרוֹן. וְהַנִּרְאֶה לְדַעְתִּי בְּשׁוּט הַתֵּבָה כִּי הָיְתָה מִפְּנֵי הֱיוֹת הַמַּיִם נוֹבְעִים מִן הַתְּהוֹמוֹת וֶהֱיוֹתָם עוֹד רוֹתְחִים כְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ, כִּי בַּעֲבוּר כֵּן תֵּלֵךְ עַל פְּנֵי הַמַּיִם, וְאִם לֹא מִפְּנֵי זֶה הָיְתָה נִטְבַּעַת בִּכְבֵדוּתָהּ, כִּי רַבִּים אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹכָהּ וְהַמַּאֲכָל וְהַמַּשְׁקֶה הָיָה הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד. וְכַאֲשֶׁר שָׁכְכוּ הַמַּיִם מִנְּבִיעָתָם אוֹ מֵרְתִיחָתָם גַּם כֵּן וְחָסְרוּ בָּרוּחַ, מִיָּד נִכְנְסָה הַתֵּבָה אֶל תּוֹךְ הַמַּיִם בְּכֹבֶד מַשָּׂאָהּ, וַתָּנַח עַל הָהָר. וְעַל דַּעַת הַמְּפָרְשִׁים (הראב"ע והרד"ק) הַמִּסְפָּר בְּתִגְבֹּרֶת הַמַּיִם חֲמִשִּׁים וּמְאַת יוֹם, וּמְנוֹחַ הַתֵּבָה וּרְאִיַּת רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים וְאַרְבָּעִים יוֹם אַחֲרֵי כֵן, הַכֹּל יָדַעְנוּ בְּדֶרֶךְ הַנְּבוּאָה, כִּי הַכָּתוּב מוֹדִיעַ אוֹתָנוּ כֵּן, אֲבָל נֹחַ לֹא יָדַע רַק שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ כִּי נָחָה הַתֵּבָה, וְהִמְתִּין לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ זְמַן שֶׁחָשַׁב כִּי קַלּוּ הַמַּיִם. וְהִנֵּה גַּם לִדְבָרֵינוּ גַּם לְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ וְכָל הַמְּפָרְשִׁים יִהְיוּ הָרֵי אֲרָרָט מִן "הֶהָרִים הַגְּבֹהִים אֲשֶׁר תַּחַת כָּל הַשָּׁמָיִם" (בראשית ז':י"ט), שֶׁהָיוּ הַמַּיִם עֲלֵיהֶם ט"ו אַמָּה. וְלָכֵן יִקְשֶׁה זֶה, כִּי הַיָּדוּעַ בָּהָר הַיְּוָנִי שֶׁגָּבוֹהַּ מֵהֶם הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד, וְאֶרֶץ אֲרָרָט בְּשֵׁפֶל הַכַּדּוּר הַקָּרוֹב לְבָבֶל. וְאוּלַי נֹאמַר כִּי הָיָה הַחֶסְרוֹן בי"ז לַחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי גָּדוֹל מְאֹד מט"ו אַמָּה, וְקֹדֶם לָכֵן נִרְאוּ רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים הַגְּבוֹהִים, לֹא הָרֵי אֲרָרָט, וַיִּקֶר מִקְרֶה הַתֵּבָה שֶׁהָיְתָה בְּאֶרֶץ אֲרָרָט בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי, וַתָּנַח עַל רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים הָהֵם. וְהִנֵּה נֹחַ מֵעֵת שֶׁכָּלָה הַגֶּשֶׁם הָיָה פּוֹתֵחַ הַחַלּוֹן וְסוֹגֵר אוֹתוֹ כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, וְאַחַר ע"ג יוֹם מִמְּנוֹחַ הַתֵּבָה הִשְׁגִּיחַ מִן הַחַלּוֹן וְנִרְאוּ לוֹ רָאשֵׁי הָרֵי אֲרָרָט, וְחָזַר וְסָגַר אוֹתוֹ. וְהִגִּיד הַכָּתוּב כִּי אַחַר אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם שָׁלַח הָעוֹרֵב, וְלֹא אָמַר הַכָּתוּב "וַיְהִי בְּחֹדֶשׁ פְּלוֹנִי וּבְיוֹם פְּלוֹנִי וַיִּפְתַּח נֹחַ", וְאָמַר "וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם", לְהַגִּיד כִּי מֵעֵת שֶׁנִּרְאוּ לְנֹחַ רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים הִמְתִּין אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם, כִּי חָשַׁב בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁבַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה נִרְאוּ הַמִּגְדָּלִים וְנִגְלוּ הָאִילָנוֹת, וְיִמְצְאוּ הָעוֹפוֹת לָהֶם מָנוֹחַ בַּאֲשֶׁר תְּקַנֵּנָּה, וּפָתַח הַחַלּוֹן לִשְׁלֹחַ הָעוֹרֵב. וּבַחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן הוּא חֹדֶשׁ תִּשְׁרֵי חָרְבוּ הַמַּיִם, וּבַחֹדֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי הוּא חֹדֶשׁ מַרְחֶשְׁוָן בְּשִׁבְעָה וְעֶשְׂרִים בּוֹ יָבְשָׁה הָאָרֶץ, וּבוֹ בַּיּוֹם יָצְאוּ מִן הַתֵּבָה. וְהִנֵּה כָּל מִנְיַן הַפָּרָשָׁה כִּפְשׁוּטוֹ וּמַשְׁמָעוֹ. וְדַע כִּי אַחֲרֵי שֶׁהִסְכִּימוּ שֶׁבְּתִשְׁרֵי נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם כַּאֲשֶׁר תִּקְּנוּ "זֶה הַיּוֹם תְּחִלַּת מַעֲשֶׂיךָ זִכָּרוֹן לְיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן", וְכֵן הוּא סֵדֶר הַזְּמַנִּים זֶרַע וְקָצִיר וְקוֹר וָחֹם, יִהְיֶה רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנִים מִתִּשְׁרֵי, וְכֵן הֶחֳדָשִׁים מִמֶּנּוּ הֵם נִמְנִים, עַד שֶׁהִגַּעְנוּ לִיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם, וְאָז צִוָּה הקב"ה לִמְנוֹת בֶּחֳדָשִׁים מִנְיָן אַחֵר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שמות יב ב) "הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם רֹאשׁ חֳדָשִׁים רִאשׁוֹן הוּא לָכֶם לְחָדְשֵׁי הַשָּׁנָה", וּמִשָּׁם וְאֵילָךְ בְּכָל הַכָּתוּב יִמְנֶה תִּשְׁרֵי הַחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי, וַעֲדַיִן נִשְׁאַר בַּשָּׁנִים הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן מִמֶּנּוּ, דִּכְתִיב (שמות לד כב) "וְחַג הָאָסִיף תְּקוּפַת הַשָּׁנָה", וְכָךְ תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן בֶּן עֻזִּיאֵל "בְּיֶרַח הָאֵיתָנִים בֶּחָג הוּא הַחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי" (מלכים א ח ב) אָמַר "בְּיַרְחָא דְּעַתִּיקַיָּא דְּקָרַן לֵיהּ יַרְחָא קַדְמָאָה וּכְעַן הוּא יַרְחָא שְׁבִיעָאָה". וּבַמְּכִילְתָּא (בא א ח) "הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם", וְלֹא מָנָה בּוֹ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן:
Radakfollows וְהַמַּ֗יִם הָיוּ֙ הָל֣וֹךְ וְחָס֔וֹר
Radak: they kept diminishing, as in 'the creatures ran and returned' (Ezekiel 1:14).

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי with a time phrase begins a new episode: 'at the end of forty days'.
  • The zaqef gadol on וַיְהִי and the etnaḥta on יוֹם set the time clause apart from the main clause וַיִּפְתַּח נֹחַ.
  • אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה is a perfect that refers back to 6:16: 'which he had made'.

'The window' is the opening of 6:16 (צֹהַר). The starting point of the forty days is not given by the Hebrew: Rashi counts from the sight of the tops of the mountains; Radak prefers from the ark's coming to rest.

8:7

He sent out the raven, and it went back and forth until the waters had dried from off the earth.

and-sent [object-marker]-the-raven and-went going-out and-returning until drying-of the-waters from-upon the-earth

Grammar
  • וַיֵּצֵא יָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב: a finite verb followed by two infinitive absolutes; the pair gives continued, repeated motion.
  • The etnaḥta on הָעֹרֵב ends the first clause; the zaqef qaton on וָשׁוֹב sets off 'went out and back' from the time clause.
  • עַד יְבֹשֶׁת הַמַּיִם: עַד with an infinitive construct (feminine form of יבשׁ) forms a time clause.
  • מֵעַל is a compound preposition, 'from upon', so 'from off'.

The Hebrew does not say whether the raven landed anywhere, nor whether it came back to the ark; the English keeps that openness with 'back and forth'. The pack lemma for the infinitive absolutes is יצא and שׁוב; the data are kept.

קִנָּהּ. וְכֵן מִנְהַג הַמְּלָכִים לְגַדְּלָהּ בְּבֵיתָם וּלְשָׁלְחָהּ בִּמְקוֹמוֹת הָרְחוֹקִים וְקוֹשְׁרִין כְּתָב בִּכְנָפֶיהָ, וְהִיא שָׁבָה אֶל שׁוֹלְחָהּ בִּכְתַב הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁקּוֹשֵׁר אוֹתָהּ בִּכְנָפֶיהָ גַּם מִי שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּלְּחָה לָהֶם. וְלָכָךְ פֵּרְשׁוּ הַגְּאוֹנִים מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בַּתַּלְמוּד (שבת מט) ״מָה יוֹנָה כְּנָפֶיהָ מְגִנּוֹת עָלֶיהָ״, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין שׁוֹחֲטִין אוֹתָהּ, כִּי בַּעֲבוּר שְׁלִיחוּתָם מְגַדְּלִים וּמְחַיִּים אוֹתָהּ, וְהִיא שָׁבָה אֶל שׁוֹלְחָהּ, וְזֶה תַּעֲשֶׂה כָּל הַפְּעָמִים שֶׁשּׁוֹלְחִים אוֹתָהּ. וְשָׁלַח נֹחַ אוֹתָהּ כִּי יָדַע שֶׁתָּבִיא לוֹ שׁוּם דָּבָר לְסִימָן אִם תִּמְצָא עָלֶה אוֹ גַּרְגִּיר. וְזֶה ״וַתָּשָׁב אֵלָיו אֶל־הַתֵּבָה״ (בראשית ח:ט), וְלֹא אָמַר ״אֵלָיו״, וְאָמַר ״אֶל־הַתֵּבָה״. ״אֵלָיו״ – לְהָשִׁיב שׁוֹלְחָהּ דָּבָר, כִּי לֹא מָצְאָה שׁוּם דָּבָר שֶׁתָּבִיא בְּפִיהָ לְסִימָן. וְאָמַר ״אֶל־הַתֵּבָה״ – שֶׁנָּחָה עַל גַּבֵּי הַתֵּבָה, כִּי לֹא רָצְתָה לִכְנֹס לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה מְבִיאָה שׁוּם דָּבָר לְסִימָן, וְלֹא Apparatus
  • Rashi and Radak differ on where the raven went; the Hebrew gives no destination.
8:8

Then he sent the dove away from him, to see whether the waters had abated from the surface of the ground.

and-sent [object-marker]-the-dove from-with-him to-see have-lightened the-waters from-upon face-of the-ground

Grammar
  • לִרְאוֹת הֲקַלּוּ: purpose clause (ל + infinitive) containing an indirect question introduced by the interrogative הֲ.
  • הֲקַלּוּ is a Qal perfect of the geminate root קלל, 'be light', here of waters 'lessening'.
  • The etnaḥta on מֵאִתּוֹ divides the sending from its purpose; in the second half the zaqef qaton on הַמַּיִם sets 'whether the waters had abated' apart from 'from the surface of the ground'.
  • הָאֲדָמָה, 'the ground', stands where verse 7 has הָאָרֶץ, 'the earth'; the same pair returns in 8:13.

'abated' keeps the sense of lightening (lessening of weight and amount). 'Sent ... away' follows Rashi: וַיְשַׁלַּח here is release (שִׁלּוּחַ), letting her go her own way, not a mission (שְׁלִיחוּת) as with the raven; if she found rest she would not come back. 'From him' renders מֵאִתּוֹ.

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וַיְשַׁלַּ֥ח אֶת הַיּוֹנָ֖ה
Rashi: the dove was sent at the end of seven days, since verse 10 says 'he waited another seven days', implying a first seven. This is an inference about dates and does not change the English.

לְסוֹף ז' יָמִים שֶׁהֲרֵי כְתִיב וַיָּחֶל עוֹד ז' יָמִים אֲחֵרִים, מִכְּלַל זֶה אַתָּה לָמֵד שֶׁאַף בָּרִאשׁוֹנָה הוֹחִיל ז' יָמִים:

8:9

But the dove found no resting place for the sole of her foot, and she returned to him, to the ark, for there was water over the surface of all the earth. So he stretched out his hand, took her, and brought her to him into the ark.

and-not found the-dove resting-place for-sole-of her-foot and-returned to-him to the-ark for waters upon face-of all-the-earth and-sent his-hand and-took-her and-brought [obj]-her to-him to the-ark

Grammar
  • מַיִם עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ gives the reason with כִּי; the clause has no verb (a nominal clause).
  • וַיִּשְׁלַח יָדוֹ, 'he sent his hand', is the idiom for reaching out; the same verb שׁלח is used of the birds in 8:7-8.
  • וַיִּקָּחֶהָ and אֹתָהּ carry the feminine object suffix: the dove is grammatically feminine.
  • The zaqef qaton after הַתֵּבָה divides the dove's failed search from the clause giving the reason.

'found no resting place' is the plain sense of מָנוֹחַ. The pronoun 'her' follows the Hebrew feminine; Rashi at 8:11 holds the dove was male.

Commentary (4)
Rambanfollows וְלֹֽא מָצְאָה֩ הַיּוֹנָ֨ה מָנ֜וֹחַ
Ramban: birds do not usually rest on the peaks of high mountains, where there are no trees, all the more so while water covered the face of all the earth; so the dove found no resting place that suited her. When the trees appeared she went off on her own, for doves nest in their branches.

8:10

He waited another seven days, and again he sent the dove away from the ark.

and-waited again seven-of days other and-added to-send [object-marker] the-dove from the-ark

Grammar
  • וַיֹּסֶף שַׁלַּח: a verb of adding with an infinitive means doing something again; 'he added to send' is 'he sent again'.
  • וַיָּחֶל is a hard form. Rashi: a term of waiting (לְשׁוֹן הַמְתָּנָה), as וְיִחֵלּוּ in Job 29:21. Radak: Hiphil of חול, 'wait', as וַיָּחִילוּ in Judg 3:25. Ibn Ezra prefers 'he began' (from תְּחִלָּה; compare וַיָּחֶל נֹחַ, 'Noah began', 9:20), since from תּוֹחֶלֶת he would expect וייחל or ייחל, but he allows an irregular form.
  • שִׁבְעַת יָמִים אֲחֵרִים: the number is in construct before the plural noun; אֲחֵרִים 'other' means a second week.

The English 'waited' follows Rashi and the context. The lexicon sense is the nearest the entry offers and may belong rather to יָחַל; that is a limit of the data.

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativefollows וַיָּ֣חֶל
Rashi: וַיָּחֶל is a term of waiting, like 'to me they listened and waited (וְיִחֵלּוּ)' (Job 29:21); there are many such in Scripture.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן הַמְתָּנָה, וְכֵן לִי שָׁמְעוּ וְיִחֵלּוּ (איוב כ"ט), וְהַרְבֵּה יֵשׁ בַּמִּקְרָא:
Ibn Ezranormativerecords וַיָּ֣חֶל ע֔וֹד
Ibn Ezra: in his view וַיָּחֶל comes from תְּחִלָּה, 'beginning' (he began another seven days); had it come from תּוֹחֶלֶת, 'waiting', it would be וייחל like וייקץ, or ייחל like וישב (37:1). He allows that it may be a word irregular in grammar. The English follows Rashi's 'waited' and records Ibn Ezra's 'began'.
Hebrew
ומלת ויחל עוד, על דעתי מתחלה כי אילו היתה מגזרת תוחלת היה וייחל כמו וייקץ או ייחל כמו וישב יעקב (בראשית לז א) ויתכן להיותה מלה זרה בדקדוק:
Ibn Ezranormativenot-applicable וַיֹּ֛סֶף שַׁלַּ֥ח אֶת הַיּוֹנָ֖ה מִן הַתֵּבָֽה׃
Ibn Ezra dates the sending to the twenty-fourth of Shevat; a calendar remark that does not bear on the English.

בארבעה ועשרים בשבט:

Radak: the root is חו״ל in the Hiphil, like 'they waited until they were ashamed' (Judges 3:25).

שָׁרְשׁוֹ חוּ״ל, מִבִּנְיַן הִפְעִיל, וְכֵן מִשָּׁרְשׁוֹ וּמִבִּנְיָנוֹ ״וַיָּחִילוּ עַד־בּוֹשׁ״ (שופטים ג:כה).

Onkelos: 'he waited (וְאוֹרִיךְ) another seven days and again sent the dove from the ark'.
Hebrew
וְאוֹרִיךְ עוֹד שַׁבְעָא יוֹמִין אָחֳרָנִין וְאוֹסֵיף שַׁלַּח יָת יוֹנָה מִן תֵּבוֹתָא:
Apparatus
  • וַיָּחֶל: Rashi and Radak 'he waited'; Ibn Ezra prefers 'he began (another seven days)', from תְּחִלָּה, and allows 'waited' only as an irregular form. The pack parses the form as Piel of חוּל; Radak calls it Hiphil.
8:11

The dove came to him at evening time, and there in her beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had abated from the earth.

and-came to-him the-dove at-time-of evening and-behold leaf-of olive plucked in-her-mouth and-knew Noah that lightened the-waters from-upon the-earth

Grammar
  • וְהִנֵּה turns the narration to what is seen at that moment: 'and there'.
  • טָרָף is the hard word. The pack parses it as an adjective, 'plucked' (BDB 'fresh-plucked'), and so Radak (an adjective with passive sense, like טָרוּף) and Onkelos (תְּבִיר). Rashi glosses it with the verb חָטַף, 'snatched'; Ibn Ezra prefers a verb, 'her mouth plucked (it)', with the ב of בְּפִיהָ superfluous, since verbs too can have qamets (כִּי הוּא טָרָף, Hos 6:1). Others cited by Ibn Ezra take it as a noun, 'leaf'.
  • The dove is feminine (בְּפִיהָ); Rashi, who reads the masculine form טָרָף, holds that the bird was male.
  • וַיֵּדַע נֹחַ כִּי־קַלּוּ: the verb of knowing takes a כִּי clause; קַלּוּ echoes הֲקַלּוּ of 8:8.

'freshly plucked' follows Radak and the BDB gloss; Rashi's 'snatched' (חָטַף) is close in sense. Beak is the bird's mouth. The feminine pronoun is kept.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativerecords טָרָ֣ף בְּפִ֑יהָ
Rashi: 'I say it was male', and that is why the text speaks of it sometimes in the masculine (טָרָף) and sometimes in the feminine (בְּפִיהָ): the feminine because every dove in Scripture is spoken of in the feminine (Song 5:12; Ezek 7:16; Hos 7:11). The English keeps the Hebrew's feminine 'her'.

Rashinormativefollows טָרָ֣ף
Rashi: טָרָף means 'snatched' (חָטַף); the Aggadah takes it as 'food' and בְּפִיהָ as 'speech', the dove saying that she would rather have bitter food from God than sweet from flesh and blood. The homily is not adopted.
Hebrew
חָטַף. וּמִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה (עיר' י"ח) לְשׁוֹן מָזוֹן; וְדָרְשׁוּ בְּפִיהָ לְשׁוֹן מַאֲמָר, אָמְרָה יִהְיוּ מְזוֹנוֹתַי מְרוֹרִין כְּזַיִת בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּבָּ"ה וְלֹא מְתוּקִין כִּדְבַשׁ בִּידֵי בָשָׂר וָדָם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows טָרָ֣ף בְּפִ֑יהָ
Ibn Ezra: some say טָרָף is a noun doubling עֲלֵה in sense, 'leaf' (cf. טַרְפֵּי צִמְחָהּ, Ezek 17:9), citing the qamets under the resh as in זָהָב. He holds rather that the ב of בְּפִיהָ is superfluous and טָרָף is a verb with qamets, as כִּי הוּא טָרָף (Hos 6:1), 'her mouth had plucked (it)'; or else that טָרָף is an adjective like חָכָם with a passive sense, like טָרוּף. Either way the dove tore the leaf off, which 'plucked' carries.
