גֻשְׁמָהּ" וְלֹא נִפְתְּחוּ בָּהּ מַעְיְנוֹת תְּהוֹם רַבָּה, אֲבָל הַמַּיִם נִתְפַּשְּׁטוּ בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם וְכִסּוּ כָּל הֶהָרִים הַגְּבֹהִים אֲשֶׁר תַּחַת כָּל הַשָּׁמָיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מְפֹרָשׁ (בראשית ז':י"ט), וְאֵין סְבִיב אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל גָּדֵר לְעַכֵּב הַמַּיִם שֶׁלֹּא יָבֹאוּ בָהּ. וְכָךְ אָמְרוּ בְּפִרְקֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר (פרק כג), אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יָרַד עָלֶיהָ מֵי הַמַּבּוּל מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם אֶלָּא נִתְגַּלְגְּלוּ הַמַּיִם מִן הָאֲרָצוֹת וְנִכְנְסוּ לְתוֹכָהּ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "בֶּן אָדָם אֱמָר לָהּ". וְהִנֵּה לְדַעַת רַבִּי לֵוִי מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא יָרַד בָּאָרֶץ הַהִיא הַגֶּשֶׁם הַשּׁוֹטֵף וְלֹא נִפְתְּחוּ עָלֶיהָ אֲרֻבּוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם נִשְׁאֲרוּ בָּהּ הָאִילָנוֹת, וּבְכָל הָעוֹלָם נִשְׁבְּרוּ וְנֶעֶקְרוּ בְּמַבּוּל וּמִטְרוֹת עֻזּוֹ. וַאֲנִי תָּמֵהַּ עַל מַאֲמָרָם "מִגַּן עֵדֶן", אִם כֵּן לֹא יָדַע נֹחַ שֶׁקַּלּוּ הַמַּיִם מֵעַל הָאָרֶץ, כִּי שָׁם לֹא נִכְנְסוּ מֵי הַמַּבּוּל. וְאוּלַי הָיוּ שְׁעָרָיו סְגוּרִים שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּנְסוּ שָׁם הַמַּיִם, וְכַאֲשֶׁר קַלּוּ הַמַּיִם נִפְתְּחוּ. וּמִדַּעְתָּם זוֹ אָמְרוּ שָׁם (ב"ר לו ג) "וַיִּטַּע כָּרֶם" (בראשית ט':כ') וּמֵהֵיכָן הָיָה לוֹ, אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר כָּהֲנָא בִּכְנִיסָתוֹ לַתֵּבָה הִכְנִיס עִמּוֹ זְמוֹרוֹת לִנְטִיעוֹת יִחוּרִים לִתְאֵנִים גְּרוֹפִיּוֹת לְזֵתִים:
Ramban טָרָ֣ף בְּפִ֑יהָ
Hebrew
כָּתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית ח':י"א): אוֹמֵר אֲנִי שֶׁזָּכָר הָיָה וּלְכָךְ קוֹרֵא אוֹתוֹ פְּעָמִים לְשׁוֹן זָכָר וּפְעָמִים לְשׁוֹן נְקֵבָה, לְפִי שֶׁכָּל יוֹנָה שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא לְשׁוֹן נְקֵבָה הוּא, טָרָף – חָטַף. וּמִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה לְשׁוֹן מָזוֹן, וְדָרְשׁוּ "בְּפִיהָ" לְשׁוֹן מַאֲמָר, אָמְרָה יִהְיוּ מְזוֹנוֹתַי מְרוּרִין כְּזַיִת וּבְיָדוֹ שֶׁל הקב"ה וְאַל יִהְיוּ מְתוּקִים כִּדְבַשׁ בְּיַד אָדָם. וְאֵין כָּל זֶה נָכוֹן בְּעֵינַי, כִּי חֲזָרַת זֵכֶר הַיּוֹנִים מִנְּקֵבָה לְזָכָר בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד מִן הַפָּרָשָׁה אֵין בּוֹ טַעַם, וְאִם הַלָּשׁוֹן לִקְרֹא כֻּלָּם בְּשֵׁם הַנְּקֵבוֹת לָמָּה שִׁנָּה בְּכָאן? וְכֵן מִדְרָשָׁם בַּהַגָּדָה לֹא שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ "בְּפִיהָ" לְשׁוֹן מַאֲמָר כְּלָל, אֲבָל מִדְרָשָׁם מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהֵבִיאָה הֶעָלֶה הַזֶּה, כִּי אִם נֹאמַר שֶׁאֵרַע כֵּן לֹא עַל חִנָּם פֵּרֵשׁ אוֹתוֹ הַכָּתוּב, כִּי הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר וְהִנֵּה עָלֶה טָרָף בְּפִיהָ, וְהַזַּיִת אֵינֶנּוּ בָּא מִן הָאִילָנוֹת הַגְּבוֹהִים מְאֹד שֶׁיִּשְׁכְּנוּ בּוֹ הָעוֹפוֹת לְאֹרֶךְ דָּלִיּוֹתָיו, וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ כִּי הָיָה בָּזֶה רֶמֶז, שֶׁהָעוֹפוֹת נוֹחַ לָהֶם לִהְיוֹת מְזֹנוֹתָם מָרִים כַּלַּעֲנָה בְּיַד הקב"ה וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיוּ טוֹבִים בִּידֵי אָדָם, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּנֵי הָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין רְצוֹנָם לְהִתְפַּרְנֵס זֶה מִזֶּה. וּלְשׁוֹן בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה לג ו): אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אִלּוּ מִגַּן עֵדֶן הֵבִיאָה אוֹתוֹ לֹא הָיָה לָהּ לְהָבִיא דָּבָר מְעֻלֶּה אוֹ קִנָּמוֹן אוֹ פְּפוּלְסְמוֹן, אֶלָּא רֶמֶז רָמְזָה לוֹ נֹחַ מַר מִזֶּה מִתַּחַת יָדוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְלֹא מָתוֹק מִתַּחַת יָדְךָ. אֲבָל בַּגְּמָרָא הוֹסִיפוּ (סנהדרין קח א): מֵאֵי מַשְׁמַע דְּהַאי טָרָף לִשָּׁנָא דִּמְזוֹנֵי הוּא, דִּכְתִיב (משלי ל ח) "הַטְרִיפֵנִי לֶחֶם חֻקִּי". כִּי מִפְּנֵי הַטַּעַם שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, עָשׂוּ לָזֶה סֶמֶךְ מִלְּשׁוֹן "הַטְרִיפֵנִי", יִרְמֹז כְּאִלּוּ אָמַר וְהִנֵּה עֲלֵה זַיִת טֶרֶף בְּפִיהָ. וּפְשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא פֵּרְשׁוּ בּוֹ (אונקלוס הראב"ע והרד"ק) שֶׁהוּא תֹּאַר לֶעָלֶה: וְהִנֵּה עֲלֵה זַיִת טָרוּף בְּפִיהָ. וְסֶמֶךְ לַדָּבָר, שֶׁהוּא קָמוּץ, כִּי כֵן מִשְׁפָּטוֹ. אֲבָל נִמְצָא מֵהֶם בְּזָרוּת, (הושע ו א): "כִּי הוּא טָרָף וְיִרְפָּאֵנוּ", (ויקרא ה כג): "וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת הַגְּזֵלָה אֲשֶׁר גָּזָל", (ויקרא ה יח): "עַל שִׁגְגָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר שָׁגָג", וְזוּלָתָם רַבִּים.

Apparatus
  • טָרָף: adjective 'plucked' (BDB, Radak, Onkelos תְּבִיר, and Ibn Ezra's second view); verb 'snatched, plucked' (Rashi חָטַף; Ibn Ezra's preferred view, with the ב of בְּפִיהָ superfluous); noun 'leaf' (others cited by Ibn Ezra). The Midrash cited by Rashi takes it as 'food'.
8:12

He waited another seven days and sent the dove away, and she did not return to him any more.

and-waited again seven-of days other and-sent [object-marker] the-dove and-not added to-return to-him again

Grammar
  • וַיִּיָּחֶל is Niphal (not Hithpael, which would have a patah under the yod); the root is יחל, 'wait'.
  • לֹא־יָסְפָה שׁוּב: 'she did not add to return', the same idiom of repetition as in 8:10, now negative.
  • The disjunctive accents divide the verse into three: the waiting, the sending, the result.
  • The two forms וַיָּחֶל (8:10) and וַיִּיָּחֶל (8:12) differ in stem but say the same.

The dove's failure to return is not explained in the text; Radak reads it as the dove finding rest.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּיָּ֣חֶל
Rashi: this is the same as וַיָּחֶל but in a reflexive stem: the first is 'he waited', the second 'he was patient'.

הוּא לְשׁוֹן וַיָּחֶל, אֶלָּא שֶׁזֶּה לְשׁוֹן וַיִּפְעַל וְזֶה לְשׁוֹן וַיִּתְפַּעֵל, וַיָּחֶל – וַיַּמְתֵּן; וַיִּיָּחֶל – וַיִּתְמַתֵּן:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיִּיָּ֣חֶל
Ibn Ezra: a Niphal form, as in וַיִּלָּחֶם and וַיִּצָּמֶד; the root is complete with the yod.

8:13

In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first of the month, the waters dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and there the surface of the ground had dried up.

and-it-was in-one and-six hundreds year in-the-first on-one of-the-month dried-up the-waters from-upon the-earth and-removed Noah [object-marker] covering-of the-ark and-saw and-behold dried-up face-of the-ground

Grammar
  • The date is given in Hebrew order: year, month, day. 'the first' (הָרִאשׁוֹן) is the first month; the day is 'one' (אֶחָד), used for 'the first'.
  • חָרְבוּ הַמַּיִם and חָרְבוּ פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה: the verb חרב (dry up) is used of the waters and then of the surface of the ground; in 8:14 the verb is the stronger יבשׁ.
  • וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה: 'he saw, and behold': a narrative view of what Noah saw when the cover was open.
  • The telisha gedola on וַיְהִי is a prepositive disjunctive accent, printed at the start of the word and again on the stressed syllable; it sets וַיְהִי apart from the date that follows.

The first month is Tishrei or Nisan (Rashi: R. Eliezer or R. Joshua). The text says only 'first'. The English keeps חרב as 'dried up' and יבשׁ in 8:14 as 'dry', following Rashi and Ibn Ezra on the difference.

Grammar
  • The date: month (the second), day (seven and twenty) of the month.
  • יָבְשָׁה הָאָרֶץ: the verb comes first and the subject, 'the earth', follows; the stem is Qal of יבשׁ.
  • The etnaḥta falls on לַחֹדֶשׁ, setting the date apart from the main clause.
  • The paragraph mark ס closes the section of the Flood's end.

The verse uses יבשׁ, 'be dry', and not חרב as in 8:13; the English contrasts 'had dried up' with 'was dry' following Rashi's 'completely dry' (גָּרִיד כְּהִלְכָתָהּ).

Grammar
  • וַיְדַבֵּר is a Piel wayyiqtol; the merkha is on the verb, the tipḥa on אֱלֹהִים.

Grammar
  • צֵא is the imperative of יצא with the first radical dropped; the tipḥa on it and the etnaḥta on הַתֵּבָה divide the command from the list of those who go.
  • The list pairs each man with his wife: 'you and your wife', then 'your sons and your sons' wives'. In 6:18 and 7:7 the men and the women are listed in separate groups on entering; here the couples are paired, the point Rashi and Radak draw from the verse. The accents divide the list step by step: the zaqef gadol on אַתָּה sets 'you' apart, the tipḥa on בָנֶיךָ sets off אִתָּךְ, and the tevir on וְאִשְׁתְּךָ divides 'and your wife' from the sons and their wives.
  • The construct plural נְשֵׁי־בָנֶיךָ is 'wives of your sons'.

The wording is plain. The couples are named together here, unlike the entry (6:18, 7:7), which Rashi and Radak take as the point of the verse.

Grammar
  • The object (כָּל־הַחַיָּה ...) comes before the verb הַיְצֵא; the zaqef and revia divide the long object from its specification, and the etnaḥta closes the command.
  • הַיְצֵא is read (qere) as a Hiphil imperative; the ketiv הוצא is the same form spelled with a vav in place of the yod.
  • The three weqatal verbs וְשָׁרְצוּ וּפָרוּ וְרָבוּ follow the imperative and give the purpose of the going out; the echo of 1:22 and 9:1 is clear.
  • רֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ is a figura etymologica, 'creeping thing that creeps'.

The ketiv/qere is kept in the token note. Following Ibn Ezra's grammar (הַיְצֵא like הַשְׁלֵם, a Hiphil), the English uses 'Bring out'. For וְשָׁרְצוּ the English follows Ibn Ezra's gloss יולידו 'let them bear young', which Radak (רבוי התולדה) and Onkelos (ויתילדון) share, and on which Rashi's deduction about the ark rests: 'breed abundantly' keeps both the teeming of שׁרץ and the bearing of young. The literal line keeps 'swarm'.

Grammar
  • The wayyiqtol וַיֵּצֵא reports the carrying out of the command; the verb is singular with Noah as its subject, and the others are added after it.
  • The order here is Noah, his sons, his wife, his sons' wives: men first, then women, unlike the paired order of 8:16.
  • אִתּוֹ 'with him' (silluq) closes the verse.

The verb is singular with Noah as its subject; the others are added as accompanying him. The English 'with' reflects that.

Grammar
  • The verb יָצְאוּ stands near the end, after a long compound subject; the etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ closes the subject, and within it the revia, pashta and zaqef qaton set off its parts. The zaqef qaton on לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתֵיהֶם belongs to the second half of the verse, with the verb.
  • כֹּל רוֹמֵשׂ עַל־הָאָרֶץ is an absolute כֹּל with a participle: 'everything creeping on the earth', summing up the groups before it.
  • לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתֵיהֶם: the preposition ל means 'by' or 'according to'; משפחה is usually 'clan', here the species.

For לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתֵיהֶם the English follows the sense on which Ibn Ezra (כמו למינם) and Rashi (לִדָּבֵק בְּמִינָן) agree, with Radak's 'each kind by itself': 'by their kinds'. Rashi adds that the animals left on the condition of keeping to their own kind. Ibn Ezra also records that some say they bred in the ark and that each family went out without mixing with another, which he calls not far-fetched. On that reading the word would mean 'families' in the literal sense.

Grammar
  • The sequence of wayyiqtol verbs (וַיִּבֶן, וַיִּקַּח, וַיַּעַל) reports Noah's acts one after another.
  • מִכֹּל is partitive: he took only some of each clean kind, not all of them.
  • The adjectives הַטְּהֹרָה and הַטָּהוֹר agree in gender with בְּהֵמָה (feminine) and עוֹף (masculine).
  • The pashta after מִכֹּל and the zaqef qaton after הַטָּהוֹר set the two lists apart.

The English 'offered burnt offerings' keeps the Hebrew's plural עֹלֹת. The orthography הַטְּהֹרָה and הַטָּהוֹר (WLC reads הַטְּהוֹרָה and הַטָּהֹר) is only spelling.

Apparatus
  • 8:20.4 vowels: WLC reads לַֽיהוָ֑ה; base לַֽיהֹוָ֑ה.
  • 8:20.8 spelling: WLC reads הַטְּהוֹרָ֗ה; base הַטְּהֹרָ֗ה.
  • 8:20.11 spelling: WLC reads הַטָּהֹ֔ר; base הַטָּה֔וֹר.

8:21

The LORD smelled the soothing aroma, and the LORD said to himself, "I will never again curse the ground because of the human, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth; and I will never again strike down every living thing as I have done."

and-smelled the-LORD (object-marker) scent-of the-soothing and-said the-LORD to his-heart not I-will-add to-curse again (object-marker) the-ground on-account-of the-human for formation-of heart-of the-human evil from-his-youth and-not I-will-add again to-strike (object-marker) all-of living as-which I-did

Grammar
  • The verse has two clauses of narration (וַיָּרַח, וַיֹּאמֶר) and then God's speech: two parallel vows, each opening לֹא־אֹסִף ... עוֹד, with a reason (כִּי ...) set between them.
  • אֹסִף is a Hiphil imperfect of יסף; with an infinitive it means 'I will do again', so לֹא אֹסִף לְקַלֵּל is 'I will not again curse'.
  • The segolta on הַנִּיחֹחַ (printed twice in this edition) closes the first clause, with the zarqa (zinor) on יְהֹוָה as a lesser divider within it. The etnaḥta on מִנְּעֻרָיו divides the verse: the first vow and its reason stand before it, and the second vow after it. The telisha gedola on אֹסִף and on כִּי is a minor disjunctive.
  • יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם is a construct chain: 'the formation of the human heart'; the adjective רַע is the predicate, and מִנְּעֻרָיו 'from his youth' modifies it.
  • The repeated אֹסִף עוֹד in two clauses is what Rashi takes as an oath.

The notes follow Ibn Ezra on the grammar: וַיָּרַח is a figure of speech (the offering was accepted, as one smells a pleasing scent); אֶל־לִבּוֹ means 'with/to his heart', that is 'to himself'; לְקַלֵּל is a curse on the ground that came through man (cf. 3:17); יֵצֶר is what was formed in the human. For מִנְּעֻרָיו Rashi reads the defective spelling (מנעריו כְּתִיב) as from נִנְעַר 'shaken out' (from birth) and Ramban records both 'from the beginning of youth' and 'because of youth'; the English keeps the plain 'from his youth'. The quoted speech is set in double quotation marks in the English only.

Apparatus
  • 8:21 Ramban and Rashi read מנעריו differently: Rashi as 'from the shaking out of the womb', Ramban as 'from the beginning of youth' or 'because of youth'.
8:22

For as long as the earth lasts, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night will never cease.

still all-of days-of the-earth seed and-harvest and-cold and-heat and-summer and-winter and-day and-night not they-cease

Grammar
  • עֹד כָּל־יְמֵי הָאָרֶץ is a time clause, 'all the days of the earth still', with the etnaḥta marking its end; the plural verb יִשְׁבֹּתוּ at the end governs all the pairs.
  • The eight nouns stand in four pairs of opposites: sowing and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, then day and night. Every noun after the first takes vav; in the second member of three pairs it is pointed וָ (וָחֹם, וָחֹרֶף, וָלַיְלָה), which binds the pair closely.
  • יִשְׁבֹּתוּ is the Qal of שׁבת 'to cease'; the same root gives the Sabbath, 'the ceasing'.
  • The unusual accents (pazer, telisha gedola, qadma) give the list a slow, rhythmical delivery.

Rashi divides the year into six seasons of two months each (half Tishri to half Kislev for sowing, and so on); Ibn Ezra divides the year first in two (sowing and harvest) and then in four (cold and heat, summer and winter), which also fits the Hebrew pairs. The English keeps the six nouns as the Hebrew pairs them. 'For as long as the earth lasts' keeps כָּל־יְמֵי הָאָרֶץ, which Ibn Ezra reads as showing that the earth has an appointed end.

9:1

God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth."

and-blessed God [object-marker] Noah and-[object-marker] his-sons and-said to-them be-fruitful and-multiply and-fill [object-marker]-the-earth

Grammar
  • The blessing is three imperatives: פְּרוּ, וּרְבוּ, וּמִלְאוּ.
  • The etnaḥta on בָּנָיו divides the narration from the speech.
  • וַיְבָרֶךְ is a Piel wayyiqtol; the verb of blessing takes the object marker twice, for Noah and for his sons.

The blessing repeats the language of 1:28 to the new beginning after the flood.

Commentary (3)
Radaknot-applicable וַיְבָ֣רֶךְ אֱלֹהִ֔ים
Radak: though they were blessed at the creation, the world was now renewed after being tohu va-vohu under water; the blessing is 'be fruitful and multiply', and their fear and dread (9:2).
Hebrew

Targum Onkelosnot-applicable the whole verse
Onkelos renders 'and the LORD blessed Noah and his sons and said to them: be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth', following the Hebrew closely.
Hebrew
וּבָרִיךְ יְיָ יָת נֹח וְיָת בְּנוֹהִי וַאֲמַר לְהוֹן פּוּשׁוּ וּסְגוּ וּמְלוּ יָת אַרְעָא:
9:2

The fear and dread of you shall be upon every animal of the earth and upon every bird of the sky, upon everything that crawls on the ground and upon all the fish of the sea; into your hand they are given.

and-fear-of-you and-dread-of-you shall-be upon every-living-thing-of the-earth and-upon every-bird-of the-sky in-all that crawls the-ground and-in-all-fish-of the-sea in-your-hand they-are-given

Grammar
  • וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם וְחִתְּכֶם is a pair of near synonyms, 'fear' and 'dread'. The suffix -כֶם is objective: the fear felt of you, not the fear you feel.
  • The mahpakh on וּמוֹרַאֲכֶם is conjunctive and joins the two nouns; the pashta on וְחִתְּכֶם and the zaqef on יִהְיֶה are disjunctive and close the subject and then the verb.
  • בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תִּרְמֹשׂ הָאֲדָמָה: the verb is feminine. Ibn Ezra gives two readings: 'on the ground' (the English), with an unstated feminine subject, or 'the ground' as the subject itself.
  • נִתָּנוּ is a Niphal perfect: the creatures have been given into human hands.

בְּכֹל is rendered 'upon' in step with the preceding עַל. Ibn Ezra offers two ways to take הָאֲדָמָה (place, or acting subject) and prefers to join בְּכֹל to מוֹרַאֲכֶם; the English takes the place sense and keeps the ordinary clause order.

Commentary (17)
Rashinormativefollows וְחִתְּכֶם֙

9:3

Every moving thing that is alive shall be food for you; as with the green plants, I have given you everything.

every-moving-thing that it living to-you shall-be for-food like-green-of plant I-gave to-you [object-marker] all

Grammar
  • The clause אֲשֶׁר הוּא חַי ('that it is alive') identifies the רֶמֶשׂ as living creatures.
  • The perfect נָתַתִּי is a performative-sounding perfect, 'I have given', set against the earlier grant of plants.
  • יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב refers back to the plants given as food in 1:29–30.

The English takes כְּיֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב as the standard of comparison, the plants already given, in line with Rashi.

9:4

Only flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat.

only flesh in-its-life its-blood not you-shall-eat

Grammar
  • אַךְ restricts the grant of v. 3 with a single exception.
  • בְּנַפְשׁוֹ דָמוֹ: the two nouns are bare in apposition, with no conjunction between them.
  • The negative with the yiqtol, לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ, is a prohibition.

The English keeps the Hebrew order and the bare apposition נַפְשׁוֹ דָמוֹ, as Ibn Ezra reads it: 'with its life, which is its blood'. Rashi reads דָמוֹ as a second object (blood from a living animal) besides the limb from a living animal; his reading is recorded.

9:5

But your blood, for your lives, I will demand; from every animal I will demand it, and from the human, from each man for his brother, I will demand the life of the human.

and-yet [object-marker] your-blood for-your-lives I-will-require from-hand-of every-living-thing I-will-require-it and-from-hand-of the-human from-hand-of man his-brother I-will-require [object-marker] life-of the-human

Grammar
  • The object, אֶת דִּמְכֶם, is fronted for emphasis and set against the earlier permission.
  • The verb דָּרַשׁ comes three times: אֶדְרֹשׁ, אֶדְרְשֶׁנּוּ (with the energic nun and the suffix 'it'), אֶדְרֹשׁ.
  • The etnaḥta on אֶדְרְשֶׁנּוּ divides the verse: the first half states the demand for your blood and names the animal; the second names the human and narrows to 'each man ... his brother'.
  • מִיַּד means 'from the hand of', an idiom for 'from, at the hands of'.

The English keeps the sense Ibn Ezra gives (any blood of yours is not permitted; I will require it) rather than Rashi's limit to suicide. מִיַּד אִישׁ אָחִיו is rendered 'from each man for his brother', leaving 'brother' as a fellow human.

Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְאַ֨ךְ אֶת דִּמְכֶ֤ם
Ibn Ezra: 'I have permitted you to shed the blood of every living thing except your blood, the blood of your persons, for you are human: that I have not permitted, but I will require it.' Then he spells it out: from the human, whether many kill one or one kills one; and from every animal, in that I will command another animal to kill it, for the animals are permitted to you, not you to them. He calls the reading of 'your blood for your lives' as one who kills himself forced, and adds that v. 6 may be a command to the sons of Noah to kill the killer, which he calls right.

9:6

Whoever sheds the blood of the human, by the human his blood shall be shed; for in the image of God He made the human.

shedder-of blood-of the-human in-the-human his-blood it-shall-be-shed for in-image-of God he-made [object-marker] the-human

Grammar
  • The verse is poetic: a chiasm of shedder and shed, blood and human, with a sound-play on שֹׁפֵךְ and יִשָּׁפֵךְ.
  • The participle שֹׁפֵךְ opens a casus pendens, resumed by דָּמוֹ.
  • בָּאָדָם can mean 'by a human (agent)' or 'for the sake of the human'.
  • The clause כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם gives the ground for the penalty. It is a verbal clause: בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים is fronted before עָשָׂה, whose subject is not named (Rashi: 'the Maker').

The English follows decisions (the human, with the article). 'By the human' is the plain agent reading; the other readings are kept in the commentary entries.

9:7 · ס

As for you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm over the earth and multiply in it.

and-you be-fruitful and-multiply swarm in-the-earth and-multiply in-it

Grammar
  • The independent pronoun וְאַתֶּם sets 'you' apart: for Ramban, from the other living creatures told to swarm and multiply in 8:17; the midrash Rashi cites sets the command beside the shedder of blood in v. 6.
  • Four imperatives close the speech: פְּרוּ, רְבוּ, שִׁרְצוּ, רְבוּ.
  • The etnaḥta on וּרְבוּ divides the verse into the repeated blessing and the new commands.
  • שִׁרְצוּ is the verb used of swarming creatures in 1:20-21 and 8:17.

Genesis 1:28 and 9:1 give the same words as a blessing; here they are in the form of a command.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows וְאַתֶּ֖ם פְּר֣וּ וּרְב֑וּ
Rashi: on the plain sense, the first (9:1) is a blessing and here a command; by midrash, the one who does not engage in procreation is likened to one who sheds blood (Yevamot 63b).

9:8

Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him:

and-said God to-Noah and-to-sons-of-him with-him to-say

Grammar
  • וַיֹּאמֶר is a wayyiqtol, the narrative tense; the subject אֱלֹהִים follows the verb.
  • The pashta on אֱלֹהִים and zaqef on נֹחַ divide the address: God, then Noah, then the sons.
  • לֵאמֹר (lamed + infinitive construct) is the standard introduction to quoted speech.
  • אִתּוֹ 'with him' is the form of אֵת with a suffix; it is distinct from the object marker אֵת.

The English omits לֵאמֹר, rendered by the colon. אֱלֹהִים is plural in form with a singular verb, as always for the God of Israel; 'God' per decisions.

9:9

As for me, I am establishing my covenant with you and with your offspring after you,

and-I behold-me establishing [object-marker] covenant-of-me with-you and-[with] seed-of-you after-you

Grammar
  • The independent pronoun וַאֲנִי is emphatic and contrasts God's act with the human task of the preceding verse.
  • הִנְנִי מֵקִים: הִנֵּה with a suffix plus a participle presents the act as happening now or about to happen ('I am establishing').
  • מֵקִים is a hifil participle of קום; הֵקִים אֶת בְּרִית is the idiom 'to establish a covenant'.
  • זֶרַע is a collective singular: 'seed' means all descendants.

The 'covenant' is God's one-sided promise, spelled out in 9:11.

and with every living creature that is with you, among the birds, among the livestock, and among every animal of the earth that is with you, from all that came out of the ark, to every animal of the earth.

Grammar
  • The object marker is absent: וְאֵת is the preposition 'with', continuing the covenant 'with' of 9:9.
  • The beth of בָּעוֹף and בַּבְּהֵמָה means 'among' or 'of': birds and livestock specify the living creatures.
  • מִכֹּל יֹצְאֵי הַתֵּבָה and לְכֹל חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ extend the list beyond those that are 'with you'; the comments below take them as additions.
  • The long verse is divided by etnaḥta after the second אִתְּכֶם, with the final clause set apart as an extension.

Rashi reads the two final clauses as including what the first part leaves out; the English follows, keeping the Hebrew's repetition. נֶפֶשׁ הַחַיָּה: 'living creature'.

9:11

I will establish my covenant with you: never again will any flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth.

and-I-will-establish [obj] covenant-of-me with-you and-not will-be-cut-off all flesh again from-waters-of the-flood and-not will-be again flood to-destroy the-earth

Grammar
  • The promise has two negated clauses: flesh will not be cut off, and no flood will ever again destroy the earth.
  • וַהֲקִמֹתִי is a weqatal with future sense, tied to 9:9.
  • מִמֵּי הַמַּבּוּל: the min marks the cause or means by which flesh would be cut off.
  • לְשַׁחֵת is a piel infinitive construct in a purpose clause: 'a flood meant to destroy'.

בָּשָׂר is rendered 'flesh', as the commentators take it as body. The weqatal is rendered as a plain future.

Grammar
  • זֹאת is feminine, while אוֹת is of both genders, as Ibn Ezra notes.
  • בֵּין is repeated before each party, as the idiom for 'between X and Y' requires.
  • אֲנִי נֹתֵן with a participle states the act in progress.
  • לְדֹרֹת is written defectively (without a vav), a point Rashi draws a lesson from.

First use of אוֹת in the story. 'Sign' because the commentators' sense is a mark of the covenant.

כְּטַעַם "עֵד הַגַּל הַזֶּה וְעֵדָה הַמַּצֵּבָה" (בראשית ל"א:נ"ב), וְכֵן "כִּי אֶת שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת תִּקַּח מִיָּדִי בַּעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה לִּי לְעֵדָה" (בראשית כ"א:ל'), כִּי כָל הַדָּבָר הַנִּרְאֶה שֶׁיּוּשַׁם לִפְנֵי שְׁנַיִם לְהַזְכִּירָם עִנְיָן נָדוּר בֵּינֵיהֶם יִקָּרֵא אוֹת, וְכָל הַסְכָּמָה – בְּרִית. וְכֵן בַּמִּילָה אָמַר "וְהָיָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵיכֶם" (בראשית י"ז:י"א) בַּעֲבוּר הַהַסְכָּמָה שֶׁיִּמּוֹלוּ כָּל זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם לְעָבְדוֹ שְׁכֶם אֶחָד. וְעוֹד כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר תֵּרָאֶה בַּהִפּוּךְ הַנִּזְכָּר יִהְיֶה זֵכֶר לְשָׁלוֹם כַּאֲשֶׁר כָּתַבְנוּ. וּבֵין שֶׁתִּהְיֶה הַקֶּשֶׁת עַתָּה בֵּין שֶׁהָיְתָה מֵעוֹלָם בַּטֶּבַע, הַטַּעַם בָּאוֹת שֶׁבָּהּ אֶחָד הוּא. אֲבָל יֵשׁ לְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ בַּפָּרָשָׁה הַזֹּאת סוֹד נֶעֱלָם, אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (בראשית רבה ל"ה:ג'), "אֶת קַשְׁתִּי נָתַתִּי בֶּעָנָן", קַשּׁוֹתִי, דָּבָר שֶׁהוּא מוֹקֵשׁ לִי. אֶפְשָׁר כֵּן, אֶלָּא קָשִׁין דְּפִרְיָא. "וְהָיָה בְּעַנְנִי עָנָן", רַבִּי יוּדָן בְּשֵׁם ר' יְהוּדָה בֵּר' סִימוֹן אוֹמֵר, מָשָׁל לְאֶחָד שֶׁבְּיָדוֹ סֹלֶת רוֹתֵחַ וּבִקֵּשׁ לִתְּנוֹ עַל בְּנוֹ, וּנְתָנוֹ עַל עַבְדּוֹ. וְשָׁם עוֹד, "וְהָיְתָה הַקֶּשֶׁת בֶּעָנָן וּרְאִיתִיהָ לִזְכֹּר בְּרִית עוֹלָם בֵּין אֱלֹהִים", זוֹ מִדַּת הַדִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה, "וּבֵין כָּל נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה בְּכָל בָּשָׂר אֲשֶׁר עַל הָאָרֶץ", זוֹ מִדַּת הַדִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה, מִדַּת הַדִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה קָשָׁה, וּמִדַּת הַדִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה רָפָה. וּכְבָר יָדַעְתָּ מַאֲמָרָם (חגיגה טז) בַּמִּסְתַּכֵּל בַּקֶּשֶׁת, כָּל שֶׁלֹּא חָס עַל כְּבוֹד קוֹנוֹ רָאוּי לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם. וְאִם זָכִיתָ לְהָבִין דִּבְרֵיהֶם תֵּדַע כִּי פֵּרוּשׁ הַכָּתוּב כֵּן, אֶת קַשְׁתִּי שֶׁהִיא מִדַּת הַדִּין הַנְּתוּנָה בֶּעָנָן בְּעֵת הַדִּין תִּהְיֶה לְאוֹת בְּרִית:

9:13

I have now set my bow in the cloud, and it will become a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.

Grammar
  • The object אֶת קַשְׁתִּי is placed first for emphasis; נָתַתִּי is a perfect.
  • קַשְׁתִּי 'my bow' has the suffix of God, a word picture that the commentators discuss.
  • וְהָיְתָה לְ is the idiom 'it shall become'.
  • בֵּינִי וּבֵין הָאָרֶץ: the earth, not only the people, is a party; verse 12 had 'every living creature'.

The perfect נָתַתִּי is a point on which the commentators divide: Ibn Ezra says the bow is newly set now; Radak records Saadya, for whom it was set in nature at creation and is now made a sign. The English follows Ibn Ezra.

and-will-be in-my-clouding cloud over the-earth and-will-be-seen the-bow in-the-cloud

Grammar
  • וְהָיָה ... וְנִרְאֲתָה: two weqatals; 'and it will be (when) ... and it will be seen'.
  • בְּעַנְנִי עָנָן pairs a denominative verb with its cognate noun, which Radak takes as strengthening the action.
  • The first nun is light (no dagesh), though the piel calls for one, as Ibn Ezra and Radak note.
  • The nifal נִרְאֲתָה with the bow as subject means 'appear' or 'be seen'; Radak adds 'to humans'.

The cognate pair is rendered by a plain English plural.

9:15

I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and between every living creature among all flesh, and never again will the waters become a flood to destroy all flesh.

and-I-will-remember [obj] covenant-of-me which between-me and-between-you and-between every being living in-all flesh and-not will-be again the-waters for-flood to-destroy all flesh

Grammar
  • זָכַר of God is anthropomorphic: Radak says Scripture speaks in human language, since there is no forgetting before the throne of glory.
  • The verb יִהְיֶה is singular and its subject הַמַּיִם is plural. Ibn Ezra says the singular verb does not prove that מַיִם is singular, since a singular verb can come before a plural subject, as in וַיְהִי אֲנָשִׁים (Numbers 9:6).
  • The clause לֹא יִהְיֶה ... לְמַבּוּל: 'the waters will not become a flood'.
  • The etnaḥta on the first בָּשָׂר divides the verse: the covenant and its parties, then the promise. In the first half the revia on בְּרִיתִי and the zaqef on וּבֵינֵיכֶם set off the parties.

Closes the section by returning to 'flesh' and 'destroy' of 9:11, framing it.

9:16

The bow will be in the cloud, and I will see it, to remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living being, among all flesh that is on the earth.

and-will-be the-bow in-the-cloud and-I-will-see-it to-remember covenant-of everlasting between God and-between all-of being living in-all-of flesh that on the-earth

Grammar
  • וְהָיְתָה and וּרְאִיתִיהָ are weqatal forms that carry on the future promise.
  • בֵּין ... וּבֵין is the usual 'between ... and' pattern: the preposition is repeated before each member.
  • אֱלֹהִים stands where the first person is expected (compare 9:17 בֵּינִי); Rashi and Radak take this as meaningful.
  • The etnaḥta on בֶּעָנָן and the zaqef on עוֹלָם and אֱלֹהִים divide the verse into the bow, the seeing, and the covenant partners.

The English keeps 'God' in the third person, as the Hebrew does. Rashi's midrash (the attribute of justice above) is recorded, not adopted. Ibn Ezra's reading (the bow is always in the cloud, unseen by people, seen by God) agrees with the English 'will be in the cloud ... I will see it'. 'Living being' renders נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה.

9:17 · פ

God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."

Grammar
  • זֹאת אוֹת־הַבְּרִית is a verbless clause: 'this (is) the sign of the covenant'.
  • הֲקִמֹתִי is a Hiphil perfect, 1st person singular; the relative אֲשֶׁר takes it as 'that I have established'.
  • The speech now uses the first person (בֵּינִי), in contrast to the third person of 9:16.
  • The etnaḥta on נֹחַ and the zaqef gadol on בֵּינִי mark the introduction, the sign, and the covenant partners.

The paragraph mark (פ) after this verse closes the covenant speech.

The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham was the father of Canaan.

and-were sons-of Noah the-coming-out from-the-ark Shem and-Ham and-Japheth and-Ham he father-of Canaan

Grammar
  • וַיִּהְיוּ is a wayyiqtol of הָיָה with a plural subject; the predicate is the list 'Shem, Ham and Japheth'.
  • הַיֹּצְאִים is a participle with the article, 'those who came out'; the participle describes a completed event.
  • וְחָם הוּא אֲבִי כְנָעַן is a nominal clause with a pronoun copula, opening a new thought; the etnaḥta on וָיָפֶת marks a break after the list.
  • The note on Canaan prepares the story of 9:22-27.

The sentence on Canaan interrupts the list; Rashi gives its reason.

9:19

These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the whole earth was dispersed.

three these sons-of Noah and-from-these was-scattered all-of the-earth

Grammar
  • שְׁלֹשָׁה אֵלֶּה בְּנֵי־נֹחַ is a verbless clause with the number first, for emphasis: 'three, these, were the sons of Noah'.
  • נָפְצָה is a Qal perfect, 3rd feminine singular; the subject is the earth, meaning its peoples.
  • The verb comes before its subject, as in much narrative.
  • The etnaḥta on נֹחַ divides the verse in two.

Radak notes that נָפַץ is intransitive in the Qal (compare 1 Samuel 13:11), so the English uses a passive-intransitive 'was dispersed'. He reads the dispersal as the one after the generation of the Division (Babel).

9:20

Noah, a man of the soil, began and planted a vineyard.

and-began Noah man-of the-soil and-planted vineyard

Grammar
  • וַיָּחֶל is a Hiphil wayyiqtol of חלל, 'begin' (BDB Hiph 2); the same root in the Niphal and Piel means 'profane', which gives the wordplay Rashi uses.
  • Two wayyiqtol verbs in a row, 'began' and 'planted', mean 'began to plant' (Radak).
  • אִישׁ הָאֲדָמָה is a construct chain: 'man of the soil', a farmer.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאֲדָמָה separates the description of Noah from the planting.

The English keeps both verbs, 'began and planted', since the Hebrew does; the reading 'began to plant' is Radak's. Rashi's reading of וַיָּחֶל as 'made himself profane' (חֻלִּין), because he should have planted something else first, is recorded, not adopted. 'Man of the soil' is read as an expert farmer (Ibn Ezra), not 'master of the soil' (Rashi), a reading Ramban rejects.

9:21

He drank some of the wine, became drunk, and uncovered himself inside his tent.

and-drank from-the-wine and-became-drunk and-uncovered-himself in-midst-of his-tent

Grammar
  • Three wayyiqtol verbs narrate the sequence: וַיֵּשְׁתְּ 'drank', וַיִּשְׁכָּר 'became drunk', וַיִּתְגַּל 'uncovered himself'.
  • וַיֵּשְׁתְּ and וַיִּתְגַּל are short (apocopated) wayyiqtol forms of verbs whose last root letter is ה; compare the full forms יִשְׁתֶּה and יִתְגַּלֶּה.
  • וַיִּתְגַּל is a Hitpael of גלה: the ת of the stem is kept, and the doubled ל of the full form is simplified at the end of the word. The stem is reflexive (Ibn Ezra; Rashi 'לשון ויתפעל').
  • אָהֳלֹה is spelled with a final ה where the pronominal suffix 'his' is normally written וֹ; the word means 'his tent'.
  • The etnaḥta on וַיִּשְׁכָּר marks the break between the drinking and the exposure.

'Uncovered himself' is the reflexive reading; the passive 'was uncovered' (Radak: 'of himself', that is, without being forced) is the same sense. The spelling אהלה is read by Ibn Ezra and Radak as אָהֳלוֹ, ה for ו. Rashi's reading, a hint of the ten tribes called Oholah, is a midrash and is recorded, not adopted.

9:22

Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside.

and-saw Ham father-of Canaan [object-marker] nakedness-of his-father and-told to-two-of his-brothers in-the-outside

Grammar
  • וַיַּרְא ... וַיַּגֵּד are two wayyiqtol verbs with the same subject, Ham.
  • אֲבִי כְנַעַן is an apposition naming Ham; it explains why Canaan is cursed later.
  • אֵת marks the definite object עֶרְוַת אָבִיו, 'the nakedness of his father' (a construct chain).
  • לִשְׁנֵי־אֶחָיו is 'to two of his brothers', a construct dual; the revia on וַיַּרְא and the etnaḥta on אָבִיו divide the clauses.

'Nakedness' keeps the ambiguity of עֶרְוָה, which can be literal exposure or a sexual euphemism. Rashi records two rabbinic readings, that Canaan did the seeing and told his father, and that Ham castrated or sodomized Noah; neither is adopted, as the plain sense (Radak) is that Ham saw and mocked.

9:23

Shem and Japheth took the garment and laid it on both their shoulders, and they walked backward and covered their father's nakedness, and their faces were backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.

and-took Shem and-Japheth [object-marker] the-garment and-put on shoulder-of both-of-them and-walked backward and-covered [object-marker] nakedness-of their-father and-their-faces backward and-nakedness-of their-father not they-saw

Grammar
  • וַיִּקַּח is singular though the subject is 'Shem and Japheth', so the verb agrees with the nearer name (Rashi finds a lesson in this); the next verb וַיָּשִׂימוּ is plural.
  • עַל־שְׁכֶם שְׁנֵיהֶם is a construct chain with a singular noun: 'on the shoulder of the two of them'. Ibn Ezra explains the singular: each put part of the garment on his own shoulder.
  • אֲחֹרַנִּית is an adverb, 'backwards'; it occurs twice, in the verb clause and in the verbless clause.
  • וְעֶרְוַת אֲבִיהֶם לֹא רָאוּ puts the object first, for contrast with the covering.

'Both their shoulders' follows Ibn Ezra: each brother took part of the garment on his own shoulder. The repeated אֲחֹרַנִּית is kept; Rashi reads the second as the turning of their faces when they had to approach. Rashi's midrash on the singular וַיִּקַּח (Shem exerted himself more) is recorded, not adopted; Radak takes the singular as a plain idiom, like Exodus 6:10.

9:24

Noah woke from his wine and learned what his youngest son had done to him.

and-awoke Noah from-his-wine and-knew [obj] what-he-did to-him his-son the-small

Grammar
  • וַיִּיקֶץ and וַיֵּדַע are wayyiqtols that carry the narrative on from the drunkenness of 9:21.
  • אֵת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה is an object marker with a relative clause: 'what he had done'.
  • הַקָּטָן is an adjective with the article after a noun with a suffix, so the pair is definite: 'his small son'.
  • The etnaḥta after מִיֵּינוֹ divides the verse into the waking and the knowing.

הַקָּטָן is ambiguous: 'small', so 'youngest', or 'lesser, despised'. Ibn Ezra reads בְּנוֹ הַקָּטָן as Canaan, the youngest of Ham's sons (10:6), the suffix of בְּנוֹ referring to Ham; the English 'his youngest son' follows him and leaves 'his' open. Rashi reads הַקָּטָן as 'the unfit and despised' (Jeremiah 49:15), not of age; in his reading (see his comment on 9:25) the son is Ham. Radak, if the son is Ham, also takes הַקָּטָן as 'the lesser', since Ham was not the youngest. The text does not say what was done (Ibn Ezra).

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativerecords בְּנ֥וֹ הַקָּטָֽן׃
Rashi: בנו הקטן means the unfit and despised one, as in 'Behold, I have made you small among the nations, despised among men' (Jeremiah 49:15). The English keeps the plain sense 'youngest' and records this.
Hebrew
הַפָּסוּל וְהַבָּזוּי, כְּמוֹ הִנֵּה קָטֹן נְתַתִּיךָ בַּגּוֹיִם בָּזוּי בָּאָדָם (ירמיה מ"ט):
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיִּ֥יקֶץ נֹ֖חַ
Ibn Ezra: Scripture does not reveal what was done; the doer was Canaan, since Ham saw and did not cover him as his brothers did but made the matter known, and Canaan heard. The English leaves the deed unstated.
Hebrew
, הכתוב לא גילה מה נעשה. והעושה היה כנען וכן היה כי חם ראה ולא כסהו כאשר עשו אחיו רק גלה הדבר ושמע כנען ולא נדע מה עשה,

To say that Noah cursed his grandson because God had blessed his sons is the way of derash. The English 'his youngest son' leaves room for this reading.

9:25

He said, "Cursed be Canaan; a slave among slaves shall he be to his brothers."

and-said cursed Canaan slave-of slaves he-will-be to-his-brothers

Grammar
  • אָרוּר כְּנַעַן is a verbless curse: passive participle then the subject.
  • עֶבֶד עֲבָדִים is a construct chain of the same noun without the article. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'a slave like one of the slaves'; with the article it would mean 'slave of the slaves', as קֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים (Exodus 26:33) differs from קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים (Leviticus 6:18).
  • יִהְיֶה is imperfect, not the short jussive יְהִי, but in a curse the sense is a wish or decree.
  • The etnaḥta under כְּנָעַן divides the curse from its content.

The English 'a slave among slaves' follows Ibn Ezra, the normative commentator on these words: עֶבֶד עֲבָדִים means 'a slave like one of the slaves'; 'slave of the slaves' would need the article. Radak reads 'slave to slaves': his brothers will be slaves too and he a slave to them, the more so to the sons of Shem and Japheth; Sforno reads a degree of servitude added for his sin. For לְאֶחָיו Ibn Ezra names Cush, Egypt and Put, Ham's sons; Rashi has Canaan serve the seed of Shem and Japheth.

Commentary (7)
Rashinormativerecords אָר֣וּר כְּנָ֑עַן
Rashi: Noah says to Ham, 'You caused me not to father another, fourth son to serve me; cursed be your fourth son, to serve the seed of these elder ones (Shem and Japheth), on whom the burden of serving me now falls.' And what led Ham to castrate him? He told his brothers that Adam had two sons and one killed the other for the inheritance of the world, and our father has three and still seeks a fourth. 'His brothers' are then Shem and Japheth; the English 'his brothers' leaves this open.

9:26

He said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem, and may Canaan be a slave to them."

and-said blessed the-LORD God-of Shem and-let-be Canaan slave to-them

Grammar
  • בָּרוּךְ יְהֹוָה is a verbless blessing formula; the passive participle precedes the subject.
  • אֱלֹהֵי שֵׁם: the construct of אֱלֹהִים is plural in form but governs a singular sense.
  • וִיהִי is a jussive, so 'may he be'; the wish repeats in 9:27.
  • לָמוֹ is a poetic form of the plural suffix: 'to them'.

לָמוֹ is ambiguous. Ibn Ezra reads 'to them' as God and Shem: Canaan will be a slave to Him and to Shem, compelled to serve; Sforno likewise, to the God of Shem and to Shem's seed. Rashi and Radak take it as Shem's descendants. The English keeps 'to them' so that the antecedent stays open.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: וַאֲמַר בְּרִיךְ יְיָ אֱלָהֵהּ דְּשֵׁם וִיהֵי כְנַעַן עַבְדָא לְהוֹן.
9:27

May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem; and may Canaan be a slave to them.

may-he-enlarge God to-Japheth and-let-dwell in-tents-of Shem and-let-be Canaan slave to-them

Grammar
  • יַפְתְּ is a hifil jussive of פתה, 'make wide', shortened from יַפְתֶּה: the final ה falls away and the word ends in two consonants, with dagesh lene in the ת, as in יַרְדְּ (Isaiah 41:2, cited by Ibn Ezra and Radak). The verb plays on the name יֶפֶת.
  • The Hebrew has no object marker after אֱלֹהִים; the preposition ל marks Japheth: 'make wide for Japheth'.
  • The pashta and zaqef qaton set אֱלֹהִים apart as the subject of the first wish.
  • The refrain וִיהִי כְנַעַן עֶבֶד לָמוֹ repeats 9:26 word for word.

The subject of וְיִשְׁכֹּן is not named. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak agree that it is God, who will dwell in the tents of Shem (Rashi: rest His Presence on Israel), and Onkelos renders 'may He make His Presence dwell'; the English 'he' continues the subject of the first wish, God. Rashi's midrash: though Cyrus, a descendant of Japheth, built the Second Temple, the Presence rested only in the First, built by Solomon of Shem. Sforno reads the tents of Shem as houses of study.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativefollows יַ֤פְתְּ אֱלֹהִים֙ לְיֶ֔פֶת
Rashi: the Targum renders יַפְתֵּי, 'may He enlarge'. The English follows this sense.
Hebrew
מְתֻרְגָּם יַפְתֵּי, יַרְחִיב:
Rashinormativefollows וְיִשְׁכֹּ֖ן בְּאׇֽהֳלֵי שֵׁ֑ם
Rashi: He (God) will rest His Presence on Israel. The Sages' midrash: although God enlarged Japheth, for Cyrus, of Japheth's line, built the Second Temple, the Presence did not rest in it; it rested in the First Temple, built by Solomon of Shem's line. The English 'he' takes God as the subject.

Rashinormativefollows וִיהִ֥י כְנַ֖עַן עֶ֥בֶד לָֽמוֹ׃
Rashi: even after the sons of Shem go into exile, slaves from Canaan's sons will be sold to them. The English 'a slave to them' fits.
Hebrew
אַף מִשֶּׁיִּגְלוּ בְנֵי שֵׁם יִמָּכְרוּ לָהֶם עֲבָדִים מִבְּנֵי כְּנַעַן:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows יַ֤פְתְּ
Ibn Ezra: יפת comes from יפה but means 'may He enlarge', like Deuteronomy 12:20, as in Aramaic, a hifil like 'and kings He subdues' (Isaiah 41:2); in this verse God blesses Japheth and Shem, since 'dwell in the tents of Shem' means God dwells in them, for the first verse blessed God. The English 'enlarge' follows.

9:28

After the flood Noah lived three hundred and fifty years.

and-lived Noah after the-flood three hundred year and-fifty year

Grammar
  • וַיְחִי is the wayyiqtol of חיה in its short form, for וַיִּחְיֶה.
  • The number is in two parts, each followed by the singular noun: שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה וַחֲמִשִּׁים שָׁנָה, 'three hundred year and fifty year'; שָׁנָה is repeated after each part.
  • מַבּוּל is used of the flood only, here with the article.
  • The etnaḥta under הַמַּבּוּל separates the time marker from the number.

The English puts 'after the flood' at the head of the sentence; the literal keeps the Hebrew order.

Radak: the number of years is given to show when the world began again, for every generation; the counter knows it from the Torah's count and from the prophets.

9:29 · פ

All the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.

and-were all-of days-of Noah nine hundred year and-fifty year and-died

Grammar
  • כָּל־יְמֵי־נֹחַ is a construct chain of three words, the subject of וַיִּהְיוּ.
  • The plural verb agrees with יְמֵי, 'days'.
  • The closing וַיָּמֹת is the formula that ends each life in the genealogy.
  • A paragraph break follows, marked פ.

The total, nine hundred and fifty, is the sum of the six hundred years before the flood and the three hundred and fifty after.

10:1

These are the descendants of Noah's sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth: children were born to them after the flood.

and-these generations-of sons-of Noah Shem Ham and-Japheth and-were-born to-them sons after the-flood

Grammar
  • תּוֹלְדֹת is a construct plural: the account of a man's descendants.
  • The etnaḥta on וָיָפֶת divides the verse: the list of names, then the new clause.
  • וַיִּוָּלְדוּ is a Niphal wayyiqtol, passive 'were born'.

The English joins the two clauses with a colon, since the second states what follows from the first.

Commentary (6)
Rambannot-applicable the whole verse
Ramban's comment here is cut off in the pack and does not bear on the plain sense.

וְטַעַם

Ramban: men of those generations begot at about sixty, yet Noah's sons had no children even by a hundred, only after the flood; God restrained their fertility so that they would not beget children who would perish in the flood, or so that He would not have to save many in the ark. He did the same with the whole line (Lamech and Noah were late fathers), as Rashi cites from Bereshit Rabbah.

Grammar
  • Kittim has no ו before it: the etnaḥta on וְתַרְשִׁישׁ divides the four names into two pairs, Elishah and Tarshish, then Kittim and Dodanim, each pair joined by ו inside it.

The lexicon links the last name to רוֹדָנִים (Rhodians), reflecting the parallel reading in Chronicles. The data is kept; the English follows the Hebrew of this verse.

וּבְנֵי יָוָן אֶלִישָׁה וְתַרְשִׁישׁ כִּתִּים וְדֹדָנִים:
Apparatus

10:5

From these the coastlands of the nations were separated in their lands, each according to its language, by their clans, in their nations.

from-these were-divided coasts-of the-nations in-their-lands man to-his-language to-their-clans in-their-nations

Grammar
  • מֵאֵלֶּה, 'from these', points back to the sons of Japheth just listed; the clause closes the list of Japheth's line.
  • נִפְרְדוּ is a Niphal perfect, 3rd plural, of פרד: 'were separated, spread apart'. Hebrew puts the verb before its subject אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם; the English puts the subject first.
  • אִיֵּי is the construct plural of אִי, 'coast, coastland, island'.
  • אִישׁ is distributive: 'each one'.
  • The four ב/ל phrases (lands, language, clans, nations) qualify the separation; the etnaḥta on לִלְשֹׁנוֹ divides them two and two.

The English renders אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם literally, 'the coastlands of the nations' (lexicon: coast, region). The peoples who settled them are implied: Ramban takes the sons of Japheth as dwellers in the islands of the sea, each apart in his own land, and Radak takes אִיִּים as districts set apart from one another.

Hebrew
כִּי בְּנֵי יֶפֶת יוֹשְׁבֵי אִיֵּי הַיָּם, וְהֵם נִפְרָדִים כָּל אֶחָד מִבָּנָיו בְּאִי אַחֵר יוֹשֵׁב לְבַדּוֹ, וְאַרְצֹתָם רְחוֹקוֹת זוֹ מִזּוֹ, וְהִיא בִּרְכַּת אֲבִיהֶם שֶׁאָמַר "יַפְתְּ אֱלֹהִים לְיֶפֶת", שֶׁיִּהְיוּ רַבִּים בְּמֶרְחֲבֵי אֶרֶץ. אֲבָל בְּנֵי חָם כֻּלָּם קְרוֹבִים יוֹשְׁבֵי הָאֲרָצוֹת, וְלָכֵן אָמַר "וַיְהִי גְּבוּל הַכְּנַעֲנִי מִצִּידֹן" וְגוֹ' (בראשית י':י"ט), וְאָמַר "בְּאַרְצֹתָם בְּגוֹיֵהֶם" (בראשית י':כ'), וְכֵן בִּבְנֵי שֵׁם. וְסִפֵּר הַכָּתוּב כָּל אֵלֶּה כִּי רָצָה לְהוֹדִיעַ יִחוּס אַבְרָהָם מִשֵּׁם וְתוֹלְדוֹת חָם, לְהוֹדִיעַ הָעַמִּים שֶׁזָּכָה אַבְרָהָם בְּאַרְצָם בַּעֲוֹן אֲבוֹתָם. וְלָכֵן סִפֵּר גַּם בְּיֶפֶת וְהַפַּלָּגָה, לְהוֹדִיעַ סִבַּת שִׁנּוּי הַלְּשׁוֹנוֹת וּפִזּוּרָם בְּקַצְוֵי הָאָרֶץ לִזְמַן מוּעָט אַחֲרֵי אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן. וְעוֹד, לְהוֹדִיעַ חַסְדֵי הַשֵּׁם וְשָׁמְרוֹ הַבְּרִית לְנֹחַ, כִּי לֹא כִּלָּה אוֹתָם. וְהָרַב אָמַר בְּמוֹרֶה הַנְּבֻכִים (ג נ) כִּי זֶה יְאַמֵּת לַשּׁוֹמְעִים חִדּוּשׁ הָעוֹלָם. וְגַם זֶה אֱמֶת, כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ יְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו וְאֶת בֵּיתוֹ אַחֲרָיו, וְיָעִיד לָהֶם עַל נֹחַ וּבָנָיו שֶׁרָאוּ הַמַּבּוּל וְהָיוּ בַּתֵּבָה, וְהִנֵּה הוּא עֵד מִפִּי עֵד בְּעִנְיַן כָּל הַמַּבּוּל וְעֵד רְבִיעִי עַל יְצִירָה, כִּי נֹחַ רָאָה אָבִיו שֶׁרָאָה אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, וְיִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב רָאוּ שֵׁם הָעֵד בַּמַּבּוּל, וְיַעֲקֹב מַגִּיד כָּל זֶה לְיוֹרְדֵי מִצְרַיִם גַּם לְפַרְעֹה וְאַנְשֵׁי דּוֹרוֹ, וְהָאֲנָשִׁים בְּכָל דּוֹר יוֹדְעִים מֵאֲבוֹתָם אַרְבָּעָה וַחֲמִשָּׁה דּוֹרוֹת מַגִּידִים מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם וְתוֹלְדוֹתֵיהֶם:

10:8

Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be a mighty man on the earth.

and-Cush begot [object-marker] Nimrod he began to-be mighty in-the-earth

Grammar
  • הוּא הֵחֵל is a fronted subject pronoun, giving emphasis: 'he, he began'.
  • גִּבֹּר is an adjective used as a noun: 'a mighty man'.
  • The etnaḥta on נִמְרֹד divides the statement of birth from the description.

The English keeps 'began' for הֵחֵל and leaves open in what his might lay. Ibn Ezra: he began to show human might over the beasts, being a mighty hunter (10:9). Rashi: his might was to make the whole world rebel against God by the counsel of the generation of the Dispersion; this is recorded. Radak warns that the verse does not say no one was mighty before him, since the Nephilim were.

10:9

He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; therefore it is said, Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD.

he-was mighty-of hunting before the-LORD on-so it-is-said like-Nimrod mighty-of hunting before the-LORD

Grammar
  • גִּבֹּר־צַיִד is a construct chain: 'mighty one of hunting'.
  • יֵאָמַר is nifal imperfect: 'it will be said', a proverbial formula, here with the saying quoted after כְּ.
  • The etnaḥta on יְהוָה divides the verse into the statement about Nimrod and the proverb it explains.
  • The saying repeats the first half, with כְּנִמְרֹד replacing הוּא הָיָה.

The Hebrew leaves the sense of לִפְנֵי יהוה open. The English keeps the words and does not choose. Rashi reads it as defiance: Nimrod trapped people's minds with his words and led them to rebel, and 'before the LORD' means he meant to provoke Him to His face. Ibn Ezra, calling his reading the plain sense, takes it that he built altars and offered the game as burnt offerings to God. Radak and Sforno read it as an intensifier ('exceedingly mighty'). Ramban quotes Rashi and the Sages and rejects Ibn Ezra, but his own reading is that Nimrod was the first to rule over men by force, a hunter of beasts as well, with 'before the LORD' as hyperbole: none under heaven was his equal in might. Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that 'it is said' introduces a proverb.

, הוּא הַגְדָּלַת הַגְּבוּרָה, כִּי כֵן מִנְהַג הַלָּשׁוֹן כְּשֶׁמְּגַדְּלִים הַדָּבָר סוֹמֵךְ אוֹתוֹ לָאֵל, כְּמוֹ ״עִיר גְּדוֹלָה לֵאלֹהִים״ (יונה ג:ג) ״כְּהַרְרֵי אֵל״ (תהלים לו:ז) ״וַעֲנָפֶיהָ אַרְזֵי אֵל״ (תהלים פ:יא) ״שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה״ (שיר השירים ח:ו) ״מֵאַפְלֵיָה״ (ירמיהו ב:לא). וְיֵשׁ מְפָרֵשׁ (אבן עזרא) שֶׁהָיָה צָד הַחַיּוֹת וּמַקְרִיבָם לִפְנֵי ה׳, וְדַעַת אֻנְקְלוֹס נוֹטָה לְפֵרוּשֵׁנוּ שֶׁתִּרְגֵּם ״גְּבַר תַּקִּיף״.

Sforno עַל כֵּן֙ יֵֽאָמַ֔ר כְּנִמְרֹ֛ד גִּבּ֥וֹר צַ֖יִד

וּלְשֵׁמַע גְּבוּרָתוֹ מָלַךְ בַּגּוֹיִם כְּאָמְרוֹ:
Apparatus
  • Onkelos renders גִּבֹּר צַיִד as גִּבַּר תַּקִּיף, 'a mighty man', with no word for hunting, and לִפְנֵי יְהוָה as קֳדָם יְיָ, 'before the LORD'. Radak takes this rendering as support for his reading of the verse as praise of Nimrod's might.
10:10

The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Akkad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

and-was beginning-of his-kingdom Babel and-Erech and-Akkad and-Calneh in-land-of Shinar

Grammar
  • וַתְּהִי is feminine because it agrees with the subject רֵאשִׁית, not with the predicate list.
  • The list is joined with ו before each name after the first; the English uses commas and a final 'and'.
  • The etnaḥta falls after כַּלְנֵה and sets בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר apart as the location of all four.

The pronominal suffix of מַמְלַכְתּוֹ refers to Nimrod, the subject of verses 8 to 9. No normative comment is anchored to this verse.

Commentary (3)
Radak וַתְּהִ֨י רֵאשִׁ֤ית מַמְלַכְתּוֹ֙ בָּבֶ֔ל
Hebrew
וּמָלַךְ עָלֶיהָ וְאַחַר כָּךְ כָּבַשׁ אֶרֶךְ אַכַּד וְכַלְנֵה, שֶׁאַרְבַּעְתָּם בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר, אוֹ אַרְבַּעְתָּם כְּבָשָׁן בַּתְּחִלָּה וְאַחַר כָּךְ כָּבַשׁ מְדִינוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת שֶׁלֹּא נִזְכְּרוּ.
Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וַהֲוָה רֵישׁ מַלְכוּתֵיהּ בָּבֶל וְאֶרֶךְ וְאַכַּד וְכַלְנֵה בְּאַרְעָא דְבָבֶל:
Sforno וַתְּהִ֨י רֵאשִׁ֤ית מַמְלַכְתּוֹ֙ בָּבֶ֔ל
Hebrew
וְזֶה לְהוֹדִיעַ שֶׁבִּימֵי מַלְכוּתוֹ קָרָה, כְּשֶׁבָּאוּ הָאֻמּוֹת בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר שֶׁנֶּעֶשְׂתָה הַמְצָאַת הָעִיר וְהַמִּגְדָּל, כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּתְפַּשֵּׁט מַלְכוּתוֹ עַל כָּל הַמִּין הָאֱנוֹשִׁי בְּאֶמְצָעוּת אֵל נֵכָר כְּלָלִי לְכָל הַמִּין, אֵלָיו גּוֹיִם יִדְרֹשׁוּ, כְּעִנְיַן עֲצַת יָרָבְעָם כַּאֲשֶׁר יָרֵא דְּרִישַׁת הַמִּקְדָּשׁ (מלכים א יב:כו).
10:11

From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah,

from-the-land the-that went-out Asshur and-he-built (object-mark) Nineveh and (object-mark) Rehoboth Ir and (object-mark) Calah

Grammar
  • מִן־הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא is placed before the verb, so the departure from Shinar is emphasised.
  • אַשּׁוּר is a personal name here (the subject of וַיִּבֶן), though it is also the name of the land.
  • Each city is marked with אֶת; the repeated אֶת־ divides the list.
  • The merkha on רְחֹבֹת and tipḥa on עִיר show the two words are read together.

אַשּׁוּר may be read as the land (to Asshur he went out, i.e. 'he went out to Assyria', Ramban). The English takes it as the person who went out, as Rashi and Ibn Ezra do. Whether עִיר is part of the name Rehoboth-Ir or means 'the wide streets of the city' (that is, of Nineveh) is left open. The final comma leaves the list to continue into verse 12.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows מִן הָאָ֥רֶץ
Rashi: when Asshur saw his sons obey Nimrod and rebel against God by building the tower, he left their midst. The English follows in taking Asshur as the subject who went out from that land.
Hebrew
כֵּיוָן שֶׁרָאָה אַשּׁוּר אֶת בָּנָיו שׁוֹמְעִין לְנִמְרוֹד וּמוֹרְדִין בַּמָקוֹם לִבְנוֹת הַמִּגְדָּל יָצָא מִתּוֹכָם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: Asshur is a son of Japheth (sic, in the text as printed); this was after the division of the earth, and Nimrod was the first king over Babel. The English follows in taking Asshur as a person who left; Ramban's reading of the verb as 'Nimrod went out to Asshur' is not adopted.

Ramban מִן הָאָ֥רֶץ הַהִ֖וא
Hebrew
בְּמָלְכוֹ עָלֶיהָ, "יָצָא אַשּׁוּר", פִּתְרוֹנוֹ יָצָא אֶל אַשּׁוּר, כִּי אַשּׁוּר מִבְּנֵי שֵׁם הָיָה, וְזֶהוּ כִּלְשׁוֹן "וְיָצָא חֲצַר אַדָּר וְעָבַר עַצְמֹנָה" (במדבר לד ד), "וַיֵּצֵא עוֹג מֶלֶךְ הַבָּשָׁן לִקְרָאתֵנוּ אֶדְרֶעִי" (דברים ג א), "וְיָשֹׁב אַרְצוֹ בִּרְכוּשׁ גָּדוֹל" (דניאל יא כח), וְרַבִּים כֵּן. וּלְכָךְ תִּקָּרֵא אֶרֶץ אַשּׁוּר "אֶרֶץ נִמְרֹד" כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (מיכה ה ה) "וְרָעוּ אֶת אַשּׁוּר בַּחֶרֶב וְאֶת אֶרֶץ נִמְרֹד בִּפְתָחֶיהָ" וְ"אֶרֶץ נִמְרוֹד" יִרְמֹז אֶל נִינְוֵה וְאֶל רְחוֹבוֹת עִיר וְאֶל כָּלַח. וְסִפֵּר עוֹד בִּגְבוּרָתוֹ כִּי הוּא גִּבּוֹר צַיִד לְהִתְגַּבֵּר גַּם עַל הַחַיּוֹת וְלָצוּד אוֹתָן. וְאָמַר "לִפְנֵי ה'", לְהַפְלִיג כִּי אֵין תַּחַת כָּל הַשָּׁמַיִם כָּמוֹהוּ בִּגְבוּרָה. וְכֵן "וַתִּשָּׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים" (בראשית ו':י"א), כִּי כָל אֲשֶׁר לְפָנָיו בָּאָרֶץ נִשְׁחֲתוּ, כְּעִנְיָן "וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִיא מִלְּפָנַי" (ויקרא כב ג), כִּי בְּכָל מָקוֹם הוּא לְפָנָיו:

מֵאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר יָצָא אַשּׁוּר. וְלֹא זָכַר בּוֹ מִי הָיָה, אוּלַי מִבְּנֵי חָם לְפִי שֶׁזְּכָרוֹ עִם בְּנֵי חָם, אוֹ הָיָה בֶּן שֵׁם. כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״בְּנֵי שֵׁם עֵילָם וְאַשּׁוּר״ (בראשית י:כב) וְזֶהוּ הַקָּטָן, וּמַה שֶּׁזְּכָרוֹ הֵנָּה עִם סִפּוּר בְּנֵי חָם, אוּלַי יָשַׁב אַשּׁוּר בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר אַחַר שֶׁגָּדַל וְהִתְגַּבֵּר עַל מֶלֶךְ הָאָרֶץ הַהִיא שֶׁהָיָה נִמְרֹד אוֹ אֶחָד מִבָּנָיו וְלָקַח הַמְּלוּכָה מִיָּדוֹ, כִּי מִן הַדּוֹמֶה כִּי הוּא לָקַח הַמְּלוּכָה מִיַּד נִמְרֹד אוֹ מִיַּד זַרְעוֹ וּמָלַךְ עַל כָּל הָאָרֶץ, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר

, יָצָא מֵאַרְצוֹ מִי שֶׁלָּקַח הַמְּלוּכָה מִיָּדוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה גִּבּוֹר, אוֹ מִיַּד זַרְעוֹ, וְנִקְרָא הָאָרֶץ אַשּׁוּר עַל שְׁמוֹ, כִּי מָצָאנוּ כִּי מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר מָלַךְ עַל בָּבֶל וְעַל כָּל הָאָרֶץ הַהִיא. גַּם בְּנֵי חָם גֹּרְשׁוּ מִשָּׁם וְהָיְתָה לִבְנֵי כֶּשֶׂד שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ כַּשְׂדִּים וְהֵם מִבְּנֵי שֵׁם. וְכָל הַסִּפּוּר הַזֶּה לְהוֹדִיעַ כִּי הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ לַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלֹא בְכֹחַ יִגְבַּר אִישׁ, וְנוֹטֵל מַלְכוּת הָאָרֶץ מִזֶּה וּנְתָנָהּ לָזֶה כַּאֲשֶׁר יָשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וּנְתַתִּיהָ לַאֲשֶׁר יָשָׁר בְּעֵינַי״ (ירמיהו כז:ה) וְהַכֹּל לְפִי מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם כִּי הוּא אֵל אֱמוּנָה וְאֵין עָוֶל. וְאֶפְשָׁר כִּי לְעִיר מְיֻחֶדֶת שֶׁבָּנָה אַשּׁוּר קָרָא שְׁמָהּ אַשּׁוּר כִּשְׁמוֹ, אוֹ לְכָל הָאָרֶץ הַהִיא כִּי מָצָאנוּ ״בֹּאֲכָה אַשּׁוּרָה״ (בראשית כה:יח), מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר, מַלְכֵי אַשּׁוּר (מלכים ב יט:יא) לְפִיכָךְ יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת שֵׁם עִיר אוֹ שֵׁם הָאָרֶץ. וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יומא י) תָּנֵי רַב יוֹסֵף: אַשּׁוּר, זֶה סְלִיק.

Apparatus
  • Ramban takes Nimrod as the subject of 'went out' and אַשּׁוּר as his destination, 'he went out to Asshur', since Asshur was of the sons of Shem (10:22). He cites verbs of motion with a bare accusative of the goal, without ה of direction (Num 34:4; Deut 3:1), and Micah 5:5, which calls Assyria 'the land of Nimrod'. Radak takes Asshur as the subject, of Ham or of Shem.
10:12

and Resen, between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.

and (object-mark) Resen between Nineveh and-between Calah she the-city the-great

Grammar
  • בֵּין is repeated before each term, as normal in Hebrew.
  • הִוא הָעִיר הַגְּדֹלָה is a verbless clause; the feminine pronoun agrees with עִיר.
  • The etnaḥta after כָּלַח separates this clause from the preceding list.
  • The grammar does not fix the pronoun's antecedent: Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as Nineveh, the first city built (10:11); Ibn Ezra allows Resen or Calah; Radak takes it as Resen, the city the verse is speaking of.

The antecedent of הִוא is ambiguous. Rashi takes it as Nineveh, citing Jonah 3:3; Ibn Ezra prefers Nineveh and allows Resen or Calah. Radak, against 'most commentators', takes it as Resen. The English keeps the pronoun as 'that' and does not name the city; the reading of the normative commentators, Nineveh, is the one the edition takes.

and-Egypt he-fathered (object-mark) Ludim and (object-mark) Anamim and (object-mark) Lehabim and (object-mark) Naphtuhim

Grammar
  • The subject מִצְרַיִם comes before the verb, which begins the genealogy of Ham's son.
  • All four names are plural gentilics in -ִים, so they name peoples, not single persons.
  • The pazer on מִצְרַיִם and the gershayim on יָלַד are disjunctive. In the list the tevir on עֲנָמִים and the tipḥa on לְהָבִים divide the names; the darga on לוּדִים is conjunctive and binds it to the next word.
  • The list continues in verse 14.

Ibn Ezra's observation that these are all plural (names of regions, each region a family) means 'fathered' is used loosely of peoples. The English keeps 'fathered' and the plural names, with the Hebrew name Mizraim given as Egypt per decisions.

Apparatus
  • The BDB entry glosses נַפְתֻּחִים as 'the northern land' and כַּפְתֹּרִי as 'Cretans'; these are data from the lexicon, not decisions of the English.
10:14 · ס

the Pathrusim, the Casluhim, from whom the Philistines came, and the Caphtorim.

and (object-mark) Pathrusim and (object-mark) Casluhim which went-out from-there Philistim and (object-mark) Caphtorim

Grammar
  • אֲשֶׁר ... מִשָּׁם is a relative clause with a resumptive adverb: 'which ... from there'.
  • The relative clause may attach to Pathrusim and Casluhim together or only to the second; the revia on כַּסְלֻחִים closes the pair.
  • The Philistines follow the verb as subject: 'went out from there, the Philistines'.
  • The verse ends the Mizraite list with Caphtorim, set after the parenthesis.

The relative clause is ambiguous in attachment. Rashi takes it as 'from both', the Philistines coming from the Pathrusim and Casluhim together; the English leaves the antecedent as the pair. The Caphtorim stand after the parenthesis. Ibn Ezra says that Mizraim fathered the Caphtorim too, and explains why ילד is said of a father: the son comes from the father's vigour and strength, in his image and likeness.

Apparatus

10:15

Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth.

and-Canaan begot [object-marker] Sidon his-firstborn and-[object-marker] Heth

Grammar
  • The verb יָלַד, with a man as subject, means 'beget'; the objects are marked by אֶת.
  • בְּכֹרוֹ stands in apposition to צִידֹן and is set off by the tipḥa.
  • The waw on וּכְנַעַן is a simple connective with the preceding sons of Ham.

The ancestor-name Canaan is also the ethnic name; the English keeps the name. Ramban's discussion of how the ten peoples relate to the land promised to Abraham is a historical comment, not about the words.

בִּימֵי אַבְרָהָם, כִּי בְּכָאן נִכְתְּבוּ בַּשֵּׁם שֶׁקְּרָאָם אֲבִיהֶם בְּיוֹם הִוָּלְדָם, וְאַחֲרֵי שֶׁנִּפְרְדוּ בְּאַרְצֹתָם לְגוֹיֵיהֶם נִקְרְאוּ בְּשֵׁמוֹת אֲחֵרִים, אוּלַי הֶעֱלוּ לָהֶם שֵׁם עַל שֵׁם הָאָרֶץ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁפֵּרַשְׁנוּ (רמב"ן על בראשית י':י"ג), וְכֵן "שֵׂעִיר הַחוֹרִי" (בראשית ל"ו:כ'), שֵׁם הָעִיר שֵׂעִיר, וְכֵן רַבִּים. אוֹ שֶׁהוֹלִידוּ הָעַרְקִי וְהַסִּינִי מִשְׁפָּחוֹת וְנִכְרְתוּ מֵהֶם, וּבְנֵיהֶם הָיוּ קֵינִי וּקְנִזִּי עַל דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל, וְהָיוּ לְרָאשֵׁי בָּתֵּי אָבוֹת, תִּקָּרֵא הָאֻמָּה בִּשְׁמָם, כַּנָּהוּג בְּשִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל. וְהִנֵּה קְרָאָם בַּשֵּׁם שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם בִּימֵי אַבְרָהָם בְּמַתְּנָתוֹ. וּרְאָיָה לַדָּבָר כִּי הַחִוִּי הַנִּזְכָּר בְּכָאן אֵינֶנּוּ נִזְכַּר בְּמַתְּנָתוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם, וְהוּא הָיָה מֵהֶם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דברים ז א) "וְנָשַׁל גּוֹיִם רַבִּים מִפָּנֶיךָ הַחִתִּי וְהַגִּרְגָּשִׁי וְהָאֱמֹרִי וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי וְהַחִוִּי וְהַיְבוּסִי שִׁבְעָה גוֹיִם", וְכֵן בְּכָל מָקוֹם, וְיִמְנֶה הַכְּנַעֲנִי עִם בָּנָיו וְלֹא יִמְנֶה בָּהֶן רַק עֲשָׂרָה, כִּי אֶחָד מִבָּנָיו לֹא גָּבַר כְּאֶחָיו וְנִקְרָא עִם אֶחָיו בְּשֵׁם אָבִיו. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁהָיָה צִידוֹן בְּכוֹרוֹ הַנִּקְרָא "כְּנַעֲנִי" עִם אֶחָד מֵאֶחָיו שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לְגוֹי. וְאַל יִקְשֶׁה עָלֶיךָ אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים שֶׁהָיְתָה לְאַבְרָהָם, כְּדִכְתִיב (בראשית כ"ו:ג') "גּוּר בָּאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת כִּי לְךָ וּלְזַרְעֲךָ אֶתֵּן אֶת כָּל הָאֲרָצֹת הָאֵל", וְהֵם מִבְּנֵי מִצְרַיִם, כִּי הַכָּתוּב אָמַר "לַכְּנַעֲנִי תֵּחָשֵׁב חֲמֵשֶׁת סַרְנֵי פְלִשְׁתִּים" (יהושע יג ג), כִּי כָּבְשׁוּ מִקְצָת הָאָרֶץ וְיָשְׁבוּ בָּהּ, וּבְכָאן תִּרְאֶה כִּי גְּבוּל הַכְּנַעֲנִי מִצִּידוֹן בֹּאֲכָה גְרָרָה עַד עַזָּה, וְאֵלֶּה עָרֵי פְּלִשְׁתִּים כִּי אֲבִימֶלֶךְ מֶלֶךְ גְּרָר וְעַזָּה לָעַזָּתִי הִיא, וְכֵן "לְעַזָּה אֶחָד" (שמואל א ו יז), וְצִידוֹן Hebrew

10:18

the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites spread out.

and-[object-marker] the-Arvadite and-[object-marker] the-Zemarite and-[object-marker] the-Hamathite and-afterward were-scattered clans-of the-Canaanite

Grammar
  • The etnaḥta on הַחֲמָתִי ends the list of Canaan's sons; a new sentence begins with וְאַחַר.
  • נָפֹצוּ is Niphal qatal of פוץ, 'were scattered' (in the sense of spreading out); the subject מִשְׁפְּחוֹת follows the verb.
  • Word order here is verb, then subject.

Radak reads 'afterward' as after the division of the peoples (הַפַּלָּגָה, the dispersion at Babel); Rashi does not give the time, only that many clans spread out from these peoples. The English 'afterward' leaves the time open, and Radak's reading is recorded.

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativefollows וְאַחַ֣ר נָפֹ֔צוּ
Rashi: from these peoples many clans were scattered. The English takes the subject as the clans of the Canaanites spreading out.

and-was border-of the-Canaanite from-Sidon as-you-come Gerar-ward as-far-as Gaza as-you-come Sodom-ward and-Gomorrah and-Admah and-Zeboiim as-far-as Lasha

Grammar
  • בֹּאֲכָה is an infinitive construct of בוא with the long form of the 2nd person masculine singular suffix (-כָה for -ךָ), 'your coming'; it works as an idiom 'as you come to', 'in the direction of'.
  • The directional he on גְרָרָה and סְדֹמָה means 'to Gerar', 'to Sodom'.
  • The etnaḥta on עַזָּה divides the verse in two: the line from Sidon toward Gerar as far as Gaza, then the line toward Sodom and the cities with it as far as Lasha. Within each half the zaqef qaton and the gershayim mark lesser breaks.
  • Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim are listed with a waw on each of the last three.

בֹּאֲכָה, literally 'your coming', is rendered 'toward'. Ibn Ezra glosses בֹּאֲכָה גְרָרָה as אֶל גְּרָר, 'to Gerar'; Rashi takes the word as a verbal noun and explains it as a man telling his friend that the border reaches until you come to the border of a given place. The two readings agree, and the English follows both.

10:20 · ס

These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, in their nations.

these sons-of Ham to-their-clans to-their-tongues in-their-lands in-their-nations

Grammar
  • A nominal clause: אֵלֶּה is the subject, בְנֵי־חָם the predicate.
  • The four phrases with ל and ב give the divisions of Ham's descendants.
  • The paragraph mark (ס) closes the section on the sons of Ham.

The prepositions ל and ב are rendered 'by' and 'in' for a smooth English line.

10:21

Children were born to Shem also, the father of all the sons of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder.

and-to-Shem was-born also he father-of all sons-of Eber brother-of Japheth the-elder

Grammar
  • יֻלַּד is a Pual perfect 3ms with no stated subject; Radak says it is general, 'children were born'.
  • גַּם־הוּא 'he also': the line resumes Shem after the sons of Ham and Japheth have been listed (Ramban).
  • אֲבִי כָּל־בְּנֵי־עֵבֶר is a construct chain of four nouns, 'father-of all-of sons-of Eber': the first three are in the construct state and only עֵבֶר is absolute.
  • הַגָּדוֹל after Japheth is ambiguous in the Hebrew: it can describe Japheth or Shem.
  • The etnaḥta on הוּא divides the verse: the first half says that Shem had children; the second gives two titles of Shem, 'father of all the sons of Eber' and 'brother of Japheth the elder', set apart by the zaqef on עֵבֶר. Silluq closes the verse on הַגָּדוֹל.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take 'the elder' to describe Japheth (Noah was five hundred when he began to beget and Shem was a hundred two years after the flood), so the English follows them. Ramban and Radak allow it to describe Shem; recorded in the apparatus. Eber is taken as the personal name, so 'sons of Eber' are his descendants. The pack gives sense Pu for יֻלַּד and no sense fits גָּדוֹל here ('elder' in age), so none is given.

Rashi: I do not know whether 'the elder' is Japheth or Shem. Since Shem was a hundred years old two years after the flood and Noah was five hundred at the first birth, the eldest son was a hundred at the flood, so 'the elder' is Japheth.

Apparatus
  • עֵבֶר: the man Eber of 10:24-25, whose descendants are the Hebrews (Ibn Ezra), or the land beyond the River, עֵבֶר הַנָּהָר, whose people all descend from Shem (Rashi, Ramban).
  • הַגָּדוֹל: Japheth the elder (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, most commentators) or Shem the elder brother of Japheth (Ramban, Radak, and some cited by Ibn Ezra).

The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram.

Grammar
  • A verbless list: the construct בְּנֵי governs שֵׁם, and the five names stand in apposition.
  • The etnaḥta on אַשּׁוּר sets Elam and Asshur apart from the other three.

Names are given in their usual English forms.

10:23

The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash.

Grammar
  • The opening ו continues the genealogy and is not translated.
  • The etnaḥta on אֲרָם separates the head of the family from the list.

Radak notes that the line begins with the youngest son, Aram, because it ends with him, and that 1 Chronicles 1:17 has מֶשֶׁךְ for מַשׁ.

Commentary (2)
Radaknot-applicable וּבְנֵ֖י אֲרָ֑ם
Radak: the descendants begin with the youngest, Aram, because the list of Shem's sons ended with him. Those of Elam, Asshur and Lud are not given, as there was no need; Aram's are, perhaps because Terah's family married into Aram's line, so that Nahor named his firstborn Uz and a grandson Aram. For Mash, Chronicles has Meshech.

10:24

Arphaxad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber.

and-Arphaxad begot [object-mark] Shelah and-Shelah begot [object-mark] Eber

Grammar
  • The object marker אֶת־ introduces the definite name that is the object.
  • Both clauses have the order subject–verb–object, unlike the usual verb-first narrative.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁלַח closes the first clause.

The Hebrew שֶׁלַח is rendered Shelah, the familiar form.

Commentary (2)
Targum Onkelos the whole verse
Hebrew
וְאַרְפַּכְשַׁד אוֹלִיד יָת שָׁלַח וְשֶׁלַח אוֹלִיד יָת עֵבֶר:
Sfornonot-applicable עֵֽבֶר׃
Sforno: Eber, by the holy spirit, foresaw what would happen in his son's day and named him Peleg; human lifespans shortened from Peleg on because of the sin of the generation of the dispersion.
Hebrew
שֶׁכִּוֵּן בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מַה שֶׁהָיָה עָתִיד אָז לִהְיוֹת בִּימֵי בְּנוֹ, וְקָרָא שֵׁם בְּנוֹ פֶּלֶג לְהוֹדִיעַ סִבַּת קִצּוּר שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי הָאָדָם מִפֶּלֶג וָהָלְאָה, כִּי אָמְנָם סִבַּת זֶה הָיָה חֵטְא בְּנֵי הַפְּלַגָּה וְעָנְשָׁם שֶׁקִּלְקֵל מִזְגָּם מֵהַשְׁתַּנּוּת הַפִּתְאוֹמִי מֵאֲוִיר לַאֲוִיר:
10:25

To Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and the name of his brother was Joktan.

and-to-Eber was-born two sons name-of the-one Peleg for in-days-his was-divided the-earth and-name-of brother-his Joktan

Grammar
  • יֻלַּד is singular, but its subject is the plural שְׁנֵי בָנִים, which follows it: a verb placed before its subject may keep the singular (Radak: said 'in a general way').
  • פֶּלֶג and נִפְלְגָה share the root פלג: a wordplay in the explanation of the name.
  • The accents mark שֵׁם הָאֶחָד פֶּלֶג off from the 'for' clause.
  • שֵׁם אָחִיו has no verb; the nominal clause runs on from the previous one.

Rashi and Radak take 'the earth was divided' as the dispersion of the peoples. They differ on its time: Rashi, after Seder Olam, puts it at the end of Peleg's days, in the year of his death; Radak says that when Peleg was born the dispersion was already being prepared. Radak ties the shortening of lifespans to the name Joktan, Sforno to the dispersion; neither takes נִפְלְגָה itself to mean it. The English keeps the plain verb.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows נִפְלְגָ֣ה
Rashi: the languages were confused, and the people scattered from the valley and were divided over the whole world. Eber was a prophet, who named his son for what was to come. Seder Olam teaches that the division came at the end of Peleg's days: not at their start, for his younger brother Joktan had already fathered many families, and not in their middle, for Scripture would have said so; so it fell in the year Peleg died.

10:30

Their homeland stretched from Mesha, as you go toward Sephar, to the eastern mountain.

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי is a wayyiqtol of הָיָה, here 'was situated' with the singular verb before the subject מוֹשָׁבָם.
  • בֹּאֲכָה is an infinitive construct with a 2nd person suffix: 'as you come'; with סְפָרָה (directional ה) the phrase means 'in the direction of Sephar'.
  • הַר הַקֶּדֶם is a construct chain: 'the mountain of the east'.
  • The etnaḥta on מִמֵּשָׁא divides the starting point from the boundary.

Hebrew has no 'to' before הַר הַקֶּדֶם. It may stand in apposition to סְפָרָה ('Sephar, the eastern mountain'), or mark the second boundary. The English follows Radak and reads it as the end of the range.

Radak: after the division they chose the land from Mesha to הַר הַקֶּדֶם, the eastern mountain, and settled there. Saadia identifies מֵשָׁא with Mecca, where the Ishmaelites go on pilgrimage.

He renders בֹּאֲכָה by מָטֵי 'reaching' and puts ל before סְפַר only, so טוּר מָדִינְחָא stands in apposition to Sephar as the one end point; the English, with Radak, takes the eastern mountain as the end of the range, and keeps his reading here.

10:31

These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, by their languages, in their lands, by their nations.

these sons-of Shem to-their-clans to-their-tongues in-their-lands to-their-nations

Grammar
  • אֵלֶּה בְנֵי־שֵׁם is a verbless clause: 'these (are) the sons of Shem'.
  • Four phrases follow with the same pronominal suffix, each with a prefix: three with ל and one with ב.
  • The zaqef on שֵׁם sets off the statement; the tipḥa and etnaḥta then divide the four categories in pairs.
  • לָשׁוֹן, 'tongue', here has the sense 'language'. The table of nations already counts languages; the story of how the one language was confused follows in 11:1–9, where the word for 'language' is שָׂפָה.

The same four-part formula closes Ham's line (10:20); here it closes Shem's.

Commentary (1)
Targum Onkelosfollows the whole verse
Onkelos renders מִשְׁפְּחֹתָם by זַרְעֲיָתְהוֹן 'their families' and גּוֹיֵהֶם by עַמְמֵיהוֹן 'their peoples'; he puts ל before 'their lands' and ב before 'their peoples', the reverse of the Hebrew's בְּ and לְ, with no change of sense.
Hebrew
אִלֵּין בְּנֵי שֵׁם לְזַרְעֲיָתְהוֹן לְלִישָׁנְהוֹן לְאַרְעָתְהוֹן בְּעַמְמֵיהוֹן:
10:32 · פ

These are the clans of the sons of Noah, by their lineages, in their nations; and from these the nations were divided on the earth after the flood.

these clans-of sons-of Noah to-their-generations in-their-nations and-from-these were-divided the-nations in-the-earth after the-flood

Grammar
  • Hebrew puts the verb before its subject: נִפְרְדוּ הַגּוֹיִם, 'were divided the nations'; the nifal gives a passive or reflexive sense.
  • The etnaḥta on בְּגוֹיֵהֶם divides the verse: the first half closes the genealogy, the second (from וּמֵאֵלֶּה) looks beyond it to the spread of the nations. The geresh on וּמֵאֵלֶּה and the tevir on הַגּוֹיִם are lesser divisions within the second half.
  • הַמַּבּוּל, 'the flood', is the word for the Flood of chapters 6 to 9; outside Genesis it occurs only in Psalm 29:10.
  • פ at the end is a paragraph break (petuḥa), which closes the whole table of nations.

The English keeps 'after the flood' as stated, attached to the dividing of the nations. Radak objects that the nations did not separate until after the dispersion (הַפַּלָּגָה) of Peleg's time (10:25), and so attaches 'after the flood' to the families: those born after the flood separated in the land when they separated, which was after the dispersion. His reading is recorded in the commentary.

Commentary (3)
Radakrecords וּמֵאֵ֜לֶּה נִפְרְד֧וּ הַגּוֹיִ֛ם אַחַ֥ר הַמַּבּֽוּל׃
Radak: in fact they did not separate until after the dispersion (הַפַּלָּגָה, in Peleg's time), so the verse cannot mean that the separation came straight after the flood; 'rather its meaning is' (אֶלָּא פֵּרוּשׁוֹ), and his explanation follows in the next comment. The English keeps the plain order and records his reading.

Radak: those born after the flood spread out over the earth when they spread out, which was after the Peleg division.

Onkelos translates 'and from these the peoples were separated in the earth after the flood', in line with the English.

אִלֵּין זַרְעֲיַת בְּנֵי נֹחַ לְתוּלְדָתְהוֹן בְּעַמְמֵיהוֹן וּמֵאִלֵּין אִתַּפְרָשׁוּ עַמְמַיָּא בְּאַרְעָא בָּתַר טוֹפָנָא:
Apparatus
  • Radak reads the dispersal as later than the flood by the interval of the Peleg division (10:25).
11:1

Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.

and-was all-of the-earth language one and-words one(pl)

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי with a subject and a following predicate (שָׂפָה אֶחָת) states a condition: 'the whole earth was of one language'.
  • כָל־הָאָרֶץ is the whole earth by metonymy for all its people (Radak: כָּל בְּנֵי הָאָרֶץ).
  • אֲחָדִים is the plural of אֶחָד, rare; it agrees in gender with דְּבָרִים (masculine), while שָׂפָה takes the feminine אֶחָת.
  • אֶחָת is the pausal form of אַחַת (segol for pataḥ) under the etnaḥta, which divides the verse: 'one language' // 'and the same words'.

'Language' is the sense of שָׂפָה here; 'lip' is the literal sense. אֲחָדִים is read as 'the same' (identical words), the sense Ibn Ezra gives (the words meant the same to all); Rashi's 'one counsel' is recorded as an alternative.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows שָׂפָ֣ה אֶחָ֑ת
Rashi: שפה אחת means the holy tongue (Hebrew). The English says 'one language'; the identification is recorded here and in the apparatus.
Hebrew
לְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶש:
Rashinormativerecords וּדְבָרִ֖ים אֲחָדִֽים׃
Rashi: they came with one counsel and said, 'He has no right to choose the upper realms for Himself; let us go up to the firmament and make war with Him.' Another interpretation: their words were against the Only One of the world. Another: they said that once every 1656 years the firmament totters, as it did in the days of the flood, so let us make supports for it (Bereshit Rabbah). The English keeps the plain sense 'the same words', with Ibn Ezra.
Hebrew
בָּאוּ בְעֵצָה אַחַת וְאָמְרוּ לֹא כָּל הֵימֶנּוּ שֶׁיָּבֹר לוֹ אֶת הָעֶלְיוֹנִים, נַעֲלֶה לָרָקִיעַ וְנַעֲשֶׂה עִמּוֹ מִלְחָמָה. דָּבָר אַחֵר עַל יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם. דָּבָר אַחֵר וּדְבָרִים אֲחָדִים – אָמְרוּ אַחַת לְאֶלֶף ותרנ"ו שָׁנִים הָרָקִיעַ מִתְמוֹטֵט כְּשֵׁם שֶׁעָשָׂה בִּימֵי הַמַּבּוּל, בֹּאוּ וְנַעֲשֶׂה לוֹ סְמִיכוֹת (ב"ר):
Ibn Ezranormativefollows שָׂפָ֣ה אֶחָ֑ת
Ibn Ezra: אֶחָת has a small pataḥ (segol) under the alef when absolute, and a big pataḥ (pataḥ) when in construct (אַחַת). The dispersion was about a hundred years after the flood, and Peleg was named for it; following Seder Olam, Abraham was among the builders, with Noah and Shem still alive. 'One language' means one tongue, most likely the holy tongue, as the names Adam, Eve, Cain, Seth and Peleg witness.
Hebrew
בפתח קטן תחת האל"ף כשהוא מוכרת, ואם הוא נסמך יבא בפתח גדול ובספר הדקדוק בארתי למה חסר דל"ת אחת והפלגה היתה נראת משקו, הדעת כי אחר מאת שנה אחר המבול היתה ונקרא פלג כי בעת הולדו נפלגה הארץ כתרגום ארמית חצי וכמוהו פלגי מים (תהלים א ג), הם חלקי המים שהנהר יחולק וכן "אי כבוד" (ש"א ד כא) גם "עמנואל" (ישעי' ז יד) שהוא בן הנביא גם דברי סדר עולם נכונים ועליו נסמוך ואם כן הוא היה אברהם מבוני המגדל ואל תתמה, כי נח ושם הי' שם, כי לא מת שם, עד שהיה יעקב אבינו בן חמשים שנה ויותר וטעם שפה אחת לשון אחת, והקרוב אלי שהיה לשון הקדש ושם אדם וחוה, וקין גם שת ופלג לעדים,
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וּדְבָרִ֖ים אֲחָדִֽים׃
Ibn Ezra: אֲחָדִים means that today words in every language are not understood by all speakers of it, but then the sayings of the wise and the foolish were 'the same'; the plural אחדים is from אֶחָד.
