הַסְכָּמָה אַחַת הָיְתָה לָהֶם, וְכֵן (יהושע ט:ב) ״וּלְהִלָּחֵם עִם יְהוֹשֻׁעַ פֶּה אֶחָד״ רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בְּהַסְכָּמָה אַחַת, וְהַסְכָּמָתָם הָיְתָה לָלֶכֶת בָּאָרֶץ וּלְבַקֵּשׁ לָהֶם מָקוֹם רְחַב יָדַיִם וְיִשְׁכְּנוּ שָׁם כֻּלָּם וְלֹא יָפוּצוּ הֵנָּה הֵנָּה בִּהְיוֹתָם לְעַם רָב. וְהָיָה זֶה שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וְאַרְבָּעִים שָׁנִים אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל. בְּהַסְכָּמָתָם זֹאת בְּנִרְאֶה לֹא הָיוּ נֹחַ וּבָנָיו שֵׁם וְעֵבֶר וְיֶפֶת, כִּי חֲכָמִים וְצַדִּיקִים הָיוּ וְכֵן הָיוּ בֶּאֱמֶת חֲכָמִים רַבִּים בַּדּוֹר, כִּי הַחָכְמוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ חֻבְּרוּ בַּזְּמַנִּים הָהֵם עִם אֹרֶךְ שְׁנוֹת הָאֲנָשִׁים הַיְחִידִים הָהֵם וְסִפְרֵי הַחָכְמוֹת אֲשֶׁר חִבְּרוּ עַד הַמַּבּוּל הָיוּ בְּיַד נֹחַ וּבָנָיו. גַּם נֹחַ שֶׁהֶאֱרִיךְ יָמִים וְכֵן שֵׁם בְּנוֹ אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא חִבְּרוּ סְפָרִים בְּחָכְמוֹת, גַּם אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ הָיָה אָז בְּדוֹר הַפַּלָּגָה בֶּן אַרְבָּעִים וְחָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים, וּבֶאֱמֶת חָכָם גָּדוֹל הָיָה וּבֶן אַרְבָּעִים שָׁנִים הִכִּיר אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ כְּדִבְרֵי קְצָת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בראשית רבה ל) וּלְדִבְרֵי קְצָתָם בֶּן שָׁלֹשׁ, וְלֹא הָיְתָה דַּעַת כָּל חַכְמֵי הַדּוֹר הַהוּא שֶׁהָאֵל בָּרָא הָאָרֶץ אֶלָּא לְיִשְׁבָּהּ כֻּלָּהּ אוֹ רֻבָּהּ, וְיָדְעוּ גַם כֵּן כִּי בִּרְבוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם לֹא יְכִילֵם מָקוֹם אֶחָד כְּבִקְעַת בָּבֶל אוֹ גְּדוֹלָה מִמֶּנָּה, אִם כֵּן הַהַסְכָּמָה הַהִיא הָיְתָה בְּטֵלָה בְּעֵינֵי חַכְמֵי הַדּוֹר הַהוּא, אֶלָּא שֶׁעַל כָּרְחָם נָטוּ אַחַר הָרֹב שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ חֲכָמִים, לִבְנוֹת הָעִיר וְהַמִּגְדָּל. וּלְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ כֻלָּם מְדַבְּרִים שָׂפָה אֶחָת הָיוּ יוֹתֵר קְרוֹבִים לִהְיוֹת בְּהַסְכָּמָה אַחַת, וּבְבראשית רבה (לח) לְשֵׁם עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִתְכַּוְּנוּ, אָמְרוּ לֹא כָּל הֵימֶנּוּ שֶׁיִּבְחַר לָנוּ אֶת הָעֶלְיוֹנִים בֹּאוּ וְנַעֲשֶׂה עִמּוֹ מִלְחָמָה.

וַהֲוָה כָל אַרְעָא לִישָׁן חָד וּמַמְלַל חָד:
Apparatus
  • Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak identify the one language with the holy tongue; Onkelos has 'one tongue and one speech'.
  • Radak (11:1:3) takes 'one words' as one agreement (cf. Joshua 9:2 'with one mouth').
11:2

As they traveled from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.

and-was in-set-out-their from-east and-they-found plain in-land-of Shinar and-they-settled there

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי בְּ + infinitive construct is the regular way to say 'it was when ...'; the main clause follows with wayyiqtol (וַיִּמְצְאוּ).
  • בְּנָסְעָם: root נסע with the preposition בְּ and a plural suffix, 'in their setting out'.
  • The wayyiqtols וַיִּמְצְאוּ and וַיֵּשְׁבוּ carry the narrative forward.
  • The etnaḥta on מִקֶּדֶם separates the journey from the finding.

מִקֶּדֶם is taken as 'from the east' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak: they came from the eastern mountains / Ararat). Another sense is 'in the east' or 'from of old', recorded in the apparatus.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows בְּנׇסְעָ֣ם מִקֶּ֑דֶם
Rashi: they had been dwelling at 'the mountain of the east' (10:30) and set out from there to find a place that would hold them all, and found only Shinar. The English 'from the east' follows him.

שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים שָׁם, כְּדִכְתִיב לְמַעְלָה וַיְהִי מוֹשָׁבָם וְגו' הַר הַקֶּדֶם וְנָסְעוּ מִשָּׁם לָתוּר לָהֶם מָקוֹם לְהַחֲזִיק אֶת כֻּלָּם וְלֹא מָצְאוּ אֶלָּא שִׁנְעָר:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: the words 'as they set out from the east' are a sign that the mountains of Ararat are in the east.

וזה שאמר הכתוב בנסעם מקדם לאות כי הרי אררט במזרח,
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַֽיִּמְצְא֥וּ בִקְעָ֛ה
Ibn Ezra: וימצאו בקעה means they sought a good place to build a city until they found this plain; בקעה is a flat, level plain, opposite of 'rough places', though it may also lie between mountains as if cleft.

פֵּרֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"א:ב') שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים שָׁם, כַּכָּתוּב לְמַעְלָה (י ל) "וַיְהִי מוֹשָׁבָם מִמֵּשָׁא בֹּאֲכָה סְפָרָה הַר הַקֶּדֶם", וְנָסְעוּ מִשָּׁם לָתוּר לָהֶם מָקוֹם הַמַּחְזִיק אוֹתָם, וְלֹא מָצְאוּ אֶלָּא שִׁנְעָר. וְאֵין זֶה נָכוֹן, כִּי תּוֹלְדוֹת שֵׁם לְבַדָּן הֵם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עֲלֵיהֶם כֵּן, וְלָמָּה יִחֵס הַפַּלָּגָה עֲלֵיהֶם, כִּי בְּנֵי יֶפֶת וּבְנֵי חָם רַבִּים מֵהֶם. וְעוֹד כִּי מוֹשָׁבָם בְּאַרְצֹתָם הָיָה מִמֵּשָׁא עַד הַר הַקֶּדֶם. וְהַפַּלָּגָה הָיְתָה טֶרֶם שֶׁהָיָה מוֹשָׁבָם, כִּי לֹא בָּאוּ בְּנֵי יֶפֶת מֵאִיֵּי הַיָּם אֶל הַבִּקְעָה אֲשֶׁר בְּאֶרֶץ שִׁנְעָר, אֲבָל בַּפַּלָּגָה הֱפִיצָם הַשֵּׁם עַל פְּנֵי כָל הָאָרֶץ, וְאָז הוּשְׁבוּ בְּאַרְצֹתָם לְגוֹיֵיהֶם. וְרַבִּי אַבְרָהָם פֵּרֵשׁ כִּי הָרֵי אֲרָרָט בַּמִּזְרָח, וְיָפֶה אָמַר, כִּי הֵם בַּמִּזְרָח קְרוֹבִים לְאַשּׁוּר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (מלכים ב יט לז) "וְהֵמָּה נִמְלְטוּ אֶרֶץ אֲרָרָט", וְנֹחַ בְּרִדְתּוֹ מִן הָהָר נִתְיַשֵּׁב בָּאֲרָצוֹת הָהֵם הוּא וְתוֹלְדוֹתָיו, וְכַאֲשֶׁר רַבּוּ נָסְעוּ מִשָּׁם אֶל הַבִּקְעָה הַזּוֹ. וְאַנְשֵׁי הַפַּלָּגָה עַל דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (סנהדרין קט) מוֹרְדִים בְּבוֹרְאָם. וְרוֹדְפֵי הַפְּשָׁט (הראב"ע והרד"ק) אוֹמְרִים שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה דַּעְתָּם אֶלָּא שֶׁיִּהְיוּ יַחַד מְחֻבָּרִים, כִּי הִגִּיד הַכָּתוּב דַּעְתָּם "פֶּן נָפוּץ" וְלֹא סִפֵּר עֲלֵיהֶם עִנְיָן אַחֵר. וְאִם כְּדִבְרֵיהֶם יִהְיוּ טִפְּשִׁים, כִּי אֵיךְ תִּהְיֶה עִיר אַחַת וּמִגְדָּל אֶחָד מַסְפִּיק לְכָל בְּנֵי הָעוֹלָם, אוֹ שֶׁמָּא הָיוּ חוֹשְׁבִים שֶׁלֹּא יִפְרוּ וְשֶׁלֹּא יִרְבּוּ וְזֶרַע רְשָׁעִים יִכָּרֵת. אֲבָל הַיּוֹדֵעַ פֵּרוּשׁ "שֵׁם" יָבִין כַּוָּנָתָם מִמָּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ "וְנַעֲשֶׂה לָּנוּ שֵׁם", וְיֵדַע כַּמָּה הַשִּׁעוּר שֶׁיָּזְמוּ בַּמִּגְדָּל לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ, וְיָבִין כָּל הָעִנְיָן, כִּי חָשְׁבוּ מַחְשָׁבָה רָעָה וְהָעֹנֶשׁ שֶׁבָּא עֲלֵיהֶם לְהַפְרִידָם בַּלְּשׁוֹנוֹת וּבָאֲרָצוֹת מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה, כִּי הָיוּ קוֹצְצִים בַּנְּטִיעוֹת. וְהִנֵּה חֶטְאָם דּוֹמֶה לְחֵטְא אֲבִיהֶם, וְשֶׁמָּא בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה דָּרְשׁוּ (ב"ר לח ט), "אֲשֶׁר בָּנוּ בְּנֵי הָאָדָם", אָמַר רַבִּי בֶּרֶכְיָה, מָה בְּנֵי חֲמָרַיָּא בְּנֵי גַּמְלַיָּא, אֶלָּא בְּנוֹי דְּאָדָם קַדְמָאָה וְכוּ'. וְהִסְתַּכֵּל כִּי בְּכָל עִנְיַן הַמַּבּוּל הִזְכִּיר "אֱלֹהִים", וּבְכָל עִנְיַן הַפַּלָּגָה הִזְכִּיר הַשֵּׁם הַמְּיֻחָד, כִּי הַמַּבּוּל בַּעֲבוּר הַשְׁחָתַת הָאָרֶץ, וְהַפַּלָּגָה בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁקִּצְּצוּ בַּנְּטִיעוֹת וְהִנָּם עֲנוּשִׁים בִּשְׁמוֹ הַגָּדוֹל. וְזֶה טַעַם הַיְּרִידָה, וְכֵן בְּמִדַּת סְדוֹם. וְהַמַּשְׂכִּיל יָבִין:

Apparatus
  • מִקֶּדֶם can also mean 'eastward' or 'of old' (lexicon senses 1.b and 2). Ramban rejects Rashi's link with 'the mountain of the east' (10:30): that verse speaks only of Shem's descendants, while Japheth's and Ham's were more numerous, and their settlement in their lands came after the dispersion. He agrees with Ibn Ezra that Ararat lies in the east, near Assyria, and that Noah's descendants moved from there to the plain.
  • Onkelos translates 'in the beginning' (בְּקַדְמֵיתָא), taking קדם as 'of old', and 'land of Babylon' for שִׁנְעָר.
11:3

They said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks and burn them hard." So brick served them as stone, and bitumen served them as mortar.

and-they-said man to-his-fellow come let-us-make-bricks bricks and-let-us-burn to-burning and-was to-them the-brick for-stone and-the-bitumen was to-them for-mortar

Grammar
  • הָבָה is the imperative of יָהַב ('give') with paragogic he, but it functions as an interjection ('come now'), and so can address women or a plural group (Radak, Ibn Ezra).
  • נִלְבְּנָה לְבֵנִים and נִשְׂרְפָה לִשְׂרֵפָה pair a cohortative verb with a cognate noun; Radak compares 'and David fasted a fast'.
  • The first clause of the second sentence (וַתְּהִי ... הַלְּבֵנָה לְאָבֶן) has verb first; the second (וְהַחֵמָר הָיָה ...) has subject first, giving the two a chiastic balance.
  • אֶבֶן and לְבֵנָה, חֵמָר and חֹמֶר form two sound-pairs: stone/brick, bitumen/mortar.
  • לְאָבֶן has qamets under the alef instead of segol (אֶבֶן): a pausal form under the zaqef qaton, as Radak notes (compare פָּרֶץ, Ruth 4:18; עָבֶד, Gen 44:17).

חֵמָר is rendered 'bitumen' (the lexicon's sense); Ibn Ezra agrees (the word as in Arabic, used in place of clay). Radak takes חֵמָר as clay kneaded with water, recorded here. Rashi's remark that there are no stones in Babylon explains why brick stood for stone.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos keeps חֵמָר as חֵימָרָא and renders לַחֹמֶר as לְשִׁיעַ ('for plaster'); for לְבֵנִים he has לִבְנִין, and for לִשְׂרֵפָה 'in fire' (בְּנוּרָא).
11:4

Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered over the face of the whole earth."

and-they-said come let-us-build for-us city and-tower and-its-head in-the-heavens and-let-us-make for-us name lest we-be-scattered upon face-of all-of the-earth

Grammar
  • The two cohortatives נִבְנֶה and נַעֲשֶׂה, each followed by לָנוּ, give the builders' plan; פֶּן + yiqtol gives their fear.
  • וְרֹאשׁוֹ בַשָּׁמַיִם is a verbless clause describing the tower: 'and its top in the heavens'.
  • The pashta on וּמִגְדָּל and the revia on עִיר divide the object phrase.
  • שֵׁם: 'a name' as fame; wordplay with שָׁם 'there' and the later explanation of בָּבֶל.

'Heavens' is kept (rather than 'sky') as the plural of the Hebrew and its hyperbole; Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as extreme height (Deut 1:28).

11:5

The LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the children of the human were building.

and-came-down the-LORD to-see the-city and-the-tower which built sons-of the-human

Grammar
  • לִרְאֹת is an infinitive of purpose: the LORD came down 'in order to see'.
  • The verb 'came down' (וַיֵּרֶד) is a human idiom for divine attention (Ibn Ezra, Radak).
  • In the relative clause אֲשֶׁר בָּנוּ בְּנֵי הָאָדָם the verb stands before the subject.
  • בְּנֵי הָאָדָם: with the article, 'the human'; Rashi asks whose sons else they could be, and takes it as the sons of the first human, who were ungrateful as he was.

'The children of the human' keeps the article, in line with the work's decision on הָאָדָם; Rashi takes the human as the first Adam. The verb is given as 'were building' since the building is unfinished (11:8); the apparatus records Ibn Ezra and Radak on this.

Apparatus
  • Radak on בנו: 'which they began to build'. Ibn Ezra on 11:8: they had built part of the city and the tower, or 'built' in their thoughts. Onkelos: 'the LORD revealed Himself to take vengeance on the deeds of the city and tower which the sons of men built'.
11:6

The LORD said, "Look, they are one people with one language for all of them, and this is what they have begun to do. Now nothing will be held back from them that they plan to do."

and-said the-LORD behold people one and-language one to-all-of-them and-this their-beginning to-do and-now not will-be-withheld from-them all which they-plan to-do

Grammar
  • הֵן ('look') and the verbless clause עַם אֶחָד וְשָׂפָה אַחַת לְכֻלָּם state the speaker's observation.
  • הַחִלָּם is a hifil infinitive construct of חלל ('begin') with suffix ם; the pataḥ under the ה is explained by the following ח (Ibn Ezra), and Rashi glosses it 'their beginning to do'.
  • לֹא־יִבָּצֵר is a nifal of בצר: 'be cut off, withheld, restrained' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak).
  • יָזְמוּ: the pack parses it as qal yiqtol of זמם 'plan, devise'. Ibn Ezra says it has the sense of זָמְמוּ but is a different root; Radak explains it as 'thought, planning'.
  • The pashtas on אֶחָד and אַחַת and the zaqef qaton on לְכֻלָּם mark the LORD's observations; the etnaḥta on לַעֲשׂוֹת closes the first half of the verse.

The sentence is given as a statement, with Ibn Ezra ('if I leave them, they will think they can do whatever they wish'); Rashi reads it as a rhetorical question (בתמיה): 'and now, shall nothing be withheld from them that they plan to do?'. 'Held back' renders the nifal of בצר (Ibn Ezra: ימנע, 'be prevented'). The speaker is given only as 'the LORD'; Ibn Ezra and Radak say he spoke to the angels.

11:7

"Come, let us go down and confuse their language there, so that they will not understand one another's language."

come let-us-go-down and-let-us-confuse there their-language so-that not they-will-hear man language-of his-fellow

Grammar
  • The cohortatives נֵרְדָה and נָבְלָה are plural (1st person), 'let us ...'; Rashi (and Radak) take the נ as the plural prefix and the final ה as the extra he like נֵרְדָה.
  • The pack parses וְנָבְלָה as qal cohortative of בלל. Ibn Ezra argues against the grammarians who derive it from the nifal, and proposes a hifil (נָבֵלָה), which is in line with 'for there the LORD confused' (11:9).
  • אֲשֶׁר לֹא is a final/result clause, 'so that not'; יִשְׁמְעוּ is 'hear' in the sense 'understand'.
  • אִישׁ שְׂפַת רֵעֵהוּ is the idiom for 'each the language of the other'.

'Let us' keeps the plural of the Hebrew, whose addressees Rashi (His court) and Ibn Ezra (the angels) both take to be the heavenly company. The pack's data parse וְנָבְלָה as qal of בלל; Ibn Ezra's hifil is recorded, but the English 'confuse' fits both. The pack gives no qal sense for שָׁמַע, so none is cited.

11:8

So the LORD scattered them from there over the face of the whole earth, and they stopped building the city.

and-scattered the-LORD them from-there upon face-of all-of the-earth and-they-ceased to-build the-city

Grammar
  • וַיָּפֶץ is a hifil wayyiqtol of פוץ; it answers the builders' fear פֶּן נָפוּץ with the same root: what they feared, He did.
  • The phrase עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ repeats 11:4 exactly.
  • חָדַל + לְ + infinitive means 'cease from doing'.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ divides the scattering from the stopping of the work.

The repeated root פוץ links 11:4 and 11:8: 'lest we be scattered' // 'and He scattered them'. The English 'So' renders the wayyiqtol as a consequence of 11:7.

Commentary (5)

11:9 · פ

Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth; and from there the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.

upon-so called its-name Babel because-there confused the-LORD lip-of all-the-earth and-from-there scattered-them the-LORD upon-face-of all-the-earth

Grammar
  • עַל־כֵּן is a stock phrase introducing an explanation of a name or custom: 'therefore'.
  • קָרָא has no stated subject; the 3rd masculine singular is impersonal, so 'its name was called'. Ibn Ezra and Radak do not change this.
  • The etiology rests on wordplay: בָּבֶל (Babel) and בָּלַל (confuse). The verb בָּלַל is a Qal perfect, 'he confused'. Ibn Ezra and Radak analyse the name as בָּא בַּל, 'confusion came'.
  • שְׂפַת כָּל־הָאָרֶץ: 'the lip of all the earth' means the one speech of 11:1, here 'the language of all the earth'.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאָרֶץ divides the verse in two: the first half gives the name and its reason (כִּי־שָׁם בָּלַל, 'because there he confused'), the second the scattering (וּמִשָּׁם הֱפִיצָם, 'and from there he scattered them'). The fronted adverbs שָׁם and מִשָּׁם make a pair: 'there ... and from there'.

שָׂפָה is rendered 'language' because 11:1 says the whole earth had one שָׂפָה and its דְּבָרִים, and Radak reads שְׂפַת as the tongues of the nations. 'Therefore its name was called' renders the impersonal active קָרָא.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וּמִשָּׁם֙ הֱפִיצָ֣ם
Rashi: 'and from there He scattered them' teaches that they have no share in the world to come. He asks which was worse, the generation of the flood or that of the dispersion, who stretched out a hand against the Root (God) to make war on Him; yet the first were swept away and the second were not destroyed. The answer: the flood generation were robbers with strife among them, while these kept love and fellowship, as it says 'one language and one set of words'; so you learn that dissension is hateful (שֶׁשָּׂנְאוּי הַמַּחֲלֹקֶת) and peace is great. This is homily and does not bear on the English.

  • Onkelos renders בָּלַל by בַּלְבֵּל and הֱפִיצָם by בַּדָּרִנּוּן; no variant in the Hebrew is recorded.

11:10

These are the generations of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arpachshad, two years after the flood.

these generations-of Shem Shem son-of hundred-of year and-fathered [object-mark] Arpachshad two-years after the-flood

Grammar
  • אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת opens a new section of the book, here the line of Shem down to Abram.
  • The name שֵׁם is repeated: first as genitive of the heading, then as subject of a new nominal clause. The zaqef qaton on the first שֵׁם closes the heading; the yetiv, a disjunctive accent set before the word, stands on אֵלֶּה and on the second שֵׁם, at the head of each part.
  • בֶּן־מְאַת שָׁנָה: age is expressed as 'son of N years', with the number in the construct state.
  • וַיּוֹלֶד is Hifil wayyiqtol of יָלַד: the father is the subject, 'he fathered'. It continues the age clause: when he was a hundred, he fathered.
  • שְׁנָתַיִם is the dual of שָׁנָה, 'two years'.

Rashi reads שֵׁם בֶּן־מְאַת שָׁנָה as the age at the time Arpachshad was born, which is two years after the flood; the English joins the age to the begetting with 'when'. On the face of 5:32 and 7:6 (Noah 500 when he fathered his sons, 600 at the flood) Shem would be a hundred at the flood, not two years after it. Ibn Ezra refers the explanation of שְׁנָתַיִם to 10:21, 'the brother of Japheth the elder': Japheth was the first-born and Shem was born later. Radak says he explained it at 5:32.

Ibn Ezranormativenot-applicable שְׁנָתַ֖יִם

He then reckons the lifespans: Shem lived 500 years after the flood, Arpachshad 438, Shelah 433, Eber 464, while Peleg lived only 239, half his fathers' years, so Peleg may have been named on the day he was gathered (died). He rejects the view that the tower's builders were seventy, matching seventy languages: Caphtorim and Pathrusim are not individuals, Noah and his sons are not counted, and by Seder Olam the builders were thousands and myriads. 11:11 · ס

And Shem lived, after he fathered Arpachshad, five hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

and-lived Shem after fathering-him [object-mark] Arpachshad five hundreds year and-fathered sons and-daughters

Grammar
  • וַיְחִי־שֵׁם is the wayyiqtol of חָיָה, 'and Shem lived'.
  • אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ is a preposition with an infinitive construct and a suffix whose referent is the subject: 'after his fathering', 'after he fathered'. The phrase runs from the revia on שֵׁם to the zaqef qaton on אַרְפַּכְשָׁד; the pashta on אַחֲרֵי is a lesser divider within it, and the conjunctive munaḥ joins הוֹלִידוֹ to its object.
  • The number precedes the noun: חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה 'five hundreds of year', with a singular noun after the number, as in the genealogy formula.
  • The repeated וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת closes each entry of the genealogy.

The unit gives no death formula; Sforno remarks that the verb וַיָּמָת does not appear in these ten generations.

Commentary (2)
Ibn Ezranormativenot-applicable אַבְרָ֔ם
Ibn Ezra: Abram was born in the place called Ur Kasdim (compare בָּאֻרִים, Isaiah 24:15). Most likely the place had another name then, since the Chaldeans (כַּשְׂדִּים) descend from Nahor, Abram's brother; Moses wrote the name known in his own day. The proof that Abram was born there is that Haran his brother died there, in 'the land of his birth'. Or Ur may be a fire (אוּר) the Chaldeans made at that place, as in 'whose fire is in Zion' (Isaiah 31:9).

נולד במקום נקרא אור כשדים וכמוהו על כן באורים כבדו ד' (ישעי' כד טו) והקרוב שהי' לו שם אחר כי כשדים מבני נחור אחי אברם רק משה כתב השם הנודע בימיו והעד כי שם נולד אברם ששם מת הרן אחיו וכתוב בארץ מולדתו ויתכן שאור עשו הכשדים במקום הנזכר, ונקרא כן כמו "אשר אור לו בציון" (ישעי' א, ט)

Grammar
  • וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת is the heading formula of Genesis; the account that follows is of what came from Terah, and the sons and Lot are its content.
  • תֶּרַח is repeated (the yetiv on the second): the name stands as the subject of the following clause.
  • The perfect הוֹלִיד (not wayyiqtol) restates 11:26 as a summary under the heading.
  • וְהָרָן הוֹלִיד אֶת־לוֹט: the clause is added to name Lot, whose line matters to the story that follows.

The English follows the commentators' sense that the heading opens the family account of Terah, who is its apparent subject. 'Generations' keeps the standard sense of תּוֹלְדֹת; the lexicon glosses it 'account of a man and his descendants'.

Radak: Nahor's descendants are not listed because he did not beget until after the binding of Isaac; Haran's are, because Lot went with Abraham.

וְלֹא זָכַר תּוֹלְדוֹת נָחוֹר כִּי לֹא הוֹלִיד אֶלָּא עַד אַחַר עֲקֵדַת יִצְחָק, וְזָכַר תּוֹלְדוֹת הָרָן לְפִי שֶׁיָּצָא לוֹט בְּנוֹ עִם אַבְרָהָם.
Targum Onkelosnot-applicable the whole verse
Targum Onkelos follows the Hebrew word for word.
Hebrew
וְאִלֵּין תּוּלְדַת תֶּרַח תֶּרַח אוֹלִיד יָת אַבְרָם יָת נָחוֹר וְיָת הָרָן וְהָרָן אוֹלִיד יָת לוֹט:
11:28

Haran died in the lifetime of his father Terah, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.

and-died Haran upon face-of Terah his-father in-land-of his-birth in-Ur Chaldeans

Grammar
  • עַל־פְּנֵי is an idiom: 'in the presence of', so 'during his life'; cf. Numbers 3:4 where Nadab and Abihu die עַל־פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן.
  • The etnaḥta on אָבִיו marks the main division: the death and its time are set apart from the place.
  • מוֹלַדְתּוֹ is a noun with a suffix, 'his kindred' or 'his birth'; it names the place of birth, 'the land of his birth'.
  • The verb comes first, as in every wayyiqtol clause (וַיָּמׇת הָרָן, 'and-died Haran'); the English puts the subject first. וַיָּמׇת is the short Qal wayyiqtol of the hollow root מות: the stress moves back to the prefix (the munaḥ on יָּ) and the last vowel shortens to qamets ḥatuf, against the long form יָמוּת.

The English follows Rashi, who takes עַל־פְּנֵי as 'in the lifetime of' his father (so Radak, citing Numbers 3:4). Ibn Ezra reads 'before his father', who saw him die; that reading is recorded. The midrash that Haran died by his father's doing (Rashi) is recorded, not adopted. 'Ur' is a proper name here; Menahem's reading 'valley' and the midrash's 'fire' are recorded in the commentary.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativefollows עַל פְּנֵ֖י תֶּ֣רַח אָבִ֑יו
Rashi: עַל פְּנֵי is 'in his father's lifetime'; the aggadic midrash that Haran died through his father (the furnace story, Bereshit Rabbah) is a homily and he cites Menahem's reading of אוּר as 'a valley'. The English adopts the plain 'lifetime'.
Hebrew

Ibn Ezranormativerecords עַל פְּנֵ֖י אָבִ֑יו
Ibn Ezra: עַל פְּנֵי means 'before (לִפְנֵי) his father': Haran died while his father looked on, as in Numbers 3:4, עַל פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֲבִיהֶם. The English 'in the lifetime of' follows Rashi; Ibn Ezra's 'in his father's sight' is recorded.
Hebrew
וטעם על פני לפני אביו שמת ואביו רואה, וכמוהו "על פני אהרן אביהם" (במדבר ג ד):
Rambanrecords עַל פְּנֵ֖י תֶּ֣רַח אָבִ֑יו בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מוֹלַדְתּ֖וֹ
Ramban: he cites Rashi's midrash of the furnace and holds the tradition true, with אוּר as 'fire'. But Abraham was not born in Chaldea. Terah's family was from Aram, across the River (Joshua 24:2-3), where Abram and Nahor were born; Terah then went to Chaldea, where his youngest son Haran was born. So 'the land of his birth, Ur of the Chaldeans' is Haran's birthplace alone. In Ur, Abram was saved by a miracle, either hidden or open (the furnace); 15:7 'who brought you out of Ur' implies it.

הַמֶּלֶךְ אוֹתוֹ בְּבֵית הַסֹּהַר, וְהָיָה עִמָּהֶם בְּתוֹכָחוֹת יָמִים רַבִּים שָׁם, אַחַר כָּךְ פָּחַד הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁיַּשְׁחִית עָלָיו אַרְצוֹ וְיָסִיר בְּנֵי הָאָדָם מֵאֱמוּנָתָם, וְגֵרֵשׁ אוֹתוֹ אֶל קְצֵה אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן אַחַר שֶׁלָּקַח כָּל הוֹנוֹ. וְהִנֵּה עַל כָּל פָּנִים בַּמָּקוֹם הַהוּא בְּאֶרֶץ כַּשְׂדִּים נַעֲשָׂה נֵס לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ, אוֹ נֵס נִסְתָּר שֶׁנָּתַן בְּלֵב אוֹתוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ לְהַצִּילוֹ וְשֶׁלֹּא יְמִיתֶנּוּ וְהוֹצִיא אוֹתוֹ מִבֵּית הַסֹּהַר שֶׁיֵּלֵךְ לְנַפְשׁוֹ, אוֹ נֵס מְפֻרְסָם שֶׁהִשְׁלִיכוֹ לְכִבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ וְנִצַּל כְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ. וְאַל יְפַתֶּה אוֹתְךָ רַבִּי אַבְרָהָם בְּקֻשְׁיוֹתָיו שֶׁאוֹמֵר שֶׁלֹּא סִפֵּר הַכָּתוּב זֶה הַפֶּלֶא, כִּי עוֹד אֶתֵּן לְךָ טַעַם וּרְאָיָה בָּזֶה וּבְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ (רמב"ן על בראשית מ"ו:ט"ו). אֲבָל הַגּוֹיִם הָהֵם לֹא הִזְכִּירוּ זֶה בְּסִפְרָם, לְפִי שֶׁהֵם חוֹלְקִים עַל דַּעְתּוֹ וְהָיוּ חוֹשְׁבִים בְּנִסּוֹ שֶׁהוּא מַעֲשֵׂה כְּשָׁפִים, כְּעִנְיַן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עִם הַמִּצְרִים בִּתְחִלַּת מַעֲשָׂיו. וּמִפְּנֵי זֶה לֹא הִזְכִּיר עוֹד הַכָּתוּב הַנֵּס הַזֶּה, כִּי הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְהַזְכִּיר דִּבְרֵי הַחוֹלְקִים עָלָיו, כַּאֲשֶׁר הִזְכִּיר דִּבְרֵי חַרְטֻמֵּי מִצְרַיִם, וְלֹא נִתְבָּאֲרוּ דִּבְרֵי אַבְרָהָם עִמָּהֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר נִתְבָּאֲרוּ דִּבְרֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ בַּסּוֹף. וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב (בראשית ט"ו:ז'), "אֲנִי ה' אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים לָתֶת לְךָ אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת לְרִשְׁתָּהּ", כִּי מִלַּת "הוֹצֵאתִיךָ" תְּלַמֵּד עַל נֵס, כִּי לֹא אָמַר "אֲשֶׁר לְקַחְתִּיךָ מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים" אֲבָל אָמַר "הוֹצֵאתִיךָ", שֶׁהוֹצִיא מִמַּסְגֵּר אַסִּיר, כְּמוֹ "אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם" (שמות כ ב). וְאָמַר "לָתֶת לְךָ אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת לְרִשְׁתָּהּ", כִּי מֵעֵת הוֹצִיאוֹ אוֹתוֹ מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים הָיָה הָרָצוֹן לְפָנָיו יִתְעַלֶּה שֶׁיְּגַדְּלֶנּוּ וְיִתֵּן לוֹ אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַהִיא. וְתֶרַח אָבִיו וְאַבְרָהָם הָיָה בְּלִבָּם מִן הַיּוֹם הַהוּא שֶׁנִּצַּל שֶׁיֵּלְכוּ אֶל אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן לְהִתְרַחֵק מֵאֶרֶץ כַּשְׂדִּים מִפַּחַד הַמֶּלֶךְ, כִּי חָרָן קָרוֹב לָהֶם וְעַם אֶחָד וְשָׂפָה אַחַת לְכֻלָּם, כִּי לְשׁוֹן אֲרָמִית לִשְׁנֵיהֶם, וְרָצוּ לָלֶכֶת אֶל עַם אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִשְׁמַע לְשׁוֹנוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ הַהוּא וְעַמּוֹ, וְזֶהוּ טַעַם "וַיֵּצְאוּ אִתָּם מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד חָרָן" אֲשֶׁר שָׁם מִשְׁפְּחוֹתֵיהֶם וַאֲבוֹתֵיהֶם מֵעוֹלָם, וְיָשְׁבוּ בֵּינֵיהֶם, וְנִתְעַכְּבוּ שָׁם יָמִים רַבִּים. וְשָׁם נִצְטַוָּה אַבְרָהָם לַעֲשׂוֹת מַה שֶׁעָלָה בְּדַעְתּוֹ, לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן, וְעָזַב אֶת אָבִיו וּמֵת שָׁם בְּחָרָן אַרְצוֹ, וְהוּא הָלַךְ עִם אִשְׁתּוֹ וְלוֹט בֶּן אָחִיו אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן. וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב (יהושע כד ג) "וָאֶקַּח אֶת אֲבִיכֶם אֶת אַבְרָהָם מֵעֵבֶר הַנָּהָר וָאוֹלֵךְ אוֹתוֹ בְּכָל אֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן", כִּי בְּעֵבֶר הַנָּהָר נִצְטַוָּה בָּזֶה, וּמִשָּׁם לְקָחוֹ וְהוֹלִיכוֹ בְּכָל אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן. וְהִנֵּה עַל דַּעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ יִהְיֶה אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים כִּפְשׁוּטוֹ, מִלְּשׁוֹן "חַמּוֹתִי רָאִיתִי אוּר" (ישעיהו מד טז), וְאָמְרוּ וַיֵּצְאוּ אִתָּם מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים , וְתֶרַח לֹא יָצָא מִן הַכִּבְשָׁן, אֲבָל אַבְרָם הוּא עִקָּר, אוֹ הַמָּקוֹם נִקְרָא כֵן בַּעֲבוּר הַנֵּס, כְּמוֹ "וּבְתַבְעֵרָה וּבְמַסָּה וּבְקִבְרֹת הַתַּאֲוָה" (דברים ט כב) וְזוּלָתָם, וְיִרְמֹז הַכָּתוּב כִּי בְּצֵאת אַבְרָם מִן הַכִּבְשָׁן בָּרְחוּ לָהֶם כֻּלָּם מִשָּׁם. וּפֵרוּשׁ "בָּאֻרִים כַּבְּדוּ ה'" (ישעיהו כד טו) עַל דַּעְתִּי כְּדִבְרֵיהֶם, כִּי הֵם הֶהָרִים הַגְּבוֹהִים שֶׁשָּׁם עוֹשִׂים אוֹרוֹת וּמַשִּׂיאִין מַשּׂוּאוֹת לְהוֹדִיעַ הַחֲדָשׁוֹת מַהֵר בַּמֶּרְחַקִּים, כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר (שם) "בְּאִיֵּי הַיָּם שֵׁם ה' אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל", וְהָעִנְיָן שֶׁיּוֹדִיעוּ בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם הַנֵּס וְהַפֶּלֶא הַנַּעֲשֶׂה לָהֶם לִכְבוֹד הַשֵּׁם. וְכֵן "מְאוּרַת צִפְעוֹנִי" (ישעיהו יא ח), הַחוֹר שֶׁלּוֹ שֶׁשָּׁם אוֹרוֹ וַחֲמִימוּתוֹ הַגָּדוֹל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁקּוֹרֵא אוֹתוֹ "שָׂרָף". וְרָאִיתִי בְּמִדְרַשׁ "קוּמִי אוֹרִי" (פסקתא דר"כ פסקא כא) "עַל כֵּן בָּאֻרִים כַּבְּדוּ ה'", בַּמֶּה מְכַבְּדִין אוֹתוֹ, ר' אַבָּא בַּר כָּהֲנָא אָמַר בְּאִלֵּן פַּנָּסַיָּא, הֵן כְּגוֹן הָעֲשָׁשִׁיּוֹת Grammar
  • The verb וַיִּקַּח is singular though it has two subjects, because it agrees with the nearer one, Abram; Radak compares Exodus 7:10.
  • נָשִׁים is the irregular plural of אִשָּׁה; the root listed is אנש.
  • שֵׁם אֵשֶׁת־אַבְרָם שָׂרָי: the construct chain 'the name of the wife of Abram' is followed by the name in apposition.
  • בַּת־הָרָן אֲבִי־מִלְכָּה וַאֲבִי יִסְכָּה: 'father of Milcah and father of Iscah' stands in apposition to הָרָן, bound to it by the conjunctive merkha on הָרָן; the English opens it with 'who was'. Radak explains why 'father of' follows 'daughter of': 11:27 named only Lot as Haran's child, so the verse adds that Haran also fathered Milcah and Iscah.

The final clause is read as 'Haran, who was the father of Milcah and Iscah'. Whether Iscah is another name for Sarah is a question the commentators discuss; the English leaves the name as it stands. Sarai is the form of the name until 17:15.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativerecords יִסְכָּֽה׃
Rashi: Iscah is Sarah, so called because she saw (סוֹכָה) by the holy spirit and because all gazed (סוֹכִין) at her beauty; also יִסְכָּה speaks of princeliness (נְסִיכוּת), as שָׂרָה speaks of rule (שְׂרָרָה). The English keeps the name Iscah and records the identification.
Hebrew
זוֹ שָׂרָה, עַל שֵׁם שֶׁסּוֹכָה בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ וְשֶׁהַכֹּל סוֹכִין בְיָפְיָהּ; וְעוֹד יִסְכָּה לְשׁוֹן נְסִיכוּת, כְּמוֹ שָׂרָה לְשׁוֹן שְׂרָרָה:
Ibn Ezranormativerecords the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: Nahor's wife is named to give the descent of Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. The ancients said Iscah is Sarah; if that is a tradition, we accept it. Those who say Abraham, not Sarah, was barren contradict the text (Ishmael, Keturah's sons). He rejects the view that Sarah was Abram's sister. He also doubts she was Lot's sister, for then 11:31 would call her Terah's daughter, or his son's daughter as it does Lot. His own view is that the call of 12:1 came before 'Terah took' (11:31), since the Torah is not always in chronological order; so Terah set out 'to go to the land of Canaan', then liked Haran, settled there and died. The English leaves the identification open.

Grammar
  • אֵין followed by ל is the Hebrew way to say 'has not': 'there is not to her a child'.
  • וָלָד is a rare noun for offspring, formed from ילד like the verbs of begetting above; Radak gives its pattern as that of חָכָם.
  • The accents: etnaḥta on עֲקָרָה divides the verse into the state of Sarai and its consequence.
  • The statement prepares the later promises to Abram; Radak reads it as a statement of the miracle.

The sentence is a plain statement. The English keeps the Hebrew's two clauses, the second restating the first in negative terms.

Grammar
  • Terah is the subject of וַיִּקַּח, the three objects are Abram, Lot, and Sarai, each with the object marker; Radak explains that Terah leads the group because he is the father.
  • וַיֵּצְאוּ is plural and has no stated subject; אִתָּם 'with them' shows the group went together, led by Abram according to Ramban and Radak.
  • לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן: infinitive construct of הלך (the Hebrew of this verb uses the form of ילך) with directional ה: 'to go to the land of Canaan'.
  • The accents: geresh on אִתָּם, revia on כַּשְׂדִּים; the departure is set off from its goal and from the stay in Haran.
  • וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד־חָרָן: 'came as far as Haran'; the verb of settling, וַיֵּשְׁבוּ, shows that the journey stopped there.

Rashi reads וַיֵּצְאוּ אִתָּם as 'Terah and Abram went out with Lot and Sarai'; the English follows, with 'they' for the group and 'with them' kept in the line. 'Settled' follows Qal 3 of יָשַׁב. The pack's entry for הָלַךְ lists no Qal sense 'go', and the entry for עַד lists only its temporal senses, so no sense is given for לָלֶכֶת or for the spatial עַד.

11:32 · פ

The days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.

and-were days-of Terah five years and-two-hundred year and-died Terah in-Haran

Grammar
  • חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים וּמָאתַיִם שָׁנָה: the smaller number comes first; 'five years and two hundred years'. The dual מָאתַיִם is 'two hundred'.
  • The verse closes the genealogy with Terah's whole life, as the genealogies of Genesis 5 do.
  • The inverted nun in בְּחָרָן, which Rashi and Radak comment on, belongs to the text's note, not to the English line.
  • Terah's death at Haran stands before Abram's departure in 12:4, a question which Rashi and Ramban discuss.

Terah lived 205 years: at Abram's birth he was seventy, so Abram was 135 at his death; yet Abram left Haran at seventy-five (12:4). Rashi and Ramban face this: the text names Terah 'dead' early. The English follows the plain reading and records the chronology problem in the commentary. The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativerecords וַיָּ֥מׇת תֶּ֖רַח בְּחָרָֽן׃
Rashi: Terah died after Abram left Haran for Canaan, since Abram was seventy-five at his departure and Terah was seventy at Abram's birth, making Terah 145; the text places the death first so that people would not say Abram failed to honor his father, and calls the wicked 'dead' even while alive. The English states the death in the verse's order and records Rashi's reading.
